_meta.purpose: Every control in the assessment as one flat record. Derived from controls/_meta.yaml and controls/**/*.yaml through the same loader the HTML build uses, so a record here is what the page shows.
_meta.never_hand_edit: Mechanical output. Edit the control YAML and regenerate; a hand edit here is overwritten and `--check` fails in CI first.
_meta.shipped_vs_authored: Top-level keys are the fields build/schema.py normalize_item() emits -- i.e. what reaches the browser. Fields the YAML carries that the page does not render are preserved under `authored_only` rather than dropped. `phase` is not among them: normalize_item RENAMES it to `ph`, so it ships. Today with_authored_only is 0, which is the measured statement that normalize_item drops nothing the YAML authors write.
_meta.order: Groups in controls/_meta.yaml `tabs` order (BASELINE first, the tab order a reader sees), sections in meta-declared order within each. The built HTML's own DATA blob is alphabetical instead (AI_SPECIFIC first) purely because build/generate.py:305 serializes it with sort_keys=True -- a serialization artifact, not an editorial choice. Do not 'fix' this to match the page: the id SETS and every field are identical, verified with 0 mismatches.

controls.q: Are AI workloads isolated into dedicated accounts or projects separate from general-purpose workloads, so a compromise in one does not cascade to the other?
controls.h: Look for a dedicated account/OU or project boundary for AI/ML workloads with its own guardrails, distinct from shared general-purpose environments.

controls.rec: Give each AI/ML workload its own dedicated AWS account placed under the Workloads OU defined by the AWS Security Reference Architecture (a Management account plus Security, Infrastructure, and Workloads OUs), grouped apart from general-purpose workload accounts so the account boundary contains blast radius (Well-Architected SEC01-BP01, Separate workloads using accounts). Govern these accounts with AWS Organizations or an AWS Control Tower landing zone and apply distinct SCP guardrails to the AI accounts (optionally under a dedicated child OU) so a compromise in one workload does not cascade to others.

controls.q: Is there a documented, enforced approval process before a new AI model, service, or third-party AI tool is adopted into production?
controls.h: Look for an intake/approval workflow (security review, data-handling review) gating new AI capabilities before they reach production.
controls.ev: Intake workflow ticket/template showing required approvals
controls.rec: Publish only pre-approved AI models, services, and tools as AWS Service Catalog products in curated portfolios, and apply the launch constraint to EVERY product individually — a launch constraint does NOT apply at the portfolio level, nor to a product across all portfolios, so any product published without its own constraint is simply unconstrained — plus IAM-scoped access to the portfolio. Require any new AI capability to pass a documented intake workflow (security review, data-handling review) before its product is reviewed, approved, and published for self-service provisioning. This gates adoption at the provisioning layer instead of relying on after-the-fact detection. Pair the gate with a sanctioned EXPERIMENTATION path, or developers will route around it: an approval process with no way to try an unapproved model is the reason shadow AI appears. Innovation Sandbox on AWS implements the pattern — pooled accounts leased for a fixed term, budget-capped, SCP-restricted to approved regions and model families, isolated from production data, and returned to the pool after automatic resource cleanup. Hard budget enforcement (breach triggers cleanup and reclaim) is appropriate HERE and nowhere else; production accounts alert and escalate to a human instead. Building it yourself is the same shape: a pooled set of accounts, time-based expiry, a budget action that triggers cleanup, and a return-to-pool step so orphaned AI resources cannot accumulate.

controls.q: Are AI budgets and cost-anomaly alerts configured with accountable recipients across production, sandbox, and UAT accounts to detect runaway spend or misuse?
controls.h: Require both AI-scoped budgets and cost-anomaly monitoring, with alert subscriptions, confirmed recipients and owners. Reconcile coverage against an agreed account/environment inventory using OU or tag classifications. Central coverage is valid when demonstrated for each account; production-only coverage or missing subscriptions is incomplete and cannot earn Yes.
controls.ev: Production/sandbox/UAT account coverage matrix with AI budget and anomaly-monitor scopes, thresholds, notification/subscription configurations, confirmed recipients, accountable owners and alert-delivery evidence
controls.rec: Create an AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitor scoped to AI spend via a Cost Category that groups Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker (Cost Anomaly Detection cannot restrict an AWS-services monitor to specific services — that monitor evaluates every service and customer-managed AWS-services monitors are not supported, so a Cost Category is the way to scope to named AI services — and note cost categories are available only to the management account of the organization, so this step is done there, not in the workload account) with an alert subscription over an SNS threshold, plus an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered to those services with staggered SNS alerts (e.g. 80/90/100%). Configure budget notifications and anomaly-monitor alert subscriptions with workload owners and the central FinOps/security team as accountable recipients. Inspect subscriptions as well as monitor/budget existence, verify required SNS confirmations and topic permissions, and retain alert-delivery evidence. Choose thresholds and escalation paths for each workload; a detected anomaly below the subscription threshold sends no alert. Right-size Bedrock RPM/TPM Service Quotas per workload account as a PREVENTIVE cap — defaults are usually far above what a workload needs, and a lowered quota bounds a runaway agent before the budget alert fires. Agree the in-scope account inventory and production, sandbox and UAT classifications using organizational units or governed tags. Build a coverage matrix joining every account to its AI budget, anomaly monitor, alert subscriptions, thresholds and owners; document justified exclusions. Use linked-account and activated cost-allocation dimensions from AIR-FND-ACC-08 to establish spend scope. A central arrangement is acceptable when its filters demonstrably include each account and relevant AI service. Where per-account budgets are used, deploy them with CloudFormation StackSets to the relevant OUs and reconcile new or moved accounts into the matrix. Recheck anomaly-monitor coverage and subscriptions separately. Production-only coverage, an unclassified account or either missing budgets or missing anomaly alerts is incomplete; assess Partial when supporting coverage exists but the full matrix is not demonstrated. Do NOT wire a budget threshold to an SCP that denies AI services in production — that converts a cost event into an outage; hard budget enforcement belongs only in experimentation accounts (see AIR-FND-ACC-03).

controls.q: Is AI service spend attributable to the team, workload, and environment that created it, through activated cost-allocation tags that resources cannot be created without?
controls.h: Two halves, both required: the tags are ACTIVATED as cost-allocation tags in the management account's billing settings (activation is a billing-console action — a tag on a resource is invisible to Cost Explorer until activated), and a tag policy on the AI OU prevents untagged or wrongly-valued resources being created. Check Billing > Cost allocation tags for active status, and Organizations > Policies > Tag policies for enforcement on the AI OU.
controls.ev: Active cost-allocation tag list + tag policy attached to the AI OU
controls.rec: Attribution is the prerequisite for every other cost control: without it a budget or anomaly monitor can only be scoped to a whole account, so a shared account's runaway agent is indistinguishable from normal growth. Agree a minimal tag set (team, workload, environment, and where it is knowable model-id or agent-id), then ACTIVATE those keys as cost-allocation tags in the management account (Billing > Cost allocation tags) — user-defined tags are inert for cost reporting until activated, it can take up to 24 hours for a tag to appear in the billing console and up to a further 24 hours for activation to take effect, so do it before the spend you want to analyze. Do NOT expect an AWS Organizations tag policy to make the tags mandatory: AWS states that basic compliance rules do not enforce tag compliance on resources created without tags, and that the capability does not enforce missing tag keys. What a tag policy actually gives you is (a) enforced_for, which standardizes the VALUE and capitalization of a tag when a tagging operation supplies one, on the resource types you list, and (b) the required-tag-key capability, whose reporting mode is enforced only for infrastructure-as-code tools (AWS CloudFormation, Terraform, Pulumi). Presence on an arbitrary API call therefore has to come from an SCP that Denies when aws:RequestTag/<key> is Null — and because aws:RequestTag support is per ACTION, not per service (only a minority of actions declare it: 33 of 262 bedrock actions, 71 of 444 sagemaker, 20 of 250 bedrock-agentcore in the service reference), that SCP must ENUMERATE the resource-creating actions that support the key rather than use bedrock:*. A Deny keyed on an action that does not define aws:RequestTag never matches and fails OPEN, granting exactly what it was written to block. For detection, read the organization-wide tag-policy compliance report (Organizations > Tag policies, or resourcegroupstaggingapi list-required-tags) — the AWS Resource Groups console does not report noncompliance for a missing required tag key. Group the activated tags into Cost Categories so Cost Explorer, Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection can all filter on the same dimension. Note that Bedrock on-demand model invocation cost attaches to the calling account and inference-profile tags rather than to a per-request tag, so application-level attribution for shared inference needs an inference profile per workload.

controls.q: Are the security services that monitor AI workloads administered from a dedicated security-tooling account designated as delegated administrator, rather than from the organization management account?
controls.h: Check each service's admin account: Security Hub CSPM, GuardDuty, AWS Config (aggregator + conformance packs), Amazon Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer and Firewall Manager all support a delegated administrator. Verify the SAME account is the admin for each -- the administrator-member relationship does NOT propagate between services, so a per-service check is required. Confirm via organizations list-delegated-administrators and each service's own get-administrator-account / describe-organization-configuration call.
controls.ev: list-delegated-administrators output plus each service's admin account, showing one non-management account
controls.rec: Designate a dedicated security-tooling account as delegated administrator for every security service that supports one, and keep the management account out of day-to-day security operations -- an operator working findings there is working in the account that can alter SCPs, Organizations and billing, which is the widest possible blast radius. Per the AWS Security Reference Architecture this is the Security Tooling account, paired with a Log Archive account for immutable centralized logging; both are foundational accounts distinct from the AI workload accounts. Use the SAME account for all of them: administrator-member relationships do NOT propagate between services (a GuardDuty administrator does not automatically see GuardDuty findings once Security Hub is enabled from a different admin), and the AWS SRA places these services together in the single Security Tooling account, which also hosts the AWS Config organization aggregator. Then drive configuration from there rather than per account: Security Hub central configuration policies (SECURITYHUB_POLICY), Config organization conformance packs and an organization aggregator, GuardDuty auto-enable for new accounts, and Inspector via INSPECTOR_POLICY. Two corrections to assumptions this control invites: the single-security-account rule is a CONVENTION you have to verify service by service, not something Organizations enforces for you, so audit it rather than assume it; and CloudTrail is not the exception it is often described as -- CloudTrail supports its own delegated administrator that creates and manages organization trails and organization event data stores on the management account's behalf (the management account remains the resource owner of those resources), so the security-tooling account can administer the organization trail too while log delivery still lands in the Log Archive account.

controls.q: Is there a single, current inventory of all AI models, agents, and AI-enabled applications in use across the organization?
controls.h: Look for a maintained registry/catalog covering owner, purpose, and status for each AI workload; ad hoc spreadsheets that go stale don't count.
controls.ev: Live registry/catalog with recent update timestamps
controls.rec: Work up the tiers rather than starting at the most complex. TIER 1, least effort: enable AWS Security Hub AI inventory, which continuously discovers AI assets across the organization from the delegated-administrator account. Know its boundary before you rely on it: managed discovery reads AWS Config configuration items, so AWS Config must be enabled in every account and Region you expect to see, and it covers a supported subset of Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon SageMaker resource types. Self-hosted models and third-party AI services are not discovered as resources at all -- they surface only indirectly, from Amazon Inspector SBOM findings for AI/ML packages and Amazon GuardDuty DNS activity to AI service domains. So TIER 1 is the fastest start and the authoritative view of managed AWS AI resources, not a complete answer to this control: everything outside those sources still has to be registered deliberately. TIER 2, when you need richer metadata or ad-hoc questions: an AWS Config organization aggregator in the delegated-administrator account plus AWS Resource Explorer multi-account views (shared via AWS RAM), queried with Config advanced queries for things a fixed inventory view cannot express — for example every Bedrock agent with no guardrail attached, or resources filtered by tag, relationship or compliance status. TIER 3, for historical analysis or an external CMDB: deliver Config configuration snapshots and history to a central S3 bucket in the Log Archive account and query it with Athena for drift over time, lifecycle tracking and compliance trending, or feed a ServiceNow/Jira CMDB. In every tier track model versions in the Amazon SageMaker Model Registry and enforce owner/purpose/status tags (see AIR-FND-ACC-08) so the inventory stays current rather than a stale spreadsheet.

controls.q: Can access to break-glass or emergency-override procedures for AI workloads be exercised without bypassing normal approval and logging controls?
controls.h: Confirm emergency-access paths (e.g., disabling a guardrail) are logged and require secondary approval, not an unmonitored superuser path.
controls.ev: Break-glass runbook showing logging + secondary approval
controls.rec: Two different mechanisms are needed here and they are routinely conflated. (1) An override you can still exercise when the normal path is DOWN: the IAM Identity Center emergency (break-glass) access configuration -- a dedicated emergency-operations account with direct SAML 2.0 federation to the IdP that bypasses Identity Center, plus an emergency-operations group carrying no standing members, populated only during an incident. Be clear what AWS designed this for: continuity during a disruption of the IdP, of a Region, or of IAM Identity Center itself. It is not an approval gate, and it deliberately has no approver in the loop. (2) The approval gate this control actually asks about -- request, approve, time-bound grant, automatic expiry, for an action such as disabling a guardrail: temporary elevated access, also called just-in-time access. There is NO native Identity Center setting that provides it; AWS documents temporary elevated access as delivered either by a validated partner solution (Apono, CyberArk, Okta Access Requests, Tenable) or by something you build on Identity Center APIs, so name the mechanism you actually run rather than assuming the platform supplies one. The control passes only if both halves hold: every assumption of an elevated or emergency role lands in CloudTrail in the target account, and the grant expires on its own rather than being revoked from memory. Alert on any assumption of the break-glass role precisely because that is the path with no secondary approval.

src.t: Emergency access configuration for IAM Identity Center (business continuity)
Temporary elevated access (just-in-time) with IAM Identity Center

controls.q: Is there a tested plan for isolating or shutting down a specific AI workload (model, agent, or pipeline) independently, without affecting unrelated workloads in the same environment?
controls.h: Verify a documented and tested procedure exists to quarantine one AI workload without causing a wider outage.

controls.q: Is access to AI models, training data, and inference endpoints restricted to specific, named identities rather than broad wildcard grants?
controls.h: Review access policies for AI-related actions and resources; look for scoping to specific resource ARNs rather than blanket allow-all.
controls.ev: Policy review showing resource-scoped grants
controls.rec: Use IAM identity-based policies that scope AI actions (e.g. bedrock:InvokeModel, sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint) to specific resource ARNs such as arn:aws:bedrock:<region>::foundation-model/<model-id> and named endpoint/training-data ARNs, never Resource '*'. Add condition keys (e.g. bedrock:InferenceProfileArn, aws:ResourceAccount) to tighten scope and validate every policy with IAM Access Analyzer policy validation before deployment. CHECK THE KEY EXISTS, AND CHECK WHO OWNS THE RESOURCE: for bedrock:InvokeModel the IAM service model defines bedrock:ModelArn, bedrock:InferenceProfileArn, bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier, bedrock:PromptRouterArn, bedrock:ProjectArn and bedrock:ServiceTier — but not bedrock:ModelId, which AWS Prescriptive Guidance nonetheless prescribes; a condition on a key an action does not define is silently ignored and enforces nothing. And aws:ResourceAccount is a resource-perimeter key for 'AWS resources that you create and manage in your AWS accounts', so it fits your S3 training data, custom models and SageMaker endpoints, but a Bedrock foundation model is an AWS-owned resource whose ARN carries no account id (arn:aws:bedrock:<region>::foundation-model/<model-id>) — AWS's documented case of 'AWS owned resources, resources that do not belong to your organization'. Because these are Allow statements both mistakes fail closed and break inference rather than widening access, the inverse of a Deny keyed on a non-existent key, which fails open; keep owned and AWS-owned resources in separate statements so neither outcome surprises you.

controls.q: Is multi-factor authentication enforced for every human identity with direct AI model-invocation or AI-administration access?
controls.h: Inventory human access to model invocation, AI configuration, guardrails, and deployments, including human-assumed roles, federated sessions, and applicable root access. Reuse root MFA evidence; exclude nonhuman workload sessions and application-only end users. Device enrollment or SSO presence alone does not demonstrate MFA enforcement.
controls.ev: Human AI-access inventory mapped to IAM or Identity Center/external-IdP MFA enforcement, session-policy evidence and sign-in tests; applicable root MFA evidence
controls.rec: Inventory every human with direct AI model-invocation or AI-administration access, including console, CLI, assumed-role and federated paths. For Identity Center-managed MFA, use 'Every time they sign in (always-on)' and require MFA device registration at sign-in or block users without a registered device; allowing sign-in without a device or using an email code does not satisfy this control. Reuse applicable root MFA evidence. Nonhuman workload sessions and application-only end users are outside this human AWS-access population; humans assuming a workload role remain in scope. BUT DO NOT BACK IT WITH A DENY ON aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: that key 'is not present for federated identities', and an IAM Identity Center principal is a federated identity, so the combination AWS recommends everywhere else — Deny with BoolIfExists on false, which fires when the key is absent as well as when it is false — denies every Identity Center principal regardless of whether they completed MFA. The two halves of that recommendation contradict each other: the workforce users you just put on always-on MFA are exactly the ones the SCP locks out, and switching to the plain Bool operator does not fix it either, it just makes the statement enforce nothing for them. AWS documents the actual mechanism: 'to enforce MFA for IAM Identity Center identities, you can enable attributes for access control to pass a SAML assertion claim with the authentication method from your identity provider to IAM Identity Center' (or pass it as a session tag through AWS STS), then key the Deny on the resulting aws:PrincipalTag rather than on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent. Keep the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent Deny for the IAM principals it does work for — IAM users and roles assumed with MFA — where it also correctly denies long-term access keys. For an external IdP, obtain its MFA and session-policy evidence because it manages MFA and the Identity Center MFA section is unavailable. Context-aware authentication can skip an MFA prompt on a trusted device even with 'Block their sign-in' enabled. Validate enforcement with sign-in tests for the inventoried human access paths, including users without an enrolled device; a device-enrollment report or an SSO-configured flag alone is insufficient.

controls.q: Are long-lived, static credentials avoided in favor of short-lived, federated credentials for anyone or anything accessing AI services?
controls.h: Use federated SSO and temporary credentials as the standard. Correlate active static credentials with effective AI access, including assumable roles; do not infer permissions from last-used service. Record owner, age, approved exception and removal date for each remaining key. Rotation or an approved exception alone cannot earn Yes while standing AI-access credentials remain.
controls.ev: Active credential inventory joined to effective AI permissions and role paths, with owner, age and time-bounded exception/removal records for remaining static credentials
controls.rec: Standardize on short-lived credentials: IAM Identity Center federated SSO for human access, IAM roles (instance, task, and Lambda execution roles) for in-AWS compute, and IAM Roles Anywhere exchanging X.509 certificates for temporary STS credentials for off-cloud workloads. Eliminate long-term IAM user access keys and other standing credentials that can reach AI services. Join an active credential inventory to effective permissions, including reachable assumed roles and applicable identity/resource policies, permissions boundaries, session policies and organization controls. Use IAM credential reports plus ListAccessKeys and ListServiceSpecificCredentials for complete key visibility: credential reports omit service-specific credentials, including Bedrock long-term API keys. Last-used service is usage history, not the set of services a key can access. For each remaining key record its owner, creation/rotation age against the organization's approved limit, business justification, exception approver, expiry and removal date. Rotation and time-bounded exceptions are interim risk treatment and merit at most Partial while standing AI-access credentials remain; apply AIR-BDR-MDL-09 to Bedrock API-key prevention.

controls.q: Is there a recurring process to detect and remediate unused or overly broad permissions granted to AI-related identities?
controls.h: Look for scheduled access reviews or automated unused-permission detection applied to roles that touch AI services.
controls.ev: Access review cadence and most recent findings/remediation
controls.rec: Enable an IAM Access Analyzer unused access analyzer at the AWS Organizations level to continuously flag unused roles, unused access keys, and UnusedPermission findings on AI-touching identities. Review the centralized dashboard on a fixed cadence and use last accessed information to right-size or remove permissions, archiving findings for intended access. TWO CORRECTIONS THAT CHANGE HOW YOU RUN THIS. First, last accessed information is an IAM feature (iam:GenerateServiceLastAccessedDetails / iam:GetServiceLastAccessedDetails), not an Access Analyzer one, and if you automate the review note that 'only the principal that generates a report can view the report details' — with a role or federated session 'you must generate and retrieve the report during the same session', so a two-step pipeline that generates in one session and reads in another gets nothing back. Unused access findings themselves 'are only available using the ListFindingsV2 API action', so a collector written against ListFindings returns an empty set and looks like a clean bill of health. Second, and decisively for this control, last accessed information CANNOT right-size the permission that actually matters here: it 'reports service management actions', 'management actions include creation, deletion, and modification actions', and 'action last accessed information is not available for any data plane event' — bedrock:InvokeModel and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint are data-plane calls, and bedrock does not appear at all among the 202 service prefixes for which action last accessed information exists, while the only sagemaker-prefixed entry is sagemaker-geospatial. So it will tell you whether a role stopped calling bedrock as a service, never which inference actions it stopped using. Two further exclusions bite AI roles specifically: iam:PassRole 'is not tracked', which is the permission that lets an identity hand a role to an agent or training job, and access granted through resource-based policies, SCPs, permissions boundaries and session policies is excluded from the report entirely. Drive action-level right-sizing for inference from CloudTrail data events instead, and keep last accessed for the control-plane half.

controls.q: Is there a tested way to immediately revoke an identity's access to AI services during an incident, without waiting for normal offboarding cycles?
controls.h: Confirm an emergency revocation path exists and has been exercised, covering both human users and machine/agent identities.
controls.ev: Incident runbook + exercise record for emergency revocation
controls.rec: Maintain a tested emergency revocation runbook: for roles use the IAM 'Revoke active sessions' action (which attaches the AWSRevokeOlderSessions inline deny policy keyed on aws:TokenIssueTime to invalidate all outstanding temporary credentials, and needs PutRolePolicy on the role), deactivate or delete any IAM access keys, end IAM Identity Center sessions for human users, and import a certificate revocation list (CRL) for IAM Roles Anywhere identities. Exercise this path periodically for both human and machine/agent identities. THREE THINGS THAT MAKE THIS NOT A LOCKOUT UNLESS YOU BUILD IT THAT WAY. (1) Revoking sessions does not stop re-entry: the policy denies credentials issued before now 'as well as approximately 30 seconds into the future' to cover propagation delay, and 'if the user assumes the role after you revoked the permissions, then the deny policy does not apply to that user' — anyone still holding sts:AssumeRole on that role simply re-assumes it half a minute later. Revocation has to be paired in the same runbook step with removing the ability to assume (tighten the trust policy or pull the identity's AssumeRole grant), and note you cannot revoke the session of a service-linked role at all. (2) This path does not work on IAM Identity Center principals, because 'you can't edit roles in IAM that were created from IAM Identity Center permission sets'. AWS's documented mechanism there is a Deny-all policy conditioned on identitystore:userId, pre-deployed as an SCP with an invalid placeholder user ID across every account the workforce can reach and edited to the real user ID during the incident — 'the recommended approach for its ease and speed of impact', and only fast because the deployment already happened, so pre-deploying it IS the runbook step. Condition on identitystore:userId rather than aws:userId, which 'can be affected by how user attributes are synchronized' and 'can change if the user's username or email address changes'. Ending the AWS access portal session does not end the role sessions already assumed from it, and the deny must stay in place 'for at least 12 hours', after which 'any roles the user has assumed expire'. (3) Roles Anywhere revocation is pull-only and manual: CRL import is 'only supported by the API and CLI' (ImportCrl / import-crl, no console path), and 'callbacks to CRL Distribution Points (CDPs) or Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) endpoints are not supported' — so revoking the certificate at your CA changes nothing in AWS until you fetch the fresh CRL and push it yourself. Exercise the timing too, not just the mechanism: already-issued STS credentials remain valid to their expiry, and the AWS CLI caches credentials, so a revoked-but-cached session keeps working until ~/.aws/cli/cache is cleared.

controls.q: When an AI workload authenticates to a non-AWS or third-party API, does it present a machine identity whose principal is attributable in the target's logs (OAuth 2.0 client credentials, mTLS, or an API key bound to a specific principal), rather than a shared, unattributable secret?
controls.h: For AWS targets this is covered by IAM roles/SigV4; this asks about the non-AWS path. Look for an OAuth 2.0 client-credentials flow, mTLS client certificates, or per-principal API keys — not one shared key reused across workloads — and confirm the presented principal shows up in the downstream system's audit log so calls can be attributed and revoked individually.
controls.ev: Third-party auth configuration showing a per-principal machine identity + attribution in the target's logs
controls.rec: Give each workload an attributable machine identity for non-AWS targets rather than a shared secret. Prefer OAuth 2.0 client-credentials with a distinct client_id per workload, mutual TLS with a per-workload client certificate, or an API key bound to a single principal. For off-cloud workloads that then call AWS, exchange an X.509 certificate for short-lived STS credentials via IAM Roles Anywhere. Broker and store the OAuth and API-key options through AgentCore Identity credential providers / the Token Vault (or AWS Secrets Manager) with rotation, never inline, and confirm the presented client_id / certificate subject / key principal is recorded in the target API's audit log so each workload's calls are independently attributable and revocable. NOTHING BROKERS OUTBOUND mTLS FOR YOU, SO DO NOT PLAN AROUND IT. AgentCore Identity supports exactly four client authentication methods for a custom OAuth provider — CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC, CLIENT_SECRET_POST, AWS_IAM_ID_TOKEN_JWT and PRIVATE_KEY_JWT — and none of them is mTLS, so the Token Vault is not the answer for the certificate option. The only client certificate AWS will present outbound on your behalf is API Gateway's backend-authentication certificate, and it fails this control on three counts: the certificates 'generated by API Gateway are self-signed, and only the public key of a certificate is visible', so no third-party CA chain and nothing you can supply yourself; once selected 'API Gateway uses the certificate for all calls to HTTP integrations in your API', which is one identity per stage rather than one per workload; and it is 'valid for 365 days' with rotation left to you. API Gateway's mutual TLS feature runs the other direction entirely — it authenticates clients calling your API, via a Regional custom domain, an ACM certificate and an S3 truststore. A client certificate for calling someone else's API is therefore your own client's to hold, present and rotate; AWS gives you key custody, not the handshake. PREFER THE KEY-CUSTODY PATH THAT DOES EXIST: with PRIVATE_KEY_JWT, AgentCore Identity signs a short-lived RFC 7523 client assertion with a customer-managed KMS asymmetric SIGN_VERIFY key via kms:Sign and 'the private key never leaves KMS' (needs kms:Sign and kms:DescribeKey, and the public key registered with the authorization server). And with AWS_IAM_ID_TOKEN_JWT the assertion is an IAM-signed JWT for the agent's own execution role obtained via sts:GetWebIdentityToken (needs iam:EnableOutboundWebIdentityFederation on the account and an authorization server that trusts AWS IAM as an issuer). Both remove the shared secret altogether, which mTLS only does if you never copy the key. And check what you actually deployed: CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC is the default, so a credential provider created without setting clientAuthenticationMethod is authenticating with a client secret — the thing this question asks you to avoid.

controls.q: Does the authorization model distinguish action-level permissions on the same resource type — for example, an identity that can read records but not delete them — rather than granting all-or-nothing access to a resource?
controls.h: Broader than scoping which resources an identity can touch (AIR-FND-IAM-01): this asks whether read, write, and delete on the same resource type are separately grantable. Look for IAM policies enumerating specific actions instead of service:* wildcards, ABAC/condition-key differentiation, permission matrices, or API method-level authorizers that separate read from write/delete.
controls.ev: Policy or authorizer showing read vs. write/delete differentiation on one resource type
controls.rec: Grant action-level permissions, not all-or-nothing on a resource. Write IAM identity-based policies that enumerate the specific actions an identity needs (e.g. allow s3:GetObject but not s3:DeleteObject; bedrock:InvokeModel but not the guardrail/model-deployment mutation actions) rather than service:* wildcards, and differentiate access with ABAC condition keys (aws:PrincipalTag / aws:ResourceTag). For application- and agent-facing APIs, enforce the same split at the request layer via API Gateway per-method authorization or Amazon Verified Permissions (Cedar actions), so read, write, and delete on the same resource type are independently authorized and an agent granted read cannot delete.

controls.q: Are messages between agents signed by the sender and verified by the receiver at the message level, so a receiving agent proves who sent an instruction and that its content is unmodified, rather than trusting the transport alone?
controls.h: Distinct from TLS and from caller authentication (AIR-FND-IAM-08), and distinct from an authenticated channel (AIR-ACR-RT-07, AIR-SLF-AGT-05): those protect the message in flight, and an asynchronous multi-agent workflow leaves it at rest in a queue or event bus where there is no channel left to trust. Look for the sender signing the serialized payload with a KMS asymmetric key, the signature traveling with the message as message metadata so it survives every intermediary, the receiver calling Verify and rejecting before it acts, and one signing key per trust zone rather than one key shared by every agent. Check the at-rest half too: SSE on the inter-agent queues with a customer-managed key per zone.
controls.ev: Signing key per trust zone + a receiving agent rejecting a message that fails Verify
controls.rec: Provision one AWS KMS asymmetric key pair per agent trust zone for message signing, choosing a signing key spec (RSA or ECC) rather than an encryption spec, so a key compromise in one zone cannot forge messages in another. Have the sending agent sign the serialized message payload with the KMS Sign API and attach the signature plus the signing key ARN as message attributes, so the signature travels with the payload through every queue, topic, and event bus rather than terminating at the transport. Have the receiving agent call the KMS Verify API and reject the message before any instruction in it is acted on, so a forged or tampered payload never reaches the agent's reasoning loop; treat a verification failure as a security event, not a parse error. Enable SQS server-side encryption with a customer-managed KMS key on every queue carrying inter-agent messages, using a separate key per trust zone so at-rest exposure is bounded to one zone; existing queues can be converted in place. Keep signing key ARNs in Parameter Store rather than in agent code, and rotate the signing keys manually on a schedule — AWS KMS automatic and on-demand rotation cover symmetric encryption keys only, and name asymmetric and HMAC keys as requiring manual rotation, so plan an overlap window in which receivers still accept signatures from the outgoing key. Alarm on signing-key usage anomalies in CloudWatch — kms:Sign called by a role that should only verify, or a sudden rise in signing volume from one agent — because a stolen signing capability is otherwise indistinguishable from normal traffic. For agents on AgentCore Runtime using the A2A protocol, layer message-level signing on top of A2A's own authentication for any exchange that crosses a trust boundary: A2A authenticates the calling agent, which is a statement about the connection rather than about a payload that outlives it.

controls.q: Is all traffic carrying prompts, model outputs, or training data encrypted in transit end to end?
controls.h: Confirm TLS is enforced for every hop that carries prompts, responses, or training data, including internal service-to-service calls.
controls.ev: Network/config review confirming TLS enforcement
controls.rec: Enforce encryption in transit by attaching an S3 bucket policy that Denies s3:* when aws:SecureTransport is false on every bucket carrying prompts, outputs, or training data, optionally adding a NumericLessThan s3:TlsVersion 1.2 condition. Rely on TLS-only AWS service endpoints plus VPC interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for Bedrock and internal service-to-service calls — the Bedrock endpoint suffixes are bedrock, bedrock-runtime, bedrock-mantle, bedrock-agent and bedrock-agent-runtime, so a private inference path needs the runtime endpoint and not only the control-plane one. WRITE THE DENY SO IT CANNOT BREAK THE INGESTION PATH: Amazon S3 redacts s3:TlsVersion, aws:SecureTransport, aws:SourceIp and aws:VpcSourceIp from the authorization context of service-to-service calls, so a blanket Deny on them can unintentionally block AWS service principals reading your training data. AWS's prescribed exception is to add Bool aws:PrincipalIsAWSService false to the same Deny statement — but note that key is true only for a direct service-principal call and is false when a service reads your bucket under a service role you supplied, which is how Bedrock model customization and knowledge-base ingestion are configured. So do not treat the exception as covering those paths on paper: run one customization or ingestion job after attaching the policy and confirm it still succeeds, and where it does not, exclude the specific role with aws:PrincipalArn or aws:ViaAWSService rather than deleting the TLS Deny.

controls.q: Is sensitive data (PII, PHI, financial, or classified) discovered and classified before it is used as AI input, training data, or grounding context?
controls.h: Look for automated or process-driven classification/discovery that runs before data reaches a model or knowledge base, not just after-the-fact audits.
controls.ev: Classification/discovery scan results for AI data sources
controls.rec: Use both Macie mechanisms, because they answer different questions and are not interchangeable. Amazon Macie automated sensitive-data discovery continually evaluates your S3 inventory but selects representative objects by SAMPLING, so it gives estate-wide sensitivity visibility and tells you where to look — it is not per-object assurance over the specific set about to be ingested, and it is per-Region over general purpose buckets. Run a targeted sensitive-data discovery job (managed plus custom data identifiers) over the actual AI source prefixes to get that assurance, and treat the automated map as what prioritizes which prefixes need one. Then use Amazon Comprehend to identify PII in text prompts and documents prior to model or knowledge-base use — DetectPiiEntities (real-time) locates PII entities. Redacting them requires an asynchronous PII detection job configured with redaction, so pair real-time detection with the batch redaction job (or an Amazon S3 Object Lambda PII access point) where content must be redacted before use.

controls.q: Is there a defined data-residency requirement for AI workloads, and is it enforced so data does not leave approved regions or jurisdictions?
controls.h: Check for a documented residency requirement plus a technical control (region restriction, data-perimeter policy) that enforces it, not just a policy statement.
controls.ev: Residency requirement doc + region-restriction control
controls.rec: Document the approved regions and enforce them with an AWS Organizations SCP that Denies actions such as bedrock:* when aws:RequestedRegion StringNotEquals the approved list, or enable the AWS Control Tower Region deny control; this technically blocks data storage and model invocations outside approved jurisdictions rather than relying on a policy statement alone. THE REGION DENY DOES NOT BOUND WHERE A PROMPT IS PROCESSED. aws:RequestedRegion is the Region you call, and cross-Region inference profiles route the request elsewhere: AWS's own table gives the SCP requirement as 'Allow all destination Regions in profile' for a Geographic profile and 'Allow "aws:RequestedRegion": "unspecified"' for a Global profile, which routes worldwide. So adding unspecified to unbreak a failing call silently permits worldwide processing — the opposite of what this control asks for. AWS also states cross-Region inference can route to Regions that are not manually enabled in your account, so leaving a Region disabled is not a residency control either. Pick Geographic profiles for a residency requirement, enumerate every destination Region of the profiles you allow in the SCP rather than only the calling Region, and evidence the outcome from CloudTrail's additionalEventData.inferenceRegion field (logged in the source Region), which records where each request was actually processed.

controls.q: Are backups or snapshots of AI training data and model artifacts protected against tampering or deletion, including by a compromised administrator?
controls.h: Look for immutability (e.g., object lock, versioning with deletion protection) on backups of training data and model artifacts.
controls.ev: Backup configuration showing immutability/versioning
controls.rec: Store backups of training data and model artifacts in S3 with Object Lock in Compliance mode (WORM) plus versioning, and lock AWS Backup vaults with Vault Lock in Compliance mode. In Compliance mode neither an IAM principal nor the account root can alter or delete recovery points before the retention period expires, protecting against a compromised administrator. TWO WAYS A COMPLIANCE-MODE VAULT LOCK IS WEAKER THAN IT READS, both of which leave the compromised-administrator window this control names still open. First, a Compliance-mode lock is immutable only after its grace time expires — you choose the grace time and it must be at least 3 days (72 hours), and AWS states that during grace time you can still remove the vault lock and change its configuration, so a lock created today is administrator-removable for at least the next three days. Track the lock's start date, not just its mode. Second, PutBackupVaultLockConfiguration selects the mode by the presence of one parameter: include ChangeableForDays and you get Compliance mode, omit it and you silently get Governance mode, which AWS documents as removable by any user with sufficient IAM permissions. Assert the mode from the vault's returned lock configuration rather than from the call you believe you made. Note also that the lock's minimum and maximum retention periods do not apply retroactively — recovery points already in the vault keep their previous lifecycle settings.

controls.q: Is there a defined data-retention and deletion schedule for prompts, model outputs, and conversation history?
controls.h: Confirm a written retention policy exists specifying how long AI interaction data is kept and when it should be deleted.
controls.ev: Documented retention/deletion policy for AI interaction data
controls.rec: Define a written retention and deletion schedule for prompts, model outputs, and conversation history, then bind it to an enforceable control by encoding the period as Amazon S3 Lifecycle expiration rules on the storage buckets (and equivalent TTLs on any DynamoDB or CloudWatch Logs stores) so the documented period maps to a technical mechanism, not just intent. THE SCHEDULE MUST ALSO COVER THE MODEL'S OWN RETENTION, NOT ONLY YOUR COPIES. Amazon Bedrock retains prompts and outputs according to a data-retention mode resolved as 'first non-inherit value of (project -> account -> model default)', and inherit is the default for new accounts and projects — so an account nobody has configured has made no retention decision and each model's built-in default governs. Under default mode AWS states it may retain the data for safety and abuse-prevention purposes, and on the Responses API store=false 'does not guarantee zero data retention'. Set the account mode explicitly with PutAccountDataRetention (mode none for zero retention, which writes no request or response data to durable storage), set it per project where projects are used, and read back each model's effective mode and allowed_modes rather than assuming — if your effective mode is outside a model's allowed_modes that model reports status unavailable and its requests are blocked, so this is an availability decision as well as a retention one. There is no console UI for this at launch; it is API or SDK only. For the DynamoDB leg, note TTL is best-effort: DynamoDB deletes expired items typically within a few days of expiry and they remain readable until it does, so a TTL is not a hard deletion deadline.

controls.q: Is the data-retention and deletion schedule for AI interaction data actually enforced, with deletion occurring automatically on schedule?
controls.h: Confirm deletion actually happens on the defined schedule (e.g., automated lifecycle/expiry), not just that a policy is written down.
controls.ev: Evidence of scheduled deletion running (lifecycle rule / job logs)
controls.rec: Enforce the schedule with S3 Lifecycle configuration Expiration actions (plus NoncurrentVersionExpiration on versioned buckets), which Amazon S3 evaluates daily to automatically delete expired objects. Confirm enforcement from an S3 Lifecycle Event Notification for an object that actually expired rather than from the lifecycle rule's status, because a present, Enabled rule is not evidence that anything was deleted. NoncurrentVersionExpiration is not optional on a versioned bucket: on a versioning-enabled bucket an Expiration action on the current version only adds a delete marker, and AWS states object expiration 'applies only to an object's current version (it has no impact on noncurrent object versions)' — so an Expiration rule alone retains every prior version of every prompt and output indefinitely while presenting as enforced. FOUR DOCUMENTED CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH EXPIRATION SILENTLY DOES NOTHING, each of which reads as compliant: Amazon S3 'doesn't take any action on noncurrent versions of objects that have the S3 Object Lock configuration applied' — which collides directly with AIR-FND-DAT-05, since applying Object Lock in Compliance mode to the same data this control expires means the expiration will not run. S3 takes no action when one or more versions exist and a delete marker is already the current version. S3 takes no action on current or noncurrent versions of objects whose replication status is Pending or Failed. For a tag-based filter S3 re-evaluates the object's tags at execution time, so removing the triggering tag after the action is queued cancels the expiration. Where the same data must be both immutable and expiring, separate them — hold the WORM copy in its own locked bucket or vault with a retention period equal to the schedule and let it expire by lifecycle completion, rather than layering a lifecycle rule over a locked object and treating the rule as the control.

controls.q: When an AI system is deprecated or a model is retired, is there a defined process to securely dispose of the associated training data, artifacts, and credentials?
controls.h: Look for a decommissioning checklist covering data deletion, credential revocation, and artifact disposal for retired AI systems.
controls.ev: Decommissioning checklist / most recent completed record
controls.rec: Maintain a decommissioning checklist that on retirement deletes S3 data and artifacts (lifecycle or explicit delete), revokes the IAM roles/access keys and Secrets Manager secrets, and calls KMS ScheduleKeyDeletion on the data-specific customer-managed key so remaining ciphertext becomes cryptographically unrecoverable (crypto-shredding); retain the completed record as evidence. NEITHER DELETION IS IMMEDIATE, SO DO NOT CLOSE THE RECORD ON THE API CALL: ScheduleKeyDeletion takes a PendingWindowInDays of 7-30 days (default 30), the actual deletion can land up to 24 hours later than the scheduled date, and CancelKeyDeletion can recover the key for the whole window. Secrets Manager likewise 'does not immediately delete secrets' but schedules them after a recovery window of a minimum of seven days. Take the closing evidence from the CloudTrail DeleteKey event, not the ScheduleKeyDeletion event. Scheduling deletion also 'might not immediately affect data keys encrypted by the KMS key', so a process already holding a decrypted data key keeps reading. THREE DOCUMENTED CASES WHERE THE DELETE SHREDS NOTHING: (1) a multi-Region REPLICA key is reversible — 'You can delete a replica key at any time' and 'if you mistakenly delete a replica key, you can recreate it by replicating the same primary key in the same Region' — so where AI data was replicated across Regions you must schedule every replica and then the primary, whose waiting period only begins when the last replica is deleted. (2) DeleteImportedKeyMaterial is 'temporary and reversible' because the material can be reimported, so a runbook step reading 'delete the key material' has not shredded anything. (3) a replicated secret cannot be deleted at all until its replicas are — 'you can't delete a primary secret if it is replicated to other Regions'. The unrecoverability the checklist depends on is guaranteed for a deleted single-Region symmetric encryption key, where metadata unique to that key is cryptographically bound to each ciphertext, so even the identical key material reimported into a new key cannot decrypt it. Order the checklist to revoke before it shreds: deleting a secret makes it inaccessible immediately even though disposal completes later, and for an asymmetric ENCRYPT_DECRYPT key the public key may already be outside AWS KMS, where 'alarms, logs, and other strategies that detect attempted use of KMS key that is pending deletion cannot detect use of the public key' — so check CloudTrail for public-key downloads as part of retirement rather than assuming the key policy bounded it.

controls.q: Where the AI pipeline uses AWS AI services covered by the AI services opt-out policy, has the organization opted out of content use for service improvement, and is that choice locked so a member account cannot override it?
controls.h: Check for an AWS Organizations AI services opt-out policy attached at the root (not just an account-level setting), and confirm child accounts cannot re-opt-in. Note this policy type covers a specific list of services (Comprehend, Textract, Transcribe, Rekognition, Lex, Polly, GuardDuty, CloudWatch, Config, Security Hub, and others) — Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI are not on that list, so absence of a Bedrock entry is expected, not a finding.
controls.ev: DescribeEffectivePolicy output for AISERVICES_OPT_OUT_POLICY on a member account
controls.rec: Enable the AISERVICES_OPT_OUT_POLICY type on the organization root (EnablePolicyType) and attach a policy that sets opt_out for the covered services the AI pipeline actually uses — or use the default services entry to cover all of them at once. LOCK IT AT ALL THREE PLACEMENTS, NOT ONE: "@@operators_allowed_for_child_policies": ["@@none"] means something different depending on where it sits, so placing it only alongside "@@assign": "optOut" does not lock the organization. Under opt_out_policy it stops a child changing that service's setting. Under the service or default key it stops a child adding keys to that entry. Only under services does it stop a child "adding any new sections for individual services". AWS's own Example 2 places the operator under both default and opt_out_policy and is documented to still resolve to a child account opting in to Amazon Lex, precisely because there is none under services — the parent's optOut keeps governing default while a one-line child policy assigning optIn to lex, textract or q takes effect for that service. The fully locked root policy therefore carries it at all three levels: {"services": {"@@operators_allowed_for_child_policies": ["@@none"], "default": {"@@operators_allowed_for_child_policies": ["@@none"], "opt_out_policy": {"@@operators_allowed_for_child_policies": ["@@none"], "@@assign": "optOut"}}}}. Capitalization is load-bearing — "the policies do not work if you use unexpected capitalization" — so optOut, not optout, and note @@append, @@remove and @@enforced_for are all unusable in this policy type, leaving @@assign as the only operator. Verify enforcement per account with organizations:DescribeEffectivePolicy --policy-type AISERVICES_OPT_OUT_POLICY rather than reading the attached policy, since the effective policy is what the inheritance chain actually resolves to. Scope the claim honestly: this policy type applies only to the services on the AWS-published supported list, so it does not govern Amazon Bedrock or Amazon SageMaker AI — for those, the no-training-on-customer-content commitment comes from the AWS Service Terms (Amazon Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence Services), not from this control. Also note that opting out deletes the associated historical content a service had stored for improvement purposes — bounded, though: the deletion 'is limited to content stored that is not required to provide service functions', so content used to provide the service to you is not deleted. THE VERIFICATION IS PER-ACCOUNT AND CANNOT BE DONE AT THE OU: DescribeEffectivePolicy states 'Specifying an organization root or organizational unit (OU) as the target is not supported', while its TargetId pattern still accepts r- and ou- ids — so an OU-scoped check fails at runtime rather than at validation, and coverage evidence has to be sampled account by account. WHY THIS IS ALSO A RESIDENCY CONTROL: for content used for service improvement AWS states 'we might store such content in an AWS Region outside of the AWS Region where you are using the service', so an un-opted-out covered service moves content out of Region by design and no aws:RequestedRegion Deny bounds it (see AIR-FND-DAT-04). AND BEDROCK IS NO LONGER SERVICE-TERMS-ONLY: Amazon Bedrock now exposes retention as an account setting (PutAccountDataRetention with mode none) that an SCP can pin org-wide on bedrock:DataRetentionMode for control-plane calls and bedrock-mantle:DataRetentionMode for inference — so treat a missing bedrock entry in this policy as expected but not as the end of the enquiry, and check that setting per AIR-FND-DAT-06.

controls.q: Is every AI workload whose data must remain inaccessible to its own operating environment identified, with decryption bound to an attested enclave measurement rather than to an IAM principal alone?
controls.h: For the highest-sensitivity inference or training, an IAM-authorized role is still a role a compromised host can use. Start by confirming the identification exists and covers every AI workload, then — for each one it placed in scope — that the KMS key policy releases the key only against a verified measurement — so decryption fails on an unmeasured or debug environment even with valid IAM permissions. Read the whole key policy, not just the statement carrying the condition: attestation binds that statement, so any other statement allowing the same actions unconditioned is a second, unattested path to the same plaintext, and it looks identical in a policy excerpt. A workload that has no such data satisfies this control on the identification alone: the empty set is a legitimate Yes, and the recorded determination — which data classes were considered, and why none of them requires host-inaccessibility — is the evidence for it. That is deliberately not a separate answer state; leaving the control unanswered instead reads as review that has not happened yet, and answering Yes without the determination asserts a scoping decision nobody made.
controls.ev: The per-workload determination of whether any data requires host-inaccessibility, naming the data classes considered — and for each workload it placed in scope, the complete KMS key policy, every statement rather than the attested one alone so an unconditioned grant of the same actions is visible, plus the trusted PCR/image-digest values, which PCRs are pinned beyond the image, and how the values are refreshed on rebuild
controls.rec: Bind decryption to attestation, not just identity. UNDERSTAND THE BUILD COST BEFORE COMMITTING: this is an application-architecture change, not a setting to switch on. You split the sensitive component out of the application, package it as a Docker image, convert that to an enclave image file with nitro-cli build-enclave. Allocate the parent's vCPUs and memory to it — run-enclave takes a minimum of 64 MiB, cannot exceed the parent's memory, must leave enough for the parent's own applications and at least 1 vCPU (2, and an even count, if the parent is multithreaded), and because the image is loaded into that memory the working figure is a multiple of the EIF size rather than the EIF size. Proxy every input, output, and AWS API call over a host-local vsock channel, because the enclave has no network interface, no persistent storage, and no SSH. The enclave must use the Nitro Enclaves SDK to obtain its attestation document, and the PCR measurements that build produces have to reach the KMS key policy on every rebuild. Plan it as a project for the one component that genuinely needs it — a decryption or signing step — not as a wrapper around a whole service. Then run the sensitive component in the enclave and write the KMS key policy so kms:Decrypt / kms:GenerateDataKey / kms:GenerateDataKeyPair / kms:DeriveSharedSecret / kms:GenerateRandom are allowed only when the request carries a signed attestation document matching your measurements: use kms:RecipientAttestation:ImageSha384 (equivalent to PCR0, the enclave image digest) and/or kms:RecipientAttestation:PCR<PCR_ID> with StringEqualsIgnoreCase and a lower-case hex value of up to 96 bytes. Note that this reaches only those five operations: kms:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext accepts none of the attestation condition keys, so a data key obtained that way cannot be gated on attestation at all. These conditions are effective only when the request's Recipient parameter supplies an enclave attestation document, so a request without one is denied. AUDIT THE WHOLE POLICY, NOT THE ONE STATEMENT: that denial is a property of the statement carrying the condition, not of the key, so a second statement allowing the same actions without a condition leaves the key decryptable off the attested path — and the key policy AWS generates when you do not supply one grants the account root full access, which allows Decrypt. A policy can therefore carry correct attestation conditions and still be bypassable; AWS's own remedy is to change the broad administrative kms:* grant to NotAction: kms:Decrypt, keeping key administration while removing the unconditioned data path. PIN DEPLOYMENT CONTEXT, NOT JUST THE IMAGE: the EIF is not a secret, so PCR0/ImageSha384 alone is satisfied by the same image rebuilt and launched anywhere by anyone holding the Principal's credentials — add PCR3 (parent IAM role) or PCR4 (parent instance ID), with AWS recommending PCR3 plus PCR8 (signing certificate) together 'for the best flexibility'; PCR1 (kernel/bootstrap) and PCR2 (application) add image integrity but no deployment binding. ONLY THREE OF THE SIX MEASUREMENTS COME OUT OF THE BUILD: an enclave has exactly six (PCR0, PCR1, PCR2, PCR3, PCR4, PCR8) and build-enclave emits only PCR0/1/2 — PCR8 appears only when you build with --private-key and --signing-certificate, and PCR3 and PCR4 are not emitted at all. You generate those two yourself as a SHA384 of the parent's IAM role ARN or its instance ID, padded with 48 null bytes, so a padding or ARN-format mistake produces a hash that can never match and presents as a broken deployment rather than as a policy error; and although the condition key accepts PCR0 through PCR31, a condition on any index outside those six can never be satisfied either. PCR8 also makes a certificate expiry an availability dependency: run-enclave fails with errors E36, E39 and E11 on an image signed by a certificate that is no longer valid, so the signing certificate's renewal belongs in the same pipeline as the key-policy update. TREAT A DEBUG ENCLAVE AS NOT AN ENCLAVE: enclaves launched with --debug-mode or --attach-console 'generate attestation documents with PCR values made up entirely of zeroes' — every PCR, not only PCR0/1/2 — and such documents 'cannot be used for cryptographic attestation'; debug mode additionally lets the parent read the enclave's console with nitro-cli console, so it gives up the isolation this control exists to obtain, and --attach-console does exactly the same thing while not reading like a debug flag. Correctly pinned PCRs already reject a zeroed document, but detect it rather than assume, by alerting on KMS CloudTrail events whose recorded attestation context shows all-zero PCRs. Treat the values as build artifacts: every enclave rebuild changes them, so the key-policy update belongs in the release pipeline — the failure is not only that the workload loses access, but that a stale policy silently keeps authorizing a retired image, so reconcile the authorized PCRs against the images your pipeline actually publishes. Note the enclave's only ingress is a host-local vsock channel: if the parent forwards a network-reachable port into the vsock proxy, an attacker who reaches that port drives a correctly-attested enclave as a confused deputy, and CloudTrail shows a clean attestation doing their decryption — so keep the proxy bound host-locally and treat the parent's own hardening as in scope. WHERE THE WORKLOAD CANNOT BE REFACTORED INTO AN ENCLAVE: an enclave partitions only vCPUs and memory with no device passthrough and no persistent storage, so a GPU-served model cannot run inside one. Use EC2 instance attestation instead — launch from an Attestable AMI with NitroTPM and gate the same five KMS operations on kms:RecipientAttestation:NitroTPMPCR<PCR_ID>, noting the PCR numbering differs from enclaves (PCR4/PCR12 validate a standard boot, PCR7 the UEFI Secure Boot policy, and PCR7 is the one that survives instance updates without a key-policy edit). This attests the host at boot rather than isolating a component at runtime — weaker, but available to workloads enclaves cannot host. Where the identification finds no data requiring host-inaccessibility, that recorded determination is what satisfies this control — answer Yes on it and rely on AIR-FND-DAT-01 encryption plus least privilege for the workload's ordinary confidentiality. Write into it which data classes were considered and the basis for excluding each, and re-run it whenever the workload's data classification changes: this is the control most likely to become applicable later without anyone noticing, because nothing about the workload's configuration changes when the data flowing through it gets more sensitive. Two other controls escalate here rather than duplicating this one, and are the usual reasons to be reading it: AIR-SLF-RT-01, when an injected secret must not be readable from the host it runs on, and AIR-SLF-CMP-08, when self-hosted model weights must stay unreadable to the instance operator.

controls.q: Do AI workloads run inside a private network boundary, without requiring direct public internet exposure for normal operation?
controls.h: Confirm AI compute/inference resources sit in private subnets or an equivalent private network boundary rather than having public endpoints by default.
controls.ev: Network diagram / config showing private placement
controls.rec: Deploy AI compute (SageMaker training/hosting, Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, Lambda/ECS inference) in private VPC subnets with no internet gateway, and for SageMaker set VpcConfig so containers have no public endpoint or default internet egress. Understand what EnableNetworkIsolation does before reaching for it, because it is stronger than private placement and not a superset of it: the container then makes no outbound network calls at all — not to Amazon S3, not to resources in your own VPC — and no AWS credentials are made available to the container runtime environment. That fits a self-contained training or inference image (and is required for AWS Marketplace algorithm and model packages), but it breaks any container that itself calls Bedrock, S3 or a private service, and the Chainer and SageMaker RL containers do not support it at all. SageMaker still performs the S3 download and upload for you outside the container, so combining it with VpcConfig routes that data movement through your subnet while the container stays isolated. For AgentCore Runtime, set network mode to VPC with private subnets rather than the default public endpoint, and check the S3 path explicitly: runtimes created before the 2026-05-05 rollout include a service-managed Amazon S3 gateway that sits outside your VPC configuration, so VPC mode alone is not yet full isolation — set requireServiceS3Endpoint to false through UpdateAgentRuntime to close it (the field cannot be set at CreateAgentRuntime), after confirming your own VPC provides the S3 access the runtime needs. Runtimes created after the rollout have no service-managed gateway, so all access including S3 is governed exclusively by your VPC configuration.

controls.q: Is traffic between AI workloads and the AWS services they call kept off the public internet (private connectivity), rather than routing over the open internet?
controls.h: Look for private connectivity (e.g., VPC endpoints or equivalent) for calls from AI workloads to the services they depend on.
controls.ev: Route table / endpoint configuration review
controls.rec: Reach dependent AWS services over AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints with Private DNS enabled, and use S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints, so traffic stays off the public internet. Scope each endpoint with a least-privilege VPC endpoint policy. Create one endpoint per API surface you actually call, because no single Bedrock endpoint covers the service: the supported suffixes are bedrock (control plane), bedrock-runtime (inference), bedrock-mantle (the newer inference endpoint, whose traffic a bedrock-runtime endpoint does not carry), bedrock-agent (build time) and bedrock-agent-runtime (agent invocation). An agentic workload needs the AgentCore endpoints as well, and they are separate service names again — com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore for the Runtime, built-in tools, Memory and Identity data plane, com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore.gateway for Gateway and MCP traffic, and com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore-control for the control plane. For SageMaker, create com.amazonaws.<region>.sagemaker.api and com.amazonaws.<region>.sagemaker.runtime, whose endpoint-specific DNS names take the form VPC_Endpoint_ID.api.sagemaker.<region>.vpce.amazonaws.com and VPC_Endpoint_ID.runtime.sagemaker.<region>.vpce.amazonaws.com. Enumerate the endpoints against the calls the workload actually makes rather than assuming one per service: an API surface with no matching endpoint is not covered by PrivateLink, and wherever the subnet still has an internet path that call quietly leaves over it.

controls.q: Is outbound network traffic from AI workloads restricted to an approved allow-list of destinations, rather than unrestricted egress?
controls.h: Check for an egress control (firewall, proxy, or security-group allow-list) that limits where AI workloads can send outbound traffic.
controls.ev: Egress policy/allow-list configuration
controls.rec: Force outbound traffic through AWS Network Firewall stateful domain allow-list rule groups, matching TLS_SNI for HTTPS and the HTTP host header for HTTP. The Allow action supplies the default drop itself — traffic of the inspected protocol that does not match the domain specifications is denied — so do not also attach Reject or Alert domain rule groups to a policy that uses default action ordering, where that implicit drop is evaluated before your other rules. Set the HOME_NET rule variable to cover every CIDR you want inspected: domain-list inspection defaults to traffic originating inside the firewall's own VPC, so traffic arriving from other VPCs or on-premises is not inspected until you widen it. Pair this with Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall allow-list rule groups and treat that pairing as required rather than defense in depth: DNS queries sent to the Route 53 Resolver are routed to a static address in the VPC and are therefore not inspected by Network Firewall at all, including by the AWS managed rule groups, and security groups cannot block them either. Keep the two domain lists in sync, end the DNS Firewall rule group with an explicit BLOCK on * so anything off the list fails to resolve, and restrict security-group egress to the required ports. Add IP and CIDR rules alongside the domain rules on your highest-value paths, because Network Firewall does not pause connections to perform out-of-band DNS lookups — it matches on the SNI or host header the client presents, not the address it actually connects to, so a client offering an approved SNI while connecting elsewhere passes the domain allow-list.

controls.q: Is inbound and outbound traffic to AI endpoints inspected for known attack patterns (e.g., injection attempts, exfiltration signatures)?
controls.h: Look for a web/network protection layer in front of AI endpoints doing signature or pattern-based inspection, not just plain routing.
controls.ev: Protection layer configuration + recent detections
controls.rec: Front public AI endpoints (API Gateway, ALB, or CloudFront) with an AWS WAF web ACL using the SQL injection and XSS attack rule statements plus rate-based rules, and set the SQLi sensitivity level to HIGH — it defaults to LOW, while AWS documents HIGH as detecting more SQL injection attacks and as the recommended setting. Then fix the limit that quietly decides whether inspection reaches an AI request at all: AWS WAF inspects the request body only up to a per-resource-type ceiling — fixed at 8 KB for Application Load Balancer and AppSync, and defaulting to 16 KB (raisable in 16 KB increments to 64 KB) for CloudFront, API Gateway, Amazon Cognito, App Runner, Verified Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Prompt bodies routinely exceed 8 KB, and the default OversizeHandling is CONTINUE, which inspects only the portion within the limit and forwards the request, so an oversized prompt passes the injection rules uninspected. Raise the limit where the resource type allows it and choose OversizeHandling deliberately (MATCH to treat oversize as a hit, or NO_MATCH with a separate size-constraint rule) rather than leaving the default; note gRPC bodies cannot be inspected. Inspect VPC egress with AWS Network Firewall Suricata-compatible IPS stateful rules, adding the AWS managed threat-signature rule groups (ThreatSignaturesBotnet, ThreatSignaturesIOC, ThreatSignaturesEmergingEvents and the other categories) and the domain and IP reputation groups (MalwareDomains, BotNetCommandAndControlDomains, AbusedLegitMalwareDomains) to catch exfiltration and command-and-control patterns — selecting the StrictOrder or ActionOrder variant of each rule-group name to match your firewall policy's rule evaluation order, since only the matching variant can be added to a given policy.

controls.q: Are network paths between different AI workloads segmented, so a compromise of one workload cannot directly reach another's network segment?
controls.h: Confirm distinct AI workloads (e.g., different agents or applications) are placed in separate network segments with controlled paths between them, not a single flat network.
controls.ev: Segmentation diagram / security-group review
controls.rec: Segment distinct AI workloads into separate subnets, VPCs or accounts so a compromise of one cannot reach another's segment, and route required cross-segment traffic through a Transit Gateway or PrivateLink with a Network Firewall inspection VPC. Then pick the enforcement mechanism per path, because security-group referencing does not work everywhere the segmentation does, and a rule that silently never matches reads as a control while enforcing nothing. Referencing a peer security group works in an inbound rule when the groups are in the same VPC, across a VPC peering connection, or across a transit gateway — but in an outbound rule only for the same VPC or a peering connection, not across a transit gateway. It is not supported across transit gateway peering connections at all (both VPCs must attach to the same transit gateway, which rules out the cross-Region case), and not supported for PrivateLink endpoints, where AWS recommends IP CIDR-based rules instead. Most importantly for the inspection path this control prescribes: if you route traffic between instances in different subnets through a middlebox appliance, each security group must reference the other instance's private IP or its subnet CIDR — referencing the other instance's security group as the source does not allow the traffic to flow — and referencing through a transit gateway does not work across a Gateway Load Balancer or AWS Network Firewall. So use peer security-group references for same-VPC and peered paths, and CIDR-based rules plus subnet network ACLs for transit-gateway, PrivateLink and inspected paths. Note also that referenced security groups are not authorized against in AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress/Egress and the matching Revoke calls — only existence is checked — so naming a referenced group in an IAM policy for those actions has no effect.

controls.q: Can an autonomous agent's ability to reach arbitrary network destinations or invoke arbitrary tools be constrained to an explicit allow-list, rather than open-ended reachability?
controls.h: Verify agent runtimes are bound to a defined set of reachable endpoints/tools rather than able to resolve and connect to anything.
controls.ev: Agent runtime network policy / allow-list configuration
controls.rec: Run agents on Bedrock AgentCore Runtime in VPC mode by setting networkConfiguration.networkMode to VPC (valid values PUBLIC | VPC) with networkModeConfig (a VpcConfig of private subnets and security groups, 1-16 of each) instead of the default PUBLIC mode, then constrain network reachability with those security groups plus Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall domain allow-lists so the agent can only resolve and connect to approved endpoints. Make VPC mode non-optional through IAM rather than convention: AgentCore defines the bedrock-agentcore:subnets and bedrock-agentcore:securityGroups condition keys, so a Deny with Null set to true on both keys rejects any call that omits a VPC configuration, and ForAnyValue:StringNotEquals on the same keys pins deployments to approved subnet and security-group ids. Scope that policy to the actions that actually define the keys — CreateAgentRuntime, UpdateAgentRuntime, CreateCodeInterpreter and CreateBrowser. The developer guide also lists CreateGatewayTarget and UpdateGatewayTarget as supporting these keys when a target configures a managed VPC resource, but the machine-readable IAM service reference lists no action condition keys for either action, and a Deny conditioned on a key an action does not define never matches — it fails open, granting exactly what it was written to block. So do not rely on the Gateway-target variant until you have proved in your own account that the Deny actually denies. Because network controls gate destinations and FQDNs rather than which tools run over a reachable endpoint, also enforce tool-level allow-listing at the application layer (the agent's registered tool set and an AgentCore Gateway with scoped authorization) to fully constrain tool invocation.
