controls.q: Are internet-facing entry points to AI workloads protected against volumetric and application-layer DDoS attacks, rather than relying on the always-on baseline protection alone?
controls.h: Check for an explicit, configured L7 mitigation on the AI entry point — not the always-on baseline. AWS Shield Standard applies to every customer at no cost and needs no configuration, so its presence is already true of an unprotected account and proves nothing here. The current mechanism is the AWS WAF Anti-DDoS managed rule group (AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet, 50 WCUs): confirm it is referenced in the web ACL associated with the entry point, and check the Block and Challenge sensitivity levels are set deliberately rather than left at defaults, since they tune independently. Note this does NOT require a Shield Advanced subscription — any AWS WAF customer can enable it — so absence of Shield Advanced is not an excuse for absence of this control. If you find Shield Advanced automatic application-layer mitigation (L7AM) instead, that is the legacy path: it was superseded by the managed rule group on 2026-03-26 and is available to new subscribers only via AWS Support, so treat it as Partial and plan the migration. Where Shield Advanced IS subscribed, verify per-resource enrollment too: CreateProtection accepts only a CloudFront distribution, Route 53 hosted zone, Global Accelerator standard accelerator, Elastic IP, Application Load Balancer or Classic Load Balancer — an EC2 instance or Network Load Balancer is protected only by association with a protected Elastic IP, so look for that association rather than the instance itself. API Gateway and Lambda function URLs are not Shield Advanced resource types, so the protectable edge is a CloudFront distribution in front of them. Finally, confirm a request-rate cap exists on the inference path specifically, because the distinctive loss on an AI endpoint is token and inference spend as much as availability.

controls.rec: Add the AWS WAF Anti-DDoS managed rule group (AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet, 50 WCUs) to the web ACL on every internet-facing AI entry point, and set the Block and Challenge sensitivity levels deliberately — they tune independently, so you can run Challenge at high sensitivity to catch more suspicious traffic while keeping Block low to avoid dropping legitimate requests. This is the current mechanism and it does NOT require a Shield Advanced subscription: any AWS WAF customer can enable it. It superseded Shield Advanced automatic application-layer mitigation (L7AM) on 2026-03-26, reacts in seconds rather than minutes, baselines in minutes, needs no health checks, and uses 50 WCUs against the previous 150; if you are still on L7AM, migrate. Pair it with your own AWS WAF rate-based rule scoped to the inference path, because the distinctive AI loss from a flood is runaway token and inference spend rather than only unavailability — cap request rate per caller even where availability is acceptable. Match on the rule group's labels (awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:*, which mark graduated suspicion levels and event-detected) where you need handling the rule group does not cover, and exclude any workload path that cannot support a Challenge action so it falls back to Block. Do not treat the baseline as the control: AWS Shield Standard is automatic and free for every customer, so it is already true of an unprotected account. Where availability is business-critical, additionally subscribe to Shield Advanced and enroll each resource with shield:CreateProtection — CloudFront, Application or Classic Load Balancer, Global Accelerator, Route 53 hosted zone, or an Elastic IP (also how an EC2 instance or Network Load Balancer is protected, by association). Front API Gateway or a Lambda function URL with CloudFront, since neither is a protectable type. Use AWS Firewall Manager to enroll org-wide rather than per account, and register for SRT proactive engagement.

controls.q: Is the audit trail that records agent and model activity protected against tampering, deletion, and retention-shortening — including by a compromised account administrator — where it actually lives, in CloudWatch Logs as well as CloudTrail?
controls.h: Most of the substantive agent audit record — input/output prompts, reasoning traces, tool invocations, session spans, and AgentCore Memory data-plane events — is delivered to CloudWatch Log groups, not CloudTrail, and CloudWatch Logs has no S3-style object lock. Individual log events are already append-only; the realistic tamper vectors are deleting the log group/stream or shortening retention. Look for log-group deletion protection, an SCP restricting delete/retention actions to a named provisioning role, KMS encryption, and an authoritative copy forwarded to a separate log-archive account or WORM store.
controls.ev: Log-group deletion-protection / SCP configuration + CloudTrail log-file validation status
controls.rec: Protect the agent audit trail where it actually lives. The substantive records — input/output prompts, reasoning traces, tool invocations, session spans, and AgentCore Memory data-plane events (CreateEvent/DeleteEvent/RetrieveMemoryRecords) — are delivered to CloudWatch Log groups (e.g. /aws/bedrock-agentcore/runtimes/*, aws/spans, and Bedrock model-invocation log groups), which have no native WORM; log events are already append-only, so the real tamper vectors are deleting the log group or stream, shortening retention, disabling the protection itself, and cutting the forwarding path. Close all four: enable log-group deletion protection (PutLogGroupDeletionProtection, or deletionProtectionEnabled at CreateLogGroup), which blocks every deletion operation on the group until it is explicitly disabled, and attach an AWS Organizations SCP denying logs:DeleteLogGroup, logs:DeleteLogStream, logs:PutRetentionPolicy, logs:PutLogGroupDeletionProtection and logs:DeleteSubscriptionFilter on the agent log groups except a single named provisioning role — omit the last two and an administrator simply turns protection off or deletes the filter forwarding the copy. Two details decide whether that SCP works at all: DeleteLogStream authorizes on the log-stream ARN, so its Resource needs the log-group ARN plus a trailing :log-stream:* rather than the log-group ARN alone, and no logs action defines a service-specific condition key, so scope the provisioning-role exception on aws:PrincipalArn — a Deny conditioned on a key the action does not define never matches and fails open, granting exactly what it was written to block. Encrypt log data with a customer-managed KMS key. For true immutability, forward those log groups to an S3 bucket with Object Lock (compliance mode) in a separate Log Archive account using a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter to Amazon Data Firehose rather than CreateExportTask: an account can run only one export task at a time, and AWS explicitly recommends subscriptions over repeated exports for continuous archiving. For the API/control-plane trail, enable AWS CloudTrail log-file integrity validation and Object Lock on the CloudTrail bucket.

controls.q: Is a threat-detection capability actively monitoring the AI account/environment for known malicious activity (e.g., credential compromise, unusual API calls)?

controls.rec: Enable Amazon GuardDuty across all accounts hosting AI workloads with GuardDuty AI Protection turned on. Credit it with what it actually detects: AI Protection analyzes CloudTrail data events from Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon SageMaker AI through a service-linked CloudTrail channel it creates for you, and it produces exactly three finding types — Impact:IAMUser/AnomalousModelInvocation, Impact:IAMUser/CostHarvesting and Impact:IAMUser/PromptInjection.Direct. Credential compromise is not among them; that detection comes from GuardDuty foundational CloudTrail analysis, which is a separate capability, so keep foundational GuardDuty enabled rather than assuming the AI plan subsumes it. Route findings into AWS Security Hub for a single view and review them on a defined cadence. Pair this runtime threat detection with the posture side: in Security Hub CSPM enable the GA 'AI Security Best Practices' standard (arn:aws:securityhub:<region>::standards/ai-security-best-practices/v/1.0.0) — a curated, AI-specific control set that continuously flags deployed AI resources (Bedrock, SageMaker, AgentCore) deviating from best practices such as network isolation, encryption at rest/in transit, VPC placement, KMS key usage, and private-registry requirements — alongside AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, and use Security Hub CSPM central configuration from the delegated administrator to enforce these standards org-wide across every AI-workload account and Region. GuardDuty finds active threats; the AI Security Best Practices standard finds misconfigurations before they are exploited.

controls.q: Are attempts to manipulate a model through its input (prompt injection, jailbreak patterns) detected and logged as security-relevant events?
controls.h: Confirm there is a mechanism (guardrail, filter, or monitoring rule) that flags suspicious input patterns as distinct, reviewable events.
controls.ev: Detection rule + example flagged event
controls.rec: Enable the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails prompt attack filter to detect jailbreak and prompt-injection inputs, and use the Standard tier if you need prompt leakage — leakage detection is Standard-tier only, so a Classic-tier guardrail does not provide it. Mark untrusted input so the filter evaluates the user turn rather than your own instructions: with InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream that means input tags, and with Converse it means a guardContent block — but note that once any guardContent block appears in the messages, the guardrail evaluates only those blocks and skips every other content block entirely, so tag every untrusted turn or none. Log each intervention (GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED) via model invocation logging and let GuardDuty AI Protection raise Impact:IAMUser/PromptInjection.Direct so manipulation attempts become distinct, reviewable security events. Then close the gap this control is most often failed by: with tool use, a guardrail passed in guardrailConfig does not evaluate messages[].content[].toolResult (tool results your application returns), toolConfig.tools[].toolSpec.description or .inputSchema (your tool definitions), or output.message.content[].toolUse.input (the arguments the model generates for a tool call) — no filter, prompt attack detection included, sees any of them. So indirect injection arriving through retrieved documents or tool output, and a coerced tool argument on the way out, are both invisible to the inline guardrail: run a separate ApplyGuardrail call over retrieved and tool-returned content before it re-enters the model context, and validate tool arguments at the tool boundary rather than trusting the guardrail to catch them.

controls.q: Can security telemetry from AI workloads be correlated with the rest of the organization's detection and SIEM pipeline, rather than living in an isolated silo?
controls.h: Verify AI workload logs/alerts flow into the same central detection pipeline used for the rest of the environment.
controls.ev: SIEM/pipeline ingestion configuration for AI telemetry
controls.rec: Use AWS Security Hub as the single aggregation point (GuardDuty AI Protection findings integrate automatically) and stream findings, plus Bedrock model invocation logs and CloudTrail events, via Amazon EventBridge to Lambda or Amazon Data Firehose into the central SIEM (e.g., Amazon OpenSearch Service or a partner SIEM) so AI telemetry is correlated with the rest of the environment instead of siloed. Where the destination would otherwise be a bespoke data store, prefer CloudWatch pipelines as the centralized analytics layer: it ingests AWS vended logs org-wide (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, WAF) plus third-party sources, applies up to 20 built-in processors to parse, enrich, filter and standardize each event, and lands output that stays compatible with Logs Insights, Logs Anomaly Detection and Live Tail — and from there export to Apache Iceberg S3 Tables for Athena or an existing SIEM. It removes the ETL pipeline this control otherwise implies, and keeps one copy of the data rather than one per tool. controls.q: For autonomous agents, is there a tested ability to detect and automatically contain runaway or looping behavior before it causes broad impact?
controls.h: Confirm a control (rate limit, circuit breaker, anomaly-triggered pause) exists and has been exercised for agents behaving outside expected bounds.
controls.ev: Containment control configuration + test/exercise record
controls.rec: Alarm on the metrics that exist. In the AWS/Bedrock namespace, dimensioned by ModelId, you get Invocations, InvocationLatency, TimeToFirstToken, InvocationThrottles, InvocationClientErrors, InvocationServerErrors, InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount — there is no loop or recursion metric, so a runaway agent must be inferred rather than read off a counter: use CloudWatch anomaly-detection alarms, or metric-math alarms on invocation rate and InputTokenCount per session, instead of a single static threshold. EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage exists but AWS states plainly that it is an approximation and must not be used as the sole indicator for quota use or capacity planning, so do not build the circuit breaker on it. Check the namespace matches your endpoint too: bedrock-mantle publishes to AWS/BedrockMantle with different metric names (Inferences, TotalInputTokens), so alarms written against AWS/Bedrock will not fire on that traffic at all. Trigger EventBridge from those alarms to a Lambda auto-pause or SNS escalation. For the hard stop, AWS Step Functions gives you duration natively — TimeoutSeconds on each Task state and on the state machine, plus HeartbeatSeconds so a stalled tool call fails rather than hanging — but it has no native tool-call-count or token-budget limit: carry the call count and token spend in the execution state and gate them in a Choice state, backed by an AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store emergency off-switch. Then exercise the containment path via a game day, because an untested circuit breaker is a claim rather than a control.

controls.q: Are coordination-level metrics for multi-agent workflows — inter-agent message rates, per-agent-pair error rates, workflow execution frequency, and communication topology — baselined and alarmed on, rather than only each agent's own health and error metrics?
controls.h: Distinct from per-agent behavioral monitoring (AIR-ACR-OBS-05, AIR-SLF-AGT-06) and from distributed tracing (AIR-SLF-AGT-04, AIR-ACR-OBS-01): tracing reconstructs one request after the fact, and per-agent alarms watch one agent's own telemetry. The unit of measurement here is the coordination itself — the pair, the workflow, the graph. Look for those metrics published as CloudWatch custom metrics, a baseline established during normal operation with anomaly detection on top, and an alert when an agent begins communicating with a peer it has never communicated with before.
controls.ev: Coordination metric definitions per workflow + an anomaly-detection alarm on a per-agent-pair metric
controls.rec: Publish the coordination measurements as CloudWatch custom metrics, dimensioned by agent pair and by workflow rather than by agent alone: inter-agent message rate, workflow execution frequency, agent response latency, and error rate per sending/receiving pair. Collect those metrics through a period of normal operation to establish a baseline, then enable CloudWatch anomaly detection on each so the alarm threshold follows the workflow's own pattern instead of a hand-picked number that is wrong for every other workflow. Derive the communication topology from AgentCore Observability session, trace, and span data together with A2A message events, and alert when the observed topology diverges from the documented trust-boundary architecture — a new edge in the graph is the cheapest available signal that one agent has been redirected. Correlate the coordination alarms with GuardDuty findings against the agents' execution roles in Security Hub, so credential misuse detected at the account layer and anomalous coordination detected at the workflow layer are read as one incident rather than two unrelated tickets. Schedule CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over the agent log groups for coordination patterns that are not expressible as a single metric — a workflow completing without one of its usual participants, or a retry storm confined to one agent pair.

controls.q: Is adversarial and penetration testing of the agent run against a scoped test environment with its own credentials, memory store, and tool endpoints, rather than against the production agent?
controls.h: AIR-FND-DET-08 asks whether the testing happens; this asks where. An agent under test executes the exploit — it really calls the tool, really sends the message, really writes to memory — so an injection payload that lands in a shared memory store shapes a real user's answer later. Look for a documented in-scope and out-of-scope list per assessment, a test agent instance with its own memory store and tool endpoints, external dependencies mocked or sandboxed, test credentials held in Secrets Manager and rotated after each cycle rather than long-lived and shared, network and IAM segmentation that stops the test instance reaching production resources, and test logs landing in your own account.
controls.ev: Per-assessment scope document + isolated test environment definition + evidence of credential rotation after a cycle
controls.rec: Stand up a test environment that replicates the agent architecture with its own AgentCore Memory resource, its own tool endpoints, and its own permission boundaries, so an attack payload that succeeds cannot persist into the memory a production user's session retrieves. Define and record the scope before each assessment — which endpoints, tools, data stores, and agent-to-agent paths are in scope, and which are explicitly excluded — so a test that reaches something unintended is detectable as a scope breach rather than absorbed as noise. Issue the test agent its own credentials from Secrets Manager and rotate them after each testing cycle, so a credential captured during a test grants nothing afterwards and no test credential outlives the assessment that needed it. Enforce the boundary at two layers rather than one: network segmentation so the test environment has no route to production endpoints, and an Organizations SCP on the test account denying access to production resources, so a misconfigured test agent is contained by policy even when the network is wrong. Capture the test agent's own logs into CloudWatch in your account and review them after each assessment against the recorded scope, so what the test actually touched is evidence rather than assumption.

controls.q: When an agent is contained automatically, is its state captured for forensics before its credentials are revoked, so the evidence needed to investigate survives the containment?
controls.h: AIR-FND-DET-07 asks whether containment is automatic and AIR-SLF-AGT-07 whether a credential kill-switch exists; this asks about the order of operations, which is where the evidence is lost. Look for an automation that snapshots the agent's current memory, active sessions, and pending operations to S3 first, then revokes credentials by attaching a deny-all policy to the agent's role while preserving the role itself for analysis, then broadcasts the quarantine event so dependent workflows trip their circuit breakers. Stopping the process first loses in-memory state; deleting the role destroys the forensic subject. Look too for restoration gated behind a runbook that needs more than one person, so a contained agent is not re-enabled before the investigation concludes.
controls.ev: Containment automation showing snapshot-before-revoke ordering + a captured snapshot from an exercise
controls.rec: Trigger containment from an EventBridge rule on the anomaly alarm into a single automation — a Lambda function or an SSM Automation runbook — so the ordering of the steps is a property of the automation rather than of whoever responds. Make the first action the snapshot: write the agent's current memory contents, active session identifiers, and pending operations to S3, with Object Lock where the snapshot has to be defensible later, because none of that state survives the revocation that follows. Only then revoke: attach a deny-all inline policy to the agent's role conditioned on aws:TokenIssueTime so existing sessions are invalidated, and keep the role in place — deleting it removes the very configuration the investigation needs to read. Broadcast the quarantine as an EventBridge event so peer agents and orchestrating workflows route to their fallback paths rather than retrying a principal that will now deny everything. Gate restoration behind an SSM Automation runbook whose aws:approve step names the Approvers and sets MinRequiredApprovals above 1 — the parameter is optional and 'the system defaults to one', so a runbook that lists several approvers but omits it resumes on the first approval and is a single-person gate that reads like a multi-person one. Then exercise the whole sequence as a fault-injection experiment rather than a tabletop: an AWS FIS experiment template whose aws:ssm:start-automation-execution action invokes the containment runbook by documentArn, with aws:cloudwatch:assert-alarm-state asserting the detection alarm actually reached ALARM, so the exercise proves the trigger fired and not merely that the runbook runs when a human starts it. Put a CloudWatch-alarm stop condition on the experiment template and rehearse in pre-production first, because FIS 'carries out real actions on real AWS resources' and a stopped experiment cannot be resumed — an experiment that revokes an agent's credentials for real needs the abort path that a tabletop does not. Grant the FIS experiment role ssm:StartAutomationExecution, ssm:GetAutomationExecution and ssm:StopAutomationExecution — plus iam:PassRole only if the containment document assumes a role — and size the exercise around the mismatch between the two timeouts: aws:ssm:start-automation-execution caps maxDuration at 12 hours, while an aws:approve step defaults to a 7-day timeout, so the approval-gated restoration half either needs approvers on standby inside the window or its own timeoutSeconds for the exercise, or the experiment expires while the runbook is still waiting and the rehearsal proves nothing.

controls.q: Is there a named owner accountable for the security of each AI workload in production?
controls.h: Confirm each production AI workload has an identifiable accountable owner, not a diffuse 'the team' answer.
controls.ev: Ownership mapping per production AI workload
controls.rec: Assign a named accountable owner to every production AI workload and encode it as an owner tag on the workload's resources, so accountability attaches to the resources themselves rather than to a diffuse 'the team' answer, and keep the value resolvable to a person or an on-call rotation. Be precise about what makes that tag stick, because the obvious mechanism does not: AWS states that a tag policy's basic compliance rules do not enforce tag compliance on resources that are created without tags, and that the capability does not enforce missing tag keys. What an AWS Organizations tag policy does give you is (a) enforced_for, which standardizes the VALUE and capitalization of owner when a tagging operation supplies one, on the resource types you list, and (b) a required-tag-key capability whose reporting mode is enforced only for infrastructure-as-code tools (AWS CloudFormation, Terraform, Pulumi). Requiring the tag on an arbitrary create call therefore needs an SCP that Denies when aws:RequestTag/owner is Null, enumerating the resource-creating actions that actually declare the key -- support is per ACTION, not per service, so a Deny written against bedrock:* silently never matches and fails OPEN. For drift, read the organization-wide tag-policy compliance report (Organizations > Tag policies, or resourcegroupstaggingapi list-required-tags) rather than the AWS Resource Groups console, which does not report noncompliance for a missing required tag key.

controls.q: For autonomous agents that can take real-world or transactional actions, is there a governance sign-off step required before granting that level of autonomy?
controls.h: Confirm a defined approval gate (security + business sign-off) exists before an agent is authorized to act rather than only answer or retrieve.
controls.ev: Sign-off record for an agent granted acting autonomy
controls.rec: Require a documented security + business sign-off gate before any agent is granted acting (transactional) autonomy beyond answer/retrieve, and retain each approval decision and its rationale as the sign-off record. You can operationalize the gate with the AWS Agent Registry approval workflow in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now generally available under the agent-registry API namespace: a publisher submits the agent as a record, Amazon EventBridge notifies approvers when it is submitted for approval, and a curator or administrator approves it before it becomes discoverable, with AWS CloudTrail logging the registry API calls. Two things turn that from a gate into a formality if missed. First, approval only gates anything while auto-approval is left OFF - with auto-approval enabled a submitted record moves straight to Approved and becomes searchable with no human in the loop - so verify that setting rather than inferring review from the workflow's existence. Second, registry approval governs catalog discoverability and reuse, not the grant of transactional autonomy itself, so provision the technical authorization to act (least-privilege IAM and AgentCore Identity permissions, plus the run-time approval gate of AIR-FND-GOV-09) only after sign-off.

controls.q: Are the agents, tools, and MCP servers that teams can discover and reuse gated by an approval/curation step, so only vetted resources become discoverable across the organization?
controls.h: Beyond simply inventorying what exists, confirm there is a curated catalog with an approval workflow: a resource (agent, tool, MCP server, skill) is not discoverable or reusable org-wide until reviewed and approved, and can be deprecated/removed. Distinct from a plain asset inventory (which records what exists) and from agent-identity enumeration.
controls.ev: Curated agent/tool registry with an enforced approval workflow
controls.rec: Use AWS Agent Registry in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore as the curated catalog. It is generally available under the agent-registry API namespace, so scope IAM policies to that namespace: support for the public-preview bedrock-agentcore namespace is being discontinued on 17 September 2026, and a policy still written against the preview namespace will stop authorizing registry calls. A publisher submits records for MCP servers, agents, tools, skills, or custom resources, and a curator or administrator approves each record before it becomes discoverable org-wide - and can deprecate it or remove it from discoverability at any time. That approval is a real curation gate only while auto-approval is OFF: with auto-approval enabled, a submitted record moves directly to Approved status and becomes visible in search results shortly after, so the vetting this control asks about rests on that setting, not on the registry being in use. Because the registry catalogs metadata, register resources regardless of where they run (AgentCore Runtime/Gateway-hosted, other-provider, or on-prem) by entering records manually or via URL-based discovery from a live MCP server or agent endpoint, so the approval workflow spans all sources, with Amazon EventBridge notifying curators when records are submitted for approval and AWS CloudTrail logging registry API calls. Scope precisely - the registry gates catalog discoverability and reuse but does not by itself stop teams from deploying or running unregistered shadow agents, so pair it with an organizational policy that only registry-approved resources may be consumed.

controls.q: For agent actions that carry material financial, legal, or safety impact, is a human approval required at run time above a defined threshold, rather than the agent executing them autonomously?
controls.h: Distinct from a one-time deployment sign-off (AIR-FND-GOV-07): confirm run-time thresholds (e.g. transaction value, data-deletion scope, external commitments) route the specific action to a human before it executes, so an agent cannot autonomously approve a high-value action that no one reviewed.
controls.ev: Configured approval threshold + a held/approved high-impact action example
controls.rec: Enforce a run-time human-approval gate for actions above a defined threshold (transaction value, data-deletion scope, external commitments) so the agent cannot autonomously execute high-impact actions. Implement it as an AWS Step Functions human-approval task using the .waitForTaskToken service-integration pattern: the state machine pauses at that task until SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure is called with the task token, which an SNS notification or API Gateway approve/reject link supplies, so only above-threshold actions wait on a human while low-impact actions proceed. Two details decide whether the gate holds up in production. Set TimeoutSeconds or a heartbeat on the waiting task - a task waiting on a token with neither can stay open up to the one-year maximum execution duration, which reads as 'pending approval' indefinitely rather than failing. And the callback must come from a principal in the SAME AWS account as the state machine, so a cross-account approval UI has to assume a role in the workflow account instead of calling SendTaskSuccess directly. Amazon A2I is an alternative for ML-prediction confidence thresholds, but only where it is already in use: A2I entered maintenance mode in July 2026 and no longer accepts new customers, and requests from accounts that were not already using it fail with an InvalidParameterException.

controls.q: For the agent actions that carry the highest impact, do two or more reviewers each decide without seeing the others' decisions, with disagreement escalating to a senior reviewer rather than defaulting to approval?
controls.h: One step beyond AIR-FND-GOV-09's single approval gate. Look for a top risk tier that requires more than one approver; notifications that omit the other reviewers' decisions, because a reviewer who can see an existing approval anchors to it and independence is lost; reviewers drawn from different teams or reporting lines; a split decision that routes to escalation rather than being settled by whoever approved; and each individual decision recorded with reviewer identity, timestamp, and rationale.
controls.ev: Multi-reviewer workflow definition + a logged split decision that escalated
controls.rec: Model the review as a Step Functions Parallel state with one branch per required reviewer, so each reviewer is solicited concurrently and no reviewer's task waits on another's outcome. Deliver each reviewer's request over SNS with the proposed action and its context but without the other reviewers' decisions or identities, so the second reviewer is not anchored by the first — a shared thread turns two reviewers into one reviewer and a witness. Resolve the branches in a consensus function: require unanimity where two reviewers are configured, and majority with mandatory escalation of the dissent where three or more are, so a disagreement is never discarded silently. Route any split decision to a senior reviewer who sees all prior decisions and rationales in full, and make the default on escalation timeout a denial, because an approval that arrives by expiry is not a review. Draw the reviewers for a given operation from different teams or reporting lines, managed through IAM Identity Center groups so reviewer eligibility is an identity-source fact rather than a list maintained inside the workflow. Persist each individual decision — reviewer identity, timestamp, decision, and rationale — to S3 tagged with the agent operation id, with Object Lock where the approval record must be provable after the fact rather than merely present.

controls.q: Is the queue of agent decisions awaiting human review prioritized by impact and monitored for backlog, per-reviewer load, and rubber-stamp indicators, rather than arriving as one undifferentiated stream?
controls.h: The failure mode is silent: a review gate that exists in the architecture and is rubber-stamped in practice scores the same as one that works. Look for review requests classified by impact — data sensitivity, reversibility, first time this agent has attempted the operation, time sensitivity — rather than first-in-first-out; alarms on backlog per priority tier, time-to-assignment, and time-to-decision; a cap on concurrent assignments per reviewer; and review-quality metrics (average review time, approval rate, reversal rate) watched for the short-review-time-with-high-approval-rate pattern that shows up when volume outruns attention.
controls.ev: Priority classification scheme + CloudWatch alarms on queue backlog and on review-quality metrics
controls.rec: Ingest review requests through SQS but do not expect the queue to order them: standard queues deliver in best-effort order and offer no priority semantics, so classification has to sit above the queue rather than inside it. Have a Lambda consumer classify each request by impact — data sensitivity, whether the action is reversible, whether this agent has performed it before, and how time-sensitive it is — and write it to a DynamoDB table whose sort key orders by priority tier then submission time, so the highest-impact item pending longest is always the next one served. Serve reviewers through an assignment function that queries the highest-priority unassigned item and marks it assigned, and cap concurrent assignments per reviewer per window so load is distributed rather than pooled on whoever answers fastest. Alarm in CloudWatch on backlog depth per priority tier, time-to-assignment, and time-to-decision, and escalate automatically when a high-priority item ages past its threshold instead of waiting for a reviewer to notice. Publish review-quality metrics — average review time, approval rate, and reversal rate per reviewer — and alarm on the combination of falling review time with rising approval rate during high volume, which is what overload looks like in the data before anyone reports it.

controls.q: When an agent action is routed to a human for approval, does the reviewer see signals independent of the agent — a grounding or policy-check result, manipulation-warning flags, and how this request compares with similar past ones — alongside the proposed action?
controls.h: Pair with AIR-FND-GOV-09: an approval gate with no context is the rubber-stamp anti-pattern in its purest form. Which signal is useful depends on the review's shape. Where the reviewer is judging whether the agent's recommendation is correct, the agent's own grounding score is informative. Where the reviewer is a policy gate on an action the agent has already committed to, the agent's self-reported confidence is close to worthless and the signal must come from something the agent does not author — a grounding or automated-reasoning check, anomaly detection, or the manipulation flags raised by input validation. Look for each number presented with a plain-language statement of what it means, and for similar past decisions surfaced so a first-of-its-kind request is visibly unusual.
controls.ev: Reviewer notification or screen showing the grounding/policy-check result, manipulation flags, and comparable past decisions
controls.rec: Where the reviewer judges whether the agent is right, surface the Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding score with the request, and present it as a sentence about what it measures rather than a bare number — a reviewer who does not know what 0.7 means will treat every score as approval. Where the reviewer is a policy gate rather than a judge of correctness, surface an automated reasoning check result as context — that the action passed a named policy check, and when — and keep it as input to the human decision rather than promoting it to the decision itself. Carry the manipulation-warning flags raised during input validation — prompt-injection detections, untrusted content in the context window, an unusual instruction source — through to the reviewer's view, because the reviewer is the control that catches what the filter only suspected. Persist each decision with its scores in DynamoDB, query comparable past decisions for the same operation type when a new request arrives, and flag a request whose confidence deviates from the historical average for that operation — the deviation is the signal, not the absolute value. Surface the AgentCore Evaluations trend for the agent alongside the request, so a reviewer can see whether this agent's recent judgment has been degrading rather than assessing each request in isolation.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — model access, invocation & inference isolation
controls.q: Is cross-region or cross-account model invocation explicitly controlled, rather than left to default routing behavior?
controls.h: Verify inference requests are constrained to approved regions/accounts, especially where inference profiles route across regions.
controls.ev: Inference-profile/region configuration review
controls.rec: Use Service Control Policies to restrict which Regions Bedrock inference actions (bedrock:InvokeModel*, bedrock:CreateModelInvocationJob) are permitted in, ensuring the allowed set includes every destination Region of any cross-Region inference (CRIS) profile in use, since a blocked destination Region fails the request. Prefer geographic inference profiles over global ones to keep routing within a defined geography for data-residency, and scope inference-profile ARNs in IAM. Handle Global profiles as a distinct case, because they change what aws:RequestedRegion holds: a Region-restricting SCP must include the literal value unspecified in its allowed list or every Global call is denied, and the way to deliberately disable Global routing while leaving in-Region and geographic inference working is Deny bedrock:* with StringEquals aws:RequestedRegion unspecified plus ArnLike bedrock:InferenceProfileArn arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/global.*. Do not write that condition against the value global — one sentence of the AWS page says the service sets the field to global while its three policy examples, the SCP guidance and the comparison table all use unspecified, and a Deny on the wrong value fails open, so confirm in your own account that the Deny denies. Two consequences to plan for: CRIS can route to Regions you have not manually enabled, so Region enablement is not the control here; and for models running under default or provider_data_share retention, retained inputs and outputs are stored in the destination Region (see AIR-BDR-MDL-10), so a data-residency review has to cover the whole destination set. If the Region-deny SCP is managed by AWS Control Tower, extend it through Control Tower rather than editing it directly, which causes drift.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — model access, invocation & inference isolation
controls.q: Is there a technical control preventing use of unapproved third-party or marketplace models alongside first-party foundation models?
controls.h: Look for allow-list enforcement that distinguishes approved first-party/marketplace models from anything a developer could otherwise enable.
controls.ev: Marketplace/model-access control configuration
controls.rec: Third-party Marketplace models (for example Anthropic Claude, Cohere, Stability AI) require an AWS Marketplace subscription, so restrict aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe, and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions via SCP/IAM — using the aws-marketplace:ProductId condition key to allow only approved product IDs — to stop developers self-enabling unapproved models. Keep ProductId on the Allow side, as AWS's own example does, and do not build a Deny on it: the key is declared per-action only on AcceptAgreementRequest and CreateAgreementRequest in AWS's generated IAM service model, so a Deny conditioned on it may never match and would fail open, whereas an over-restrictive Allow fails closed and is visible. A Subscribe restriction does not block usage on its own for three separate reasons: Bedrock automatically initiates the subscription in the background on a role's first invocation of a third-party model; once the model is enabled at account level any role can invoke it with no AWS Marketplace permissions at all; and a subscription taken in one Region makes the model requestable in every Region where it is available even where Subscribe is denied. The definitive technical control is therefore the Deny-based bedrock:InvokeModel allow-list from AIR-BDR-MDL-01 scoped to approved foundation-model ARNs, which is also the only option for providers not sold through AWS Marketplace (Amazon, Meta, Mistral AI, DeepSeek, Qwen, OpenAI) because they have no product ID to scope. Where the EULA has to be reviewed before use, follow AWS's stated sequence: block model access with SCP/IAM first, review the terms, then open access only for approved models — invoking a third-party model is itself acceptance of its EULA.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — model access, invocation & inference isolation
controls.q: Is the compute capacity backing model inference isolated per workload or tenant, so one workload's usage cannot exhaust capacity needed by another?
controls.h: Check for provisioned throughput, dedicated capacity, or per-tenant quotas rather than a single shared pool with no isolation.
controls.ev: Capacity allocation / quota configuration per workload
controls.rec: Purchase Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput (CreateProvisionedModelThroughput, allocating model units per workload) to give latency-sensitive or tenant-isolated workloads dedicated inference capacity separate from the shared on-demand pool; custom and imported models can be served with either on-demand custom model deployments (CreateCustomModelDeployment, available in select Regions such as US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon)) or Provisioned Throughput, so reserve Provisioned Throughput for steady high-volume or latency-sensitive workloads. Where on-demand is used, note that Bedrock TPM/RPM Service Quotas are enforced per-model, per-Region, per-account only — they cap the account as a whole and cannot isolate one tenant/role from another, and a model's bedrock-runtime quota is shared across every inference API (InvokeModel, Converse, Responses, Chat Completions), so splitting tenants across APIs isolates nothing. Do not assume an RPM ceiling exists to lean on: RPM is enforced for some bedrock-runtime models and not others (Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 and Claude Opus 4.8, for example, have no RPM quota and are governed by token quotas alone), and the bedrock-mantle endpoint is counted separately again, with distinct input-token and output-token per-minute quotas rather than a single combined TPM. For genuine per-tenant capacity isolation on on-demand, use Provisioned Throughput (dedicated model units) or separate AWS accounts (independent quota pools), and use application inference profiles / IAM-principal attribution plus CloudWatch quota-consumption alarms to track and alert on per-workload usage. Note that cross-Region inference profiles do not support Provisioned Throughput, so a workload cannot have both CRIS routing and dedicated capacity on the same call path.

controls.q: For high-autonomy use cases, can inference be traced end to end from the invoking identity through to the specific model version and response, for forensic reconstruction?
controls.h: Verify logs link caller identity, model version, and response together so an incident can be reconstructed without gaps.
controls.ev: End-to-end trace example for a single invocation

Centralize both in CloudTrail Lake or query via Athena for forensic reconstruction. Check which CloudTrail category your APIs fall into before relying on this: InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse and ConverseStream are logged as management events and are therefore captured by default, but InvokeModelWithBidirectionalStream, StartAsyncInvoke, GetAsyncInvoke, InvokeAgent and InvokeInlineAgent are data events, which CloudTrail does not log unless you add advanced event selectors for the AWS::Bedrock::Model, AWS::Bedrock::AsyncInvoke, AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias and AWS::Bedrock::InlineAgent resource types — a high-autonomy agent using those paths leaves no trail at all until those selectors exist. If any traffic goes to the bedrock-mantle endpoint, cover it too: it is a separate endpoint with its own CloudTrail integration and its own IAM action namespace, so a trail scoped to bedrock-runtime does not see it.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — model access, invocation & inference isolation
controls.q: Are the production prompts that drive model behavior managed as controlled, versioned artifacts in a central catalog, rather than hardcoded ad hoc in application code?
controls.h: Prompts are executable logic: a changed system prompt can alter safety behavior or leak instructions. Confirm prompts are stored centrally, versioned with an immutable production snapshot, access-controlled, and encrypted — not free-floating strings edited inline and shipped without review.
controls.ev: Prompt catalog + immutable production version reference + access/encryption configuration
controls.rec: Treat prompts as code artifacts — AWS prescriptive guidance for agentic AI BP 2.2 accepts either a managed prompt registry or Git-based prompt-as-code (a hybrid of the two is its advanced pattern), so pick one and govern it; Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management (BedrockAgent API, bedrock-agent-2023-06-05) is the managed-registry option and is what the rest of this recommendation describes. Author and iterate a prompt with CreatePrompt/UpdatePrompt, then cut an immutable production snapshot with CreatePromptVersion and reference that specific numeric version at runtime (never the mutable DRAFT), so a prompt change goes through review and a versioned release instead of an inline edit. Encrypt each prompt with a customer-managed KMS key via customerEncryptionKeyArn on CreatePrompt, and scope the prompt-management IAM actions (bedrock:CreatePrompt, bedrock:CreatePromptVersion, bedrock:UpdatePrompt, bedrock:GetPrompt, bedrock:ListPrompts, bedrock:DeletePrompt) so only an approved release role can modify catalog entries. Grant runtime roles read only — but note that reading is not enough to use a cataloged prompt at inference time: bedrock:RenderPrompt is a separate permission-only action that renders a Prompt Management prompt for InvokeModel/Converse, so it belongs in the runtime role and must not be left in the release role by accident. RenderPrompt is a CloudTrail data event, so add an advanced event selector for the AWS::Bedrock::Prompt resource type if you want an audit trail of which prompt version actually served traffic. Pair the catalog with change review and prompt-injection-resistant construction (delimit untrusted user input from system instructions) so the governed prompt is also a hardened one.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — model access, invocation & inference isolation
controls.q: Are Amazon Bedrock API keys governed so production access uses short-term keys, and long-term keys — which create a standing IAM user with a static credential — cannot be created without an expiration or used in production?
controls.h: Bedrock API keys are a bearer-token path to model invocation that bypasses the usual role-assumption flow. Check whether long-term keys exist in the account (they appear as IAM users, conventionally named BedrockAPIKey-*, holding a service-specific credential for bedrock.amazonaws.com), whether any were created with no expiration, and whether a preventive policy caps key lifetime and blocks long-term-key usage in production.
controls.ev: Inventory of bedrock.amazonaws.com service-specific credentials with expiration dates + SCP/IAM policy capping key age and restricting bearerTokenType
controls.rec: Treat long-term Bedrock API keys as static credentials and govern them preventively. A long-term key is an IAM service-specific credential for ServiceName bedrock.amazonaws.com attached to a dedicated IAM user (created via CreateServiceSpecificCredential, with AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess attached when generated from the console) and can be configured with no expiration, so it is a standing bearer token outside the short-lived-credential model of AIR-FND-IAM-03. Cap lifetime with an SCP/IAM policy on iam:CreateServiceSpecificCredential conditioned on iam:ServiceSpecificCredentialServiceName equal to bedrock.amazonaws.com plus NumericLessThanEquals on iam:ServiceSpecificCredentialAgeDays (for example 90), which forces an expiry rather than an indefinite key. Keep long-term keys out of production by denying their use where it matters, and pair each action with the condition key its own endpoint publishes: bedrock:CallWithBearerToken takes bedrock:BearerTokenType, and bedrock-mantle:CallWithBearerToken takes bedrock-mantle:BearerTokenType — writing one Deny over both actions with only the bedrock: key silently fails open on the Mantle endpoint, because a condition on a key an action does not define is ignored and enforces nothing. With values SHORT_TERM and LONG_TERM, Deny on LONG_TERM in production accounts while still permitting short-term keys, which are SigV4-derived and inherit the calling principal's permissions. This is worth doing even where model access is already locked down, because bedrock:CallWithBearerToken is a required action across the Bedrock control-plane API and not only the inference operations, so a long-term key is a static credential for far more than InvokeModel — though it cannot reach Agents, Data Automation or InvokeModelWithBidirectionalStream, which do not accept API keys at all. Inventory existing keys with iam:ListServiceSpecificCredentials per user and revoke with UpdateServiceSpecificCredential (Status=Inactive), ResetServiceSpecificCredential, or DeleteServiceSpecificCredential. Note the audit asymmetry when investigating: long-term key creation is recorded in CloudTrail, but short-term keys are generated client-side and their creation is not, and the key value itself is never logged for either type.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — model access, invocation & inference isolation
controls.q: Is the Amazon Bedrock data-retention mode explicitly set and pinned org-wide, so no account or project can opt into sharing prompts and outputs with a model provider?
controls.h: New accounts and projects default to the inherit mode, not zero retention, so an account that has never been configured is not automatically at zero retention. Check the account's effective mode (GetAccountDataRetention), confirm it was explicitly set rather than left at inherit, and confirm a preventive policy blocks any principal — including an account administrator — from setting provider_data_share at either the account or the project scope.
controls.ev: GetAccountDataRetention output showing the explicitly-set mode + SCP denying non-approved modes on both the bedrock and bedrock-mantle write actions
controls.rec: Set the retention mode explicitly and pin it preventively; do not rely on defaults. The mode acts as a ceiling, not a floor — a model whose allowed_modes include none still runs at zero retention regardless of the account setting — but inherit is the default for new accounts and projects, so an unconfigured account has made no decision at all. Set each account with bedrock:PutAccountDataRetention (aws bedrock put-account-data-retention --mode none), whose valid values are default, none, provider_data_share and inherit, then attach an SCP that Denies the write actions unless the mode equals your approved value. Cover both endpoints, because they publish separate condition keys: Deny bedrock:PutAccountDataRetention on StringNotEquals bedrock:DataRetentionMode, and Deny bedrock-mantle:PutAccountDataRetention plus bedrock-mantle:CreateProject and bedrock-mantle:UpdateProject on StringNotEquals bedrock-mantle:DataRetentionMode — the project actions matter because bedrock-mantle allows a per-project override that would otherwise bypass the account-level setting. Verify with GetAccountDataRetention per account rather than by reading the SCP, and check a specific model's effective mode and allowed_modes to see which scope (project, account, or model default) is actually deciding. Both checks are API- or SDK-only, because there is no console UI for data retention at launch — an assessment that goes looking for a console setting will find nothing and wrongly record the control as absent. Understand the trade-off before pinning to none: models whose only allowed mode is provider_data_share (currently Claude Mythos 5 and Claude Fable 5) become unavailable org-wide, surfacing as status unavailable in the models list rather than as an invocation error, and on the Responses API store=true is rejected while background mode is unavailable — that is the intended consequence of requiring zero retention, not a misconfiguration. Where a specific model is genuinely needed under zero retention, the documented route is a per-account, per-model ZDR exception requested through your AWS account team (Anthropic manages eligibility for Claude models), after which none appears in that model's allowed_modes for the approved account only — so treat allowed_modes as an account-specific value to be read per account, not a fixed property of the model. Two residual limits to record rather than assume away: where cross-Region inference is enabled for a retaining model, retained inputs and outputs are stored in the destination Region that processed the request, so a data-residency review has to cover the whole destination set (see AIR-BDR-MDL-03); and AWS's abuse-detection page states, without qualifying it by retention mode, that apparent CSAM in image inputs is blocked and the flagged input or output may be stored and reviewed and reported to NCMEC — so none should not be presented to an auditor as an unqualified guarantee that no content is ever stored.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — model access, invocation & inference isolation
controls.q: When a model is fine-tuned or continued-pretrained on private data, is the risk that it memorizes and reproduces that data verbatim assessed and mitigated before the model serves production traffic?
controls.h: Distinct from filtering sensitive data out of prompts and responses (AIR-BDR-GRD-03): a customized model can emit training content it was never asked for, so an output filter is a backstop rather than the control. Confirm the training corpus was minimized and de-identified before customization, and that the resulting model was probed for regurgitation of identifiable records — not simply assumed safe because the source bucket was encrypted.
controls.ev: De-identification record for the customization corpus + extraction-probe results for the resulting model version
controls.rec: Treat a customized model as a potential disclosure path for its own training data, across all three customization types CreateModelCustomizationJob accepts (FINE_TUNING, CONTINUED_PRE_TRAINING, DISTILLATION). Before the job runs, minimize and de-identify the corpus — run Amazon Macie over the S3 training prefix and an Amazon Comprehend PII redaction job (StartPiiEntitiesDetectionJob with Mode ONLY_REDACTION), or AWS Glue sensitive-data detection, so identifiers are removed or tokenized rather than merely encrypted at rest, since encryption protects the bucket and not the model's weights. Point trainingDataConfig.s3Uri at the redaction job's output prefix, not the original: ONLY_REDACTION writes a redacted copy to the output location and leaves the input documents untouched, so a job still aimed at the source prefix trains on the raw corpus while the evidence file says redaction ran. Check which corpus the job actually reads, because trainingDataConfig also accepts invocationLogsConfig instead of an S3 URI — that path fine-tunes directly on your own model invocation logs, narrowed only by requestMetadataFilters, with usePromptResponse deciding whether model responses join the prompts, so there is no curated prefix to Macie-scan and production traffic becomes training data; for restricted data either exclude that path or move de-identification upstream to what gets logged (see AIR-BDR-MDL-02). After customization, probe the resulting model version for regurgitation before it takes production traffic: run a targeted extraction set (known records, rare identifiers, and prefix-completion prompts drawn from the training data) through the customized model and confirm it does not complete them verbatim, recording the run as evidence alongside the AIR-BDR-GRD-06 red-team cadence. Scope invocation of the customized model on the ARN it is actually reached by, which is not a foundation-model ARN: on-demand custom models are invoked with the custom model deployment's ARN as modelId (resource type custom-model-deployment, from CreateCustomModelDeployment), Provisioned Throughput ones with the provisioned-model ARN, and SageMaker-trained imports with imported-model — all three are accepted resource types on bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, so name the specific deployment ARN per tenant rather than wildcarding custom-model-deployment/*, and remember that an allow-list from AIR-BDR-MDL-01 written only over foundation-model ARNs neither authorizes nor restrains a customized model. Retain the Guardrail sensitive-information filter as a residual output backstop. AWS documents no native memorization-mitigation or differential-privacy option for Bedrock customization, so corpus minimization plus extraction testing is the enforceable part; the assessment answer should reflect that this is a process control with a testable artifact, not a service setting.

controls.q: Is a content-safety guardrail applied to model input and output for every production use case, rather than left optional per application?
controls.h: Confirm a guardrail (or equivalent content-safety layer) is attached and enforced on both the input and output path for production traffic.
controls.ev: Guardrail attachment confirmed on input and output path
controls.rec: Attach an Amazon Bedrock Guardrail to every production use case and enforce it on both the input and output path by passing guardrailIdentifier and guardrailVersion on each Converse or InvokeModel call — both are required together, and the request is rejected if contentType is not application/json. For self-hosted or third-party models that do not run through Bedrock inference, call the ApplyGuardrail API directly instead — once with source=INPUT before the model sees the prompt, and again with source=OUTPUT before the response reaches the user. Make enforcement mandatory rather than optional per application: deny bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream unless the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key matches your approved guardrail, so an application cannot simply omit the parameter.

config_rule.note: Periodic Lambda rule, NOT Guard: AWS Config does not record AWS::Bedrock::Agent or ::AgentAlias (its Bedrock types are ApplicationInferenceProfile, DataSource, FlowAlias, Guardrail, KnowledgeBase, Prompt), so there is no configuration item for a Guard policy to evaluate. The rule must call GetAgent/GetAgentAlias itself and report with put_evaluations.

controls.q: Are attempts to bypass safety controls through prompt injection or jailbreak techniques specifically detected, not just generic harmful-content filtering?
controls.h: Look for a dedicated prompt-attack/jailbreak detection capability distinct from topic or profanity filtering.
controls.ev: Prompt-attack detection configuration + example catch
controls.rec: Enable the dedicated Prompt Attack filter within the Guardrail content-filter policy (Standard tier, which adds prompt-leakage detection) to catch jailbreaks and prompt injections separately from topic and profanity filters; set the filter action to BLOCK and tune filter strength (high/medium/low) against production-like traffic. Input tagging is mandatory here, not a false-positive nicety: with InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream you must wrap the user-supplied portion in guardrail input tags (the amazon-bedrock-guardrails-guardContent tag named by amazon-bedrock-guardrailConfig tagSuffix) — with no tags, prompt attacks are not filtered for those calls at all, so an untagged prompt silently bypasses the filter it appears to have. With Converse and ConverseStream, mark the user turn with guardContent content blocks instead, since XML input tags apply only to the Invoke APIs. The filter reads message text only and never evaluates toolSpec, toolUse input or toolResult content, so screen tool payloads separately, and for multi-turn agents call the InvokeGuardrailChecks API each turn with its promptAttack check (JAILBREAK, PROMPT_INJECTION, PROMPT_LEAKAGE) on the current system and user messages.

controls.h: Confirm output filtering includes sensitive-data detection/redaction, not only topic-based content moderation.
controls.ev: Sensitive-data output filter configuration
controls.rec: Configure the Guardrail sensitive-information filter (sensitiveInformationPolicyConfig) with the required PII entity types (piiEntitiesConfig) set to BLOCK or ANONYMIZE on the output path, and add custom regexesConfig patterns for secrets, credentials, and internal identifiers not covered by the built-in PII types; enable the same checks on the input path to stop echoed exfiltration. controls.q: When a guardrail blocks or modifies a request, is that event logged as a security-relevant signal that feeds detection/monitoring?
controls.h: Verify guardrail intervention events are captured in logs/metrics reviewed by security, not silently dropped.
controls.ev: Guardrail intervention log/metric feeding monitoring
controls.rec: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging (to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3) so the full request/response and guardrail trace are captured; note the intervention signal differs by API — InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream return amazon-bedrock-guardrailAction (INTERVENED|NONE) plus the amazon-bedrock-trace block, while Converse/ConverseStream return stopReason=guardrail_intervened plus the trace.guardrail assessment. Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter that matches the intervention field, alarm on intervention spikes, and forward the invocation logs to your SIEM so guardrail interventions feed security detection instead of being silently dropped. Model invocation logging is off by default and covers only those four bedrock-runtime inference APIs, so it does not capture an intervention raised by ApplyGuardrail or InvokeGuardrailChecks — for those, log ApplyGuardrail calls (including an AccessDenied when a required guardrail was not passed) through CloudTrail, have the caller emit its own record of each detect-mode decision it acted on, and alarm on the guardrail CloudWatch metrics as well, so a workload that filters outside the inference call is not an unmonitored gap.

controls.ev: Action-level policy check configuration + example decision
controls.rec: Add an action-level authorization check that is independent of the language-output content filter: scope the agent's execution/service role with least-privilege IAM so it can only call approved tools and APIs, and for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore route every tool through the AgentCore Gateway and enforce its fine-grained access control there. Gateway REQUEST interceptors are your own Lambda functions, invoked before the gateway calls the target, that allow or deny specific tools and MCP operations such as tools/call from the caller's JWT claims; RESPONSE interceptors run after the target responds and can filter what comes back, for example removing unauthorized tools from a tools/list result — this authorizes what the agent is about to do, separate from filtering what it says. Keep the three gateway mechanisms distinct rather than describing them as one: interceptors are custom code you write, a gateway resource-based policy is standard AWS-style IAM access control on the gateway itself, and AgentCore Policy is a separate Cedar evaluation layer (pattern matching on principal.id). Follow the interceptor security guidance and fail safe — deny when an interceptor errors or times out instead of falling through to allow — and keep the content-safety guardrail on the output path as a further distinct layer.

controls.q: Is an agent's original objective protected from being redirected over the course of a session by accumulated conversation history or injected content?
controls.h: Beyond single-turn injection detection (AIR-BDR-GRD-02): confirm a control anchors the agent to its authorized goal — e.g. re-asserting the system objective, or checking that requested actions still serve the original task — so a slow, multi-turn manipulation cannot steer it to a different objective (biased recommendations, skipped review steps, preferred-vendor selection).
controls.ev: Goal-anchoring / objective-consistency control example
controls.rec: No single Amazon Bedrock feature anchors an agent to its objective, so combine native checks with process: re-assert the authorized system prompt/objective on every turn instead of trusting accumulated conversation history, and call the InvokeGuardrailChecks API each turn with its promptAttack check on the current system+user messages to catch slow, multi-turn injection and goal hijacking that a single-turn scan would miss. Because those checks only inspect language, anchor behavior at the action layer too by reusing the AIR-BDR-GRD-07 Gateway/IAM authorization so a drifted action still fails allow/deny, and require human-in-the-loop approval plus session review for high-impact or irreversible actions.

controls.q: Is model output validated for factual grounding in its provided source context, so ungrounded or off-topic (hallucinated) responses are detected or blocked rather than returned as authoritative?
controls.h: Distinct from content-safety filtering: confirm a grounding/relevance check evaluates each response against the supplied source context and the user's query, so a fabricated or irrelevant answer is caught. For domains with fixed rules, look for a formal validation step that proves whether a response contradicts an encoded policy, not just a probabilistic classifier.
controls.ev: Contextual-grounding filter configuration + a scored/blocked ungrounded response example
controls.rec: Enable the Guardrail contextual grounding filter (GuardrailContextualGroundingFilterConfig) with both filter types — GROUNDING (is the response factually supported by the provided source?) and RELEVANCE (does it address the user's query?) — each with action BLOCK and a threshold between 0 and 0.99, raising the value to block more; 1 is not a valid threshold because it would block all content. The filter evaluates the model output only and needs the reference source and the user query supplied alongside it: call ApplyGuardrail with source=OUTPUT and tag the content with the grounding_source, query and guard_content qualifiers, or supply the same qualifiers through the Invoke or Converse APIs. grounding_source and query are reference material for this check and are not themselves evaluated by the other policies, and the response returns a per-type score (0-1) with a detected flag you can log. On a knowledge base the plumbing is not equivalent: RetrieveAndGenerate accepts only generationConfiguration.guardrailConfiguration (guardrailId plus guardrailVersion), with no documented way to pass the retrieved passages as the grounding source, and the check is unsupported there on Claude 3 Sonnet and Haiku — so score grounding explicitly through ApplyGuardrail rather than assuming the knowledge base wires it up. Know the limits before relying on it: conversational QA and chatbot use cases are not supported, the grounding source, query and response are capped at 100,000, 1,000 and 5,000 characters, and with response streaming an ungrounded answer can reach the user before it is flagged. For domains governed by fixed rules, layer Automated Reasoning checks (GuardrailAutomatedReasoningPolicyConfig — up to two Automated Reasoning policy ARNs plus a confidenceThreshold from 0.0 to 1.0) which use formal logic to mathematically prove whether a response contradicts your encoded policy and return verifiable explanations, rather than acting as a binary content gate. Feed the grounding/relevance scores and Automated Reasoning findings into Bedrock model invocation logging so ungrounded or contradictory responses surface to monitoring.

controls.q: Is a single approved guardrail enforced centrally across the organization, rather than left to each application to attach the right one?
controls.h: Confirm the org mandates content safety on model invocation from the management side — either auto-applying a central guardrail to every Bedrock call, or denying invocation unless the approved guardrail is passed — so a team cannot ship an application with no guardrail or a weaker one.
controls.ev: Organizations bedrock policy (auto-apply) or SCP with bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier + cross-account share
controls.rec: Enforce a single approved guardrail org-wide from the management side rather than per application. Preferred: enable the BEDROCK_POLICY policy type in AWS Organizations (EnablePolicyType — a distinct policy type, not an SCP) and attach a Bedrock policy that auto-applies a management-account-owned guardrail (non-DRAFT numeric version, with a resource-based policy allowing org members to bedrock:ApplyGuardrail) on every Bedrock model invocation across the OU or account — callers need not pass a GuardrailIdentifier, and you set guardrail_inference, selective_content_guarding and model_enforcement. selective_content_guarding takes a system and a messages setting, each selective or comprehensive, and both default to comprehensive, which evaluates the entire prompt and overrides any caller input tagging; the Automated Reasoning policy is unsupported in enforcements and configuring one causes runtime failures. The same mechanism exists as account-level enforcement for a single account, org, OU and account policies layer as a union with the most restrictive setting winning, and DescribeEffectivePolicy tells you which guardrail an account actually gets. Complement or fall back with an SCP that denies bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream unless bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier StringEquals your approved guardrail ARN and version — those two are the only IAM actions that accept the condition key, and since Converse and ConverseStream are authorized by bedrock:InvokeModel, denying it covers them too (there is no bedrock:Converse action to name). Share the guardrail (and any guardrail-profile) cross-account via its resource-based policy (AWS::Bedrock::ResourcePolicy) scoped by aws:PrincipalOrgID, which works only within a single organization; use system-defined guardrail profiles (crossRegionConfig) for cross-region evaluation. Caveats: on the IAM/SCP route input tagging lets callers leave sections unevaluated (output is always fully checked), and don't reuse a guardrail-required role for RetrieveAndGenerate, InvokeAgent or InvokeInlineAgent, whose internal InvokeModel calls may omit the guardrail and throw AccessDenied.

controls.q: For agentic workloads, are content-safety checks applied per step of the agent loop (each turn, tool input/output), not only once on the final user-facing text?
controls.h: Agentic apps make many model and tool calls per request. Confirm safeguards run at each step — evaluating the current turn's messages and tool payloads — using the agentic guardrail check API in detect mode with caller-enforced thresholds, so injection or sensitive-data leakage mid-trajectory is caught rather than only at the final output.
controls.ev: Per-step InvokeGuardrailChecks configuration (content/promptAttack/sensitiveInformation) in the agent loop
controls.rec: Use the agentic guardrail API, InvokeGuardrailChecks (POST /guardrail-checks/invoke, IAM action bedrock:InvokeGuardrailChecks), to apply inline safeguards at each step of the agent loop without creating a guardrail resource: it runs in detect-only mode, returning per-check severity/confidence scores (contentFilter VIOLENCE/HATE/SEXUAL/MISCONDUCT/INSULTS, promptAttack JAILBREAK/PROMPT_INJECTION/PROMPT_LEAKAGE, sensitiveInformation PII, up to 31 entity types) on the current messages so the caller enforces thresholds/actions and can add or drop checks per turn as the trajectory evolves. Because it is text/message-oriented (not a tool-action evaluator), enforce action-level authorization separately (AIR-BDR-GRD-07 / AIR-ACR-POL-01) — and where enforcement should be deterministic at the gateway, compose Guardrails into AgentCore Policy via the Cedar `when guardrails{}` block so the same check drives a permit, forbid or suppressOutput decision on a BedrockGuardrails::ContentFilter, PromptAttack or SensitiveInformation safeguard (see AIR-ACR-POL-06). Two preconditions gate that path: grant bedrock:InvokeGuardrailChecks to the gateway execution role, because Policy calls the guardrail data plane with the forwarded caller credentials rather than its own, and confirm region support first — guardrails in policy are available in only five of the regions AgentCore Policy otherwise supports (us-east-1, London, Stockholm, Sydney and Tokyo).

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — Knowledge Bases & RAG data security
controls.q: Does retrieval from a knowledge base respect the original document-level access controls of the source data, rather than exposing everything to every querying user?
controls.h: Verify retrieval filters results by the requesting user's entitlements against the source system's access model, not a flat retrieval scope.
controls.ev: Access-control propagation test between source and retrieval
controls.rec: Metadata filtering alone is not an authorization boundary — the RetrievalFilter is a caller-supplied request field, so it enforces only what the calling application chooses to send. Bedrock's native mechanism is ACL-aware retrieval, enabled per data source on a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base: each document's allowed/denied users and groups are crawled at ingestion, and you pass userContext.userId on Retrieve to filter results to that principal. The identifier is an email address — the only one supported, with no alias resolution or cross-IdP mapping. It fails closed: deny overrides allow, a document with no ACL metadata is not ingested at all, and omitting userContext returns zero results from ACL-enabled data sources. Coverage differs by connector, so do not generalize: SharePoint, OneDrive, Google Drive and Confluence get pre-retrieval filtering plus real-time ACL verification against the source system. Amazon S3 and custom data sources get pre-retrieval filtering only, from ACLs you supply yourself (set aclEnabled on the connector and provide either a global ACL file via aclConfiguration.globalAccessControlListS3Uri or a per-document <file>.metadata.json accessControlList — a document with neither is silently skipped, with no error). Web Crawler does not support ACLs at all. Group membership is only as fresh as the last sync and IdP credentials are cached up to an hour, so revocations are eventually consistent. AWS states plainly that ACL awareness is not authorization and that Bedrock does not authenticate end users, so keep the identity check upstream and derive both userContext and any RetrievalFilter (tenant, department, clearance from each object's <file>.metadata.json) server-side from the authenticated session — never from client input.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — Knowledge Bases & RAG data security
controls.q: Is the underlying vector store / index for a knowledge base encrypted and access-restricted the same way as the source data it was built from?
controls.h: Check that the vector database or search index storage carries equivalent encryption and access restrictions to its source data.
controls.ev: Vector store encryption/access configuration
controls.rec: Do not assume one customer managed key covers the whole knowledge base — the default is an AWS owned key, and how far a CMK reaches depends on the vector store. On a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base the CMK set at creation covers transient ingestion storage and the managed vector store through a Bedrock-created KMS grant, so the creating identity needs kms:CreateGrant, kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt on that key conditioned with kms:ViaService bedrock.<region>.amazonaws.com, while the knowledge base service role needs no KMS permissions at all. On a bring-your-own vector store the Bedrock CMK covers only transient ingestion storage and the retrieval session (kmsKeyArn on RetrieveAndGenerate); it reaches the index itself only where Bedrock created that store for you (quick create for OpenSearch Serverless or Amazon S3 Vectors). Otherwise encrypt each store on its own terms: an OpenSearch Serverless collection is always encrypted at rest but uses a CMK only when an encryption policy sets AWSOwnedKey false with KmsARN (or CreateCollection names the key), and the choice is immutable — changing it means recreating the collection. Aurora pgvector inherits the DB cluster's own StorageEncrypted KMS key. Pinecone, Redis Enterprise Cloud and MongoDB Atlas are third-party SaaS that AWS KMS does not encrypt, so the AWS-side controls there are a CMK on the Secrets Manager secret holding the credentials plus TLS in transit. Set serverSideEncryptionConfiguration.kmsKeyArn on each data source. Critically, the key is not the access boundary: OpenSearch Serverless does not check a caller's permissions on the CMK, so anyone a data access policy admits can query the encrypted vectors — restrict the index with the collection's data access policy and network policy plus aoss:APIAccessAll scoped to that one collection ARN.

config_rule.note: AWS managed. NON_COMPLIANT if a Bedrock data source has no ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration.KmsKeyArn. Records AWS::Bedrock::DataSource. Not available in GovCloud.
