controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — Knowledge Bases & RAG data security
controls.q: Is ingestion of new documents into a knowledge base screened to prevent injection of malicious instructions embedded in the content (indirect prompt injection)?
controls.h: Look for a scanning/sanitization step on ingested content aimed at instruction-like patterns, not just malware scanning.
controls.ev: Content-screening step in the ingestion pipeline
controls.rec: Treat retrieved chunks as untrusted and screen them with a Bedrock guardrail prompt attack filter (contentPolicyConfig filter type PROMPT_ATTACK), which flags jailbreak, prompt-injection, and prompt-leakage patterns in text marked as user input. Because that filter only evaluates content wrapped in the input tags <amazon-bedrock-guardrails-guardContent_{tagSuffix}> (with a fresh random tagSuffix per request on InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream, or the equivalent guardrailConfiguration content block on Converse), you must run a self-managed Retrieve-then-generate flow to tag the retrieved chunks — the managed RetrieveAndGenerate call builds the prompt internally and cannot selectively tag them. Guardrails is a probabilistic classifier that will not catch every injection payload, so retain the pre-ingestion sanitization step that strips instruction-like patterns before chunking and embedding, plus source review and least-privilege on downstream agent/tool actions as residual app-layer controls.

controls.q: For knowledge bases spanning multiple tenants or business units, is retrieval strictly partitioned so one tenant's query cannot surface another tenant's data?
controls.h: Where multi-tenant, confirm a hard partition (separate index, or enforced filter) prevents cross-tenant retrieval, verified by testing, not assumed.
controls.ev: Cross-tenant isolation test result
controls.rec: Enforce a hard multi-tenant partition using either the silo pattern (a separate knowledge base / OpenSearch Serverless collection per tenant) or the pool pattern (a single KB with a tenantId attribute in each object's .metadata.json and a mandatory RetrievalFilter on tenantId injected server-side from the authenticated identity). The pool pattern carries a store-specific prerequisite that fails silently when missed: an OpenSearch Serverless index must use the faiss engine, because an nmslib index ignores metadata files entirely, and an Aurora pgvector table needs its custom metadata column (or one column per attribute) created before the knowledge base exists and unchangeable afterwards. So prove the filter actually filters, then validate with cross-tenant retrieval tests that one tenant's query cannot surface another tenant's data.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — Knowledge Bases & RAG data security
controls.q: Are the vector embeddings generated from source documents protected and governed as sensitive data derived from that source, rather than treated as opaque numeric arrays?
controls.h: Embeddings are not anonymized source data — embedding-inversion research shows source text can be substantially reconstructed from vectors alone. Confirm the embedding store inherits the source's classification and access controls, that nobody has read access to the raw index who is not cleared for the underlying documents, and that embeddings are not exported to a lower-trust store or third-party service without the same controls.
controls.ev: Classification of the embedding store matching the source corpus + read-access principal list for the vector index
controls.rec: Treat the embedding index as a derived copy of the source corpus at the same classification, because embedding inversion can partially reconstruct source text from vectors. AIR-BDR-KB-03 already encrypts the vector store with a customer-managed key; extend that to the governance question by carrying the source's data-classification tag onto the vector store, and hold direct read access to the raw index to only the knowledge-base service role plus named break-glass operators — not to the broader analytics or application population who are authorized to query through Retrieve but not to read the index. What that scoping looks like differs per store: for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless it takes both aoss:APIAccessAll on the one collection ARN and the collection's data access policy, since IAM alone is not the gate and the CMK is no help here (OpenSearch Serverless does not check a caller's key permissions, so a data access policy grant is sufficient to read the encrypted vectors). For OpenSearch Managed Clusters it is es:ESHttpGet/ESHttpPost on the domain and index. For Aurora pgvector it is rds-data:ExecuteStatement on the cluster plus the database grants. For Amazon S3 Vectors it is s3vectors:GetVectors and s3vectors:QueryVectors on the index. And for Pinecone, Redis Enterprise Cloud or MongoDB Atlas the boundary is the provider's own access model plus whoever can read the Secrets Manager secret. Where embeddings leave AWS or move to a lower-trust store, apply the same classification and encryption, and record the transfer. Note this is a governance and access-scoping control, not a cryptographic one: there is no AWS feature that makes an embedding non-invertible, so containment of who can read the vectors is the control.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — Knowledge Bases & RAG data security
controls.q: Is the number of retrieved chunks and the retrieval strategy bounded per request, so poisoned or low-relevance content cannot crowd legitimate context out of the model's window?
controls.h: A retrieval call that returns a large numberOfResults can fill the context window with attacker-influenced or marginal chunks, displacing the content that should have answered the query. Confirm the application sets an explicit, reviewed numberOfResults rather than relying on defaults or a caller-supplied value, and that the search type is deliberate. These are per-request parameters, so the control is in the calling application's code and its review — not a setting readable back off the knowledge base.
controls.ev: Application code or config showing a fixed server-side numberOfResults and search type, plus the review record for that value
controls.rec: Set numberOfResults explicitly in the KnowledgeBaseVectorSearchConfiguration on Retrieve/RetrieveAndGenerate (valid range 1-100) to the smallest value that answers the use case, and set it server-side so an end user cannot raise it — a caller-controlled result count is a context-stuffing lever. Choose overrideSearchType deliberately (HYBRID, which combines vector and raw-text matching, is available only on an OpenSearch Serverless vector store with a filterable text field; otherwise only SEMANTIC applies) rather than leaving strategy selection implicit. Where relevance ordering matters, configure rerankingConfiguration (VectorSearchRerankingConfiguration) so a reranker model reorders results instead of trusting raw similarity order, and pair this with the AIR-BDR-KB-02 metadata RetrievalFilter so the candidate set is scoped before it is ranked. Because these are request-body fields with no IAM condition key and no persisted knowledge-base setting, this control is verified by code review and the pinned value in the calling application, not by a describe/get on the knowledge base.

controls.section_title: Amazon Bedrock — Knowledge Bases & RAG data security
controls.q: Is the knowledge-base index monitored for unexpected change in content or embedding distribution, so corpus poisoning or a bad ingestion is detected rather than silently serving retrievals?
controls.h: Distinct from AIR-SGM-EP-06, which watches inference-time model drift: this is drift in the retrieval corpus itself. A sudden shift in document count, chunk count, or embedding distribution can indicate poisoned ingestion, an unintended bulk sync, or a source compromise. Confirm something baselines the index and alerts on deviation, rather than the index changing unobserved between syncs.
controls.ev: Baseline of index statistics + the alarm/alert configuration and a sample deviation review
controls.rec: Baseline the corpus and alert on deviation. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases publishes no embedding-drift metric — the AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases namespace carries only Invocations, ClientErrors, ServerErrors, Throttles and RawDataSize (the total raw size of the source data, emitted after each ingestion job) — so build the check from the ingestion path. On a managed knowledge base, enable ingestion log delivery (PutDeliverySource with logType APPLICATION_LOGS against the knowledge base ARN, then PutDeliveryDestination and CreateDelivery to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Firehose; the caller needs bedrock:AllowVendedLogDeliveryForResource) and baseline the per-document records, which carry a crawl_action of ADD, DELETE or UNMODIFIED plus chunk_statistics for created, deleted, failed_to_create and failed_to_delete. Where log delivery is not available, poll GetIngestionJob after each StartIngestionJob and publish IngestionJobStatistics — numberOfDocumentsScanned, numberOfNewDocumentsIndexed, numberOfModifiedDocumentsIndexed, numberOfDocumentsDeleted, numberOfDocumentsFailed, numberOfDocumentsSkipped — as CloudWatch custom metrics. Alarm when indexed or deleted counts, or RawDataSize, deviate materially from the established baseline: an unexpected bulk delete or a spike in new documents is the detectable signal of a poisoned or runaway ingestion. Complement with a periodic canary-query set whose expected top results are known, run on a schedule, and alert when the retrieved chunk set for a fixed query changes, which catches ranking-level corpus manipulation that document counts miss. Route both to the same EventBridge/SNS path used by AIR-FND-DET-03 so corpus anomalies reach the on-call owner rather than a dashboard nobody reads.

controls.q: Does each agent act under its own distinct identity, so its actions are traceable separately from the end user it is acting for?
controls.h: Confirm agents use delegation (a distinct agent identity bound to the user) rather than impersonation (reusing the raw user token), so audit records show agent + user + target. Whether each action is authorized outside the model is assessed at the gateway/policy layer.
controls.ev: Delegation vs. impersonation configuration + audit trail sample
controls.rec: Adopt the AgentCore Identity delegation model: configure CUSTOM_JWT inbound auth so Runtime/Gateway exchanges the validated user token for a Workload Access Token via GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT, which cryptographically binds the agent's own workload identity (its ARN in the agent identity directory) to the user. Give each agent a distinct workload identity and reach downstream via per-target scoped credential providers rather than forwarding the raw user JWT (impersonation). AgentCore Identity spans then record the chain in two halves — the GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT span carries workload.identity.id plus issuer and user_sub (agent + user), and the GetResourceOAuth2Token span carries workload.identity.id plus credential.provider.name (agent + target) — but those spans are opt-in: enable observability on the workload identity and credential-provider resources, or CloudTrail is the only record you get.

controls.q: Is every request to invoke an agent authenticated and its identity claims validated before the agent's code runs?
controls.h: Confirm inbound calls pass an identity check (a validated JWT from your IdP, or signed AWS requests) before execution — verifying the token signature and expected claims (issuer, audience, scopes) rather than trusting unvalidated input. Malformed, expired, or wrong-audience requests should be rejected up front.
controls.ev: Inbound authorizer configuration (validated claims / signed-request enforcement)
controls.rec: Configure the AgentCore Runtime/Gateway inbound authorizer at CreateAgentRuntime/CreateGateway time: for end-user apps set the customJWTAuthorizer with the IdP discoveryUrl (must match ^.+/\.well-known/openid-configuration$) plus allowedClients, allowedAudience, and allowedScopes so AgentCore validates the JWT signature against the IdP's JWKS and checks iss, aud, client_id, exp and scopes before agent code runs. For AWS principals use IAM SigV4 instead — on a gateway that is authorizerType AWS_IAM, while CreateAgentRuntime exposes no authorizerType field at all, so a runtime's mode follows from whether customJWTAuthorizer is configured and a runtime supports one method at a time (use separate versions per method). Do not try to tighten the invoke call itself with IAM claim conditions: InvokeAgentRuntime's only condition key is aws:ResourceTag/${TagKey}, and bedrock-agentcore:InboundJwtClaim/iss, /aud, /client_id and /scope are accepted only by GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and CompleteResourceTokenAuth — a Deny written against InvokeAgentRuntime on those keys never matches and fails open. Pin the issuer/audience/client set in the authorizer allow-lists, and apply the claim condition keys on the token-minting path instead (see AIR-ACR-ID-11).

controls.q: Are the credentials an agent uses to call downstream systems short-lived and scoped to that specific agent, rather than long-lived shared secrets?
controls.h: Check that downstream credential issuance is per-agent, time-limited, and does not rely on static shared keys.
controls.ev: Credential issuance configuration showing scope + TTL
controls.rec: Issue downstream credentials through AgentCore Identity credential providers rather than static keys: agents present a short-lived Workload Access Token (WAT) bound to a specific agent+user pair and call GetResourceOauth2Token (OAuth 2LO/3LO) or GetResourceApiKey to obtain per-target OAuth tokens/API keys from the Token Vault. Request only the required scopes per target and scope the IAM policy granting GetResourceOauth2Token/GetResourceApiKey to the specific workload-identity ARN and credential-provider ARN so each agent gets least-privilege, time-limited credentials. Where the downstream IdP supports it, prefer Private Key JWT client authentication over a shared OAuth 2.0 client secret: you register a public key with the IdP while the private key stays in AWS KMS, AgentCore Identity calls KMS to sign each client assertion, so there is no shared secret to leak or rotate and every signing operation lands in CloudTrail. It works across all three grant flows (M2M, on-behalf-of, and user-delegated) and supports RS256, PS256, and ES256 — scope the KMS key policy to the signing operation and alarm on unexpected sign calls, since the key is now the credential. For the 3LO leg specifically, bind the consent to the user who asked for it, because GetResourceOauth2Token returns an authorization URL and a URL is forwardable: a user who sends theirs to somebody else has that person's consent stored against the first user's session, and the agent then reads the wrong person's resource with a token AgentCore considers valid. Register your callback on the workload identity as an AllowedResourceOAuth2ReturnUrl via UpdateWorkloadIdentity, and in that callback verify the logged-in user matches the originating user BEFORE calling CompleteResourceTokenAuth, reading the identity from the live browser session (cookie or local storage) and not from a remote session cache that an attacker's request would hit just as well. Pass an opaque state to GetResourceOAuth2Token so the callback can reject requests your own application did not start, and note each authorization URL and session URI is valid for 10 minutes. Do not read local development as evidence this is handled: `agentcore dev` hosts the callback itself and calls CompleteResourceTokenAuth for you, so the verification step you must write for production is the one step that never runs on a developer's machine. A deployed agent has to host its own public HTTPS callback, and adopting a consent portal narrows this exposure without removing it, since a target called directly with no stored credential still returns an authorization URL under the same session-binding rules.

controls.q: Is there an org-wide preventive control preventing an agent runtime from being deployed with an authentication mode that does not propagate a real user identity?
controls.h: Look for a guardrail (policy or automated check) that blocks deploying agent runtimes configured to skip user-identity propagation.
controls.ev: Preventive guardrail configuration/policy
controls.rec: Deploy an AWS Organizations SCP at the OU level, and for each surface deny the CREATE and the UPDATE action, as AWS's own gateway SCP examples do — a create-only guardrail is walked past by creating compliant and then updating. Runtimes: bedrock-agentcore:RuntimeAuthorizerType is listed on CreateAgentRuntime and UpdateAgentRuntime in the Service Authorization Reference and in the machine-readable service model, so deny both with StringNotEquals against your required JWT-based authorizer value — AWS publishes no accepted values for this key anywhere (there is no runtime counterpart of the gateway condition-key page), so read one out of a CloudTrail event or a test-OU call before you rely on the literal. Gateways: the developer guide declares bedrock-agentcore:GatewayAuthorizerType on CreateGateway and UpdateGateway with valid values AWS_IAM, CUSTOM_JWT and NONE, so deny both with StringNotEquals against CUSTOM_JWT; the same page's EnforceGatewayIdP example shows exactly this shape on both actions. Both IAM sources omit the key from those actions (they carry only aws:RequestTag/${TagKey} plus aws:TagKeys on CreateGateway, and aws:ResourceTag/${TagKey} on UpdateGateway) — the developer guide governs feature availability, and request-time enforcement has been confirmed empirically: under a Deny keyed on this condition a compliant CUSTOM_JWT CreateGateway still succeeds, while the same policy with the key name misspelled denies every create. Run exactly that pair in a test OU before org-wide rollout, because it is what distinguishes a populated key from a null match: an unpopulated or misspelled key makes StringNotEquals match the absent value (inverted operators match a null value) and blocks compliant creates too — visible rather than silent, but still a broken guardrail. Keep the Deny in the StringNotEquals-against-your-approved-value shape rather than a StringEquals deny-list of bad values: AUTHENTICATE_ONLY is a fourth valid gateway authorizerType that the condition key's documented value list does not enumerate, so a deny-list would not name it. Back both surfaces with a detective audit of GetGateway/ListGateways and GetAgentRuntime on a schedule, alarming on (or auto-remediating) any resource whose authorizer type is not CUSTOM_JWT — neither AWS_IAM nor NONE propagates a validated end-user identity. Validation of the actual user claims (iss/aud/sub) remains an inbound-authorizer concern (see AIR-ACR-ID-08).

controls.q: Is there a tested, time-bounded procedure to stop a specific agent invoking services or retrieving credentials and to revoke its provider-side access during an incident?
controls.h: Confirm a scoped runbook and measured containment time for invocation, active sessions, future credential retrieval and already-issued provider tokens. Clearing an AgentCore refresh token and revoking a provider access token are separate steps; test that other agents remain available.
controls.ev: Single-agent containment runbook + measured propagation/session/token outcomes + separate provider-revocation evidence
controls.rec: Document and rehearse a graduated kill-switch runbook for a single agent, and scope every step to an ARN the action actually operates on — the failure mode here is a Deny that never matches. (1) Cut invocation with a resource-based policy: PutResourcePolicy an explicit Deny on that agent's runtime for bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime (plus InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser, InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand and the WebSocket-stream variants as applicable). Explicit deny always wins over any identity-based allow, and because runtime invocation is authorized hierarchically across both the runtime and the endpoint, a deny on the runtime covers every endpoint. Do not scope this deny to a workload-identity ARN: InvokeAgentRuntime operates on runtime and runtime-endpoint ARNs only, so a workload-identity-scoped deny never matches and fails open. (2) Cut outbound credentials with an identity-policy or SCP Deny on GetResourceOauth2Token/GetResourceApiKey/GetWorkloadAccessToken*, which DO take workload-identity ARNs, scoped to that agent's workload identity. (3) StopRuntimeSession (also a supported resource-policy action) to terminate sessions already running. Note the known gaps: there is no single-token revocation API. GetResourceOauth2Token with forceAuthentication=true clears the stored refresh token and forces the complete federation flow. It does not establish that previously issued provider access tokens have been invalidated; carry out provider-side revocation separately and verify both new retrieval and use of an already-issued token. The inbound authorizer validates JWTs using the IdP's JWKS; provider revocation may not immediately invalidate JWT acceptance. Determine the effective acceptance window from token exp and the deployed signing-key, authorizer and containment behavior, and measure when an already-issued token is actually rejected. Document provider revocation, token lifetime and signing-key response procedures, and measure their observed timing instead of promising immediate invalidation. Rehearse invocation denial, active-session termination, blocked credential retrieval and provider-token rejection independently, proving the targeted agent is contained without disrupting others.

controls.q: Is agent code prevented from directly minting or retrieving its own access tokens, so a compromised agent cannot extract credentials for other users?
controls.h: For runtime/gateway-hosted agents, confirm the platform delivers the agent its scoped token but blocks the agent's own code from calling the token-issuance APIs directly (service-managed identity) — so compromised or manipulated code cannot mint tokens for arbitrary users. Self-hosted agents that manage their own identity must enforce the equivalent restriction themselves.
controls.ev: Service-managed identity confirmation / token-issuance API restriction
controls.rec: For Runtime/Gateway-hosted agents, rely on AgentCore's service-managed workload identity: identities auto-created by Runtime or Gateway are service-linked and cannot retrieve workload access tokens directly — the attempt fails with 'WorkloadIdentity is linked to a service and cannot retrieve an access token by the caller' — and Runtime instead delivers the token to agent code as an invocation payload header, so compromised agent code cannot mint tokens for arbitrary users. This is a service-side restriction, not an IAM one, so do NOT try to reproduce it by removing GetWorkloadAccessToken* from the execution role: AWS's own reference AgentCore Runtime execution role grants GetWorkloadAccessToken, GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId (Sid GetAgentAccessToken) and the documented caller requirements include all three, so stripping them breaks the agent. Do this instead — scope those actions to the agent's own workload-identity ARN pattern rather than the directory or a wildcard resource. For any workload that always has a JWT available, explicitly Deny bedrock-agentcore:GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId and bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser so all user identification goes through the cryptographically verified JWT path. Keep broad managed policies such as BedrockAgentCoreFullAccess out of production roles. And for self-hosted agents that manage their own identity, issue tokens only from a trusted broker whose IAM policy is scoped to specific workload identities, never from agent code. Know that AWS's own published consent-portal execution role does NOT meet this bar, so copying it forward carries the widest grant on the page: it allows bedrock-agentcore:CompleteResourceTokenAuth, GetResourceOauth2Token and GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT on Resource '*'. That wildcard is not a limitation of the actions. The service-authorization reference marks a resource type as REQUIRED on all three (workload-identity and workload-identity-directory for GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT; those two plus oauth2credentialprovider and token-vault for CompleteResourceTokenAuth), so '*' is a widening you can narrow. Narrow it to the portal's own workload identity, credential provider and token vault, and add the InboundJwtClaim conditions from AIR-ACR-ID-11 on the same two token-minting actions, where they are among the few places those keys are accepted.

controls.q: Is inbound access to agents restricted to only your approved identity provider(s) and client applications, so a validly-signed token from an unapproved issuer cannot invoke them?
controls.h: Beyond requiring a validated token (AIR-ACR-ID-08): confirm the trusted issuer, audience, and client set is pinned — both in the inbound authorizer's allow-lists and, defensively, via IAM condition keys on the token-minting path — so only tokens from your specific IdP and client apps are accepted, not any token the authorizer can validate.
controls.ev: Inbound authorizer issuer/audience/client allow-lists + InboundJwtClaim condition keys pinning the IdP
controls.rec: Pin inbound access to your approved IdP(s) and client apps at two layers. In the CUSTOM_JWT authorizer, the discoveryUrl fixes the trusted issuer, and you must populate at least one meaningful constraint — allowedAudience (singular) and allowedClients, plus custom claims (tenant_id/department via EQUALS/CONTAINS/CONTAINS_ANY) where multi-tenant — so a broadly-configured authorizer doesn't accept any validly-signed token. Then defensively constrain the token-minting/identity APIs (GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT, CompleteResourceTokenAuth) with the bedrock-agentcore:InboundJwtClaim/iss, /aud, /client_id, and /scope condition keys (and bedrock-agentcore:userid for GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId) in the execution-role policy, combined with aws:SourceVpc/aws:SourceVpce, so only approved issuers, audiences, and clients from approved network paths can mint a Workload Access Token even if the authorizer config drifts. Add the network keys as an Allow condition (which fails closed and breaks visibly) and test them against the Runtime-initiated automatic token exchange first — aws:SourceVpc/aws:SourceVpce are only in the request context when the call actually traverses a VPC endpoint. Gateways get a third, preventive layer: the developer guide declares bedrock-agentcore:DiscoveryUrl on CreateGateway and UpdateGateway and ships an EnforceGatewayIdP SCP denying both with StringNotEquals against your IdP's discovery URL, which pins the issuer at configuration time so a gateway cannot be pointed at another IdP later. Both IAM sources attach that key only to CreatePaymentManager/UpdatePaymentManager, so prove the SCP in a test OU before rollout; and note it governs how a gateway may be configured, not who may invoke it, so it supplements rather than replaces the two layers above.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Does each agent session run in an isolated execution environment that does not leak state or data to unrelated sessions?
controls.h: Confirm one session cannot read or influence another's compute, memory, or filesystem. Note: if sessions share persistent storage (e.g. a mounted shared bucket), per-session isolation becomes the application's responsibility and must be enforced in code, not assumed from the runtime.
controls.ev: Session isolation architecture + shared-storage partitioning (if any)
controls.rec: Know which compute type you are on, because the isolation guarantee differs. On the default serverless (microVM) compute, each SESSION runs in its own microVM with an isolated kernel, memory, and filesystem, and on session completion the microVM is terminated and its memory sanitized — so one session cannot read or influence another's compute. On AgentCore Instances (EC2 managed instances in your account) that guarantee does not hold between agents: AWS states agents on an instance are not isolated from each other, multiple agents can share the instance filesystem, and all agents sharing an instance must be mutually trusted — the SESSION is the isolation unit (capacity provider + session ID maps 1:1 to one instance), so use a separate capacity provider per trust boundary. If sessions share persistent storage, prefer managed session storage, which the platform isolates per session (a session cannot read or write another session's storage, or any session of a different runtime), over a bring-your-own S3 Files or EFS mount. A BYO mount CANNOT be narrowed per session: the access point's root directory and POSIX UID/GID are fixed in filesystemConfigurations and AgentCore mounts that same access point into every session at the configured path. So per-session partitioning has to be enforced by the agent's own file paths (e.g. sessions/{session_id}/), or structurally by a separate runtime and access point per tenant — not by scoping the mount.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Is an agent's ability to invoke tools limited to an explicit, approved set, rather than open-ended tool discovery and use?
controls.h: Check for an allow-list of tools/actions bound to the agent's configuration, verified against what the agent can actually invoke at runtime.
controls.ev: Tool allow-list configuration + runtime verification
controls.rec: Front tools with AgentCore Gateway and enforce an explicit allow-list via AgentCore Policy (Cedar) in default-deny mode; Cedar is evaluated on every tool invocation (tools/call). Tool DISCOVERY is also policy-filtered — listing is treated as a meta action, so a principal only sees tools it would be permitted to call — but do not read that as an authorization guarantee: a tool is listable if there exists ANY set of circumstances under which calling it would be permitted, and AWS states plainly that a tool appearing in the list does not mean a subsequent call to it will be authorized. The genuinely unprotected surface is MCP prompts and resources: regardless of the policy evaluation mode, the gateway ALWAYS allows prompts/list, prompts/get, resources/list, resources/read and resources/templates/list, because policy evaluation applies only to MCP tools. That is where a Lambda request/response interceptor earns its place — use one to filter or deny prompt and resource access, and verify at runtime with a tools/list plus resources/list call as an unprivileged principal. For direct Runtime tool access scope the execution role and credential-provider ARNs so the agent cannot reach tools outside the approved set.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Is the execution role available to code-execution and browser tools scoped to least privilege, on the assumption that any code in the sandbox can assume it?
controls.h: Code-execution/browser tools run in an isolated per-session sandbox, but any code inside it — including model-generated code — can retrieve the tool's execution-role credentials. The execution role is therefore the blast radius: confirm it is scoped to only the specific resources the tool needs (no broad service-wide grants) and is not shared across tool types or environments.
controls.ev: Tool execution-role policy showing resource-scoped, least-privilege grants
controls.rec: Treat the tool execution role as the blast radius: any code in the microVM (including LLM-generated code) can read its temporary credentials via MMDS regardless of network mode. Scope the role to specific resource ARNs (never s3:* or bedrock:*), keep it at equal-or-fewer privileges than the invoking user, use a separate role per tool type (Code Interpreter vs Browser) and per environment, trust bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com with aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn conditions, and audit continuously with IAM Access Analyzer. Interactive shells widen who can reach that blast radius, so gate them separately: InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell opens a persistent WebSocket terminal inside a live session where, in AWS's own words, shell commands have full access to the container filesystem and any credentials or secrets configured — the microVM is the only boundary. Restrict bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell (and InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand for one-shot execution) to a named break-glass or developer role rather than granting it alongside InvokeAgentRuntime, and deny it outright in production accounts where interactive access is not a requirement. Mind the audit gap: CloudTrail records WHO opened a shell and when but not the payload, and terminal stdin/stdout is streamed to the client and NEVER logged by the service — so the commands actually run are unrecoverable after the fact. Compensate with a CloudWatch Logs metric filter and alarm on shell-connection request IDs in the agent log group, correlate to the CloudTrail event, and treat any production shell connection as an incident to review. State persists across commands within a session and reconnection replays up to 256 KB of buffered output, so a detached shell remains a live foothold until closed — 10 concurrent shells per runtime, 1-hour connection TTL.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Are resource limits (time, memory, cost) enforced per agent session to prevent a single runaway task from consuming disproportionate resources?
controls.h: Look for session-level quotas/timeouts that cap runtime resource use, distinct from account-wide service quotas.
controls.ev: Per-session resource limit configuration
controls.rec: Set AgentCore Runtime LifecycleConfiguration explicitly rather than relying on the defaults: idleRuntimeSessionTimeout defaults to 900s and maxLifetime to 28800s (8h), but both accept anything from 60s up to 1209600s (14 days), so the defaults are the only thing keeping a session from living for two weeks — set both to the lowest values the workload tolerates. On the default serverless (microVM) compute each session also carries a fixed maximum hardware allocation (2 vCPU / 8 GB) and billing tracks actual CPU consumption and peak memory per second, so compute and memory are bounded per session without extra configuration; on AgentCore Instances that ceiling is instead the capacity provider's instance type, which you choose, so size it deliberately. Monitor per-session consumption with the vended USAGE_LOGS log delivery (1-second granularity, session.id / elapsed_time_seconds / vCPU-hours / memory-GB-hours) — it is not on by default, so enable it — alarm on the ActiveSessionCount metric and on cost anomalies, and cap concurrent sessions per user in the application backend.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Is tool input/output validated against an expected schema before being passed between the model and the tool, to prevent malformed or malicious payloads?
controls.h: Confirm schema or type validation runs on both directions of tool invocation, not just on the initial user prompt.
controls.ev: Schema validation configuration for tool I/O
controls.rec: Use AgentCore Gateway tool definitions as the canonical schema and validate both directions with Lambda interceptors: a request interceptor validates/transforms inbound tool calls and a response interceptor validates/redacts target output, configured fail-safe to deny when validation cannot be completed. Add Cedar context.input conditions for parameter-level checks, and for direct Runtime tool use validate payloads against the tool's input and output schema in agent code. Do not overlook custom HEADERS as a second, unvalidated input channel into agent code: the runtime's requestHeaderAllowlist now forwards any non-restricted header (up to 20 headers, 4KB per value), where it used to permit only Authorization and X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Custom-*. Keep the allowlist to the minimum each agent reads, and treat every forwarded header as untrusted input — a webhook signature or X-Api-Key arrives verbatim from the caller, so the agent must verify it rather than trust its presence, and header values must never be interpolated into a prompt, a shell command, or a tool argument without validation. AWS restricts the dangerous classes for you (x-amz-*, x-amzn-* apart from the Custom- prefix, plus the proxy/IP-spoofing, CORS, and security-header families), so a header that is forwardable is not thereby safe. Note Authorization is only forwardable when the runtime has a customJWTAuthorizer, and forwarding it puts a live user token inside agent code — allowlist it only if the agent genuinely needs to re-present that token, and never log it (see AIR-ACR-OBS-04).

controls.q: Is there monitoring that can detect an agent attempting to use a tool or take an action outside its approved scope, even if the attempt is blocked?
controls.h: Look for logging/alerting on denied or out-of-scope tool-invocation attempts, treated as a security signal.

DenyDecisions, AllowDecisions, DeterminingPolicies and NoDeterminingPolicies land in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore CloudWatch namespace by DEFAULT, dimensioned by ToolName, Policy and TargetResource — so a deny-rate alarm per tool needs no instrumentation. To see WHICH policy decided, enable traces on the attached Gateway: the aws/spans log group then carries aws.agentcore.policy.authorization_decision, .authorization_reason, .determining_policies and .effects (plus .denied_tools on PartiallyAuthorizeActions). Investigate NoDeterminingPolicies as a default-deny outcome with no determining policy: check both policy-coverage gaps and out-of-scope attempts. Monitor the Mode/PolicyEnforcementMode dimensions and LogOnlyDecisionFlips so shadow evaluation is not mistaken for enforced denial. controls.q: For multi-agent or agent-to-agent workflows, is trust between agents established and re-verified per interaction, rather than assumed once an agent is deployed?
controls.h: Confirm agent-to-agent calls carry their own authorization check rather than an agent being implicitly trusted because it exists in the environment.
controls.ev: Agent-to-agent authorization check example
controls.rec: Require every agent-to-agent call to carry its own authorization rather than implicit trust: use AgentCore Identity delegation (not impersonation) so each hop gets a Workload Access Token bound to the agent+user pair and a separately scoped OAuth token per target, validate JWT claims (iss/aud/scope) on each inbound call via the authorizer, and enforce per-invocation authorization at Gateway with Cedar policies and interceptors. Restrict which callers and IdPs are trusted on the INBOUND AUTHORIZER, not with an IAM condition key: a runtime or gateway configured with customJWTAuthorizer validates discoveryUrl (the OIDC issuer), allowedAudience against aud, allowedClients against client_id, allowedScopes against scope, and customClaims — inboundTokenClaimName plus authorizingClaimMatchValue and a claimMatchOperator such as CONTAINS_ANY — so a token that does not match is rejected before agent code runs. Set customClaims to the calling agent's own claim (e.g. a department or agent-id claim) so each hop is authorized on who it is, not merely on holding a valid token from the same IdP. For SigV4 hops, restrict the caller with a resource-based policy on the target runtime keyed on aws:PrincipalArn instead. Note bedrock-agentcore:InboundJwtClaim/* is NOT a control on invocation: it conditions only the token-exchange actions (GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT, CompleteResourceTokenAuth), so it governs which issuers and audiences may be traded for a workload access token, and a Deny written on it will not stop an inbound invoke.

controls.q: Is outbound network access from code-execution and browser tools restricted to only what the workload needs, rather than open internet egress?
controls.h: Code-execution and browser tools can reach the network on the agent's behalf, which is a data-exfiltration path. Confirm the tool's network mode is constrained to the minimum required (isolated / storage-only / your-VPC-only), and that unrestricted public egress is not used for sensitive workloads. Where egress is needed, confirm domains are filtered rather than fully open.

controls.rec: Constrain the tool network mode to the minimum required, and note the two tools do NOT offer the same modes. Code Interpreter supports PUBLIC | SANDBOX | VPC, so SANDBOX (AWS/S3 access only, no open internet) is the right production default there and VPC mode the choice for regulated data. Never use PUBLIC egress for sensitive workloads. controls.q: For browser-based agent tools, is there a forensic record of what the agent did in the browser session (pages visited, actions taken)?
controls.h: Browser tools navigate real sites and handle credentials on the agent's behalf. Confirm a capability to observe or replay browser-session activity for investigation, so an incident responder can see what a browsing agent actually did rather than inferring it from outcomes.
controls.ev: Protected browser-session capture/replay + sampled browser API audit correlated to the same session
controls.rec: Create the browser tool with session recording enabled — recording.enabled plus an s3Location (bucket + prefix) on CreateBrowser, and an execution role allowed to write there — because it is a create-time property of a custom browser, not something you can switch on after an incident. Recording captures far more than page URLs: session DOM changes and mutations, user actions including clicks, scrolls and form interactions, console logs and error messages, Chrome DevTools Protocol events, and network events and HTTP requests, which is what lets a responder reconstruct what the agent actually did rather than infer it. Add Live View for real-time monitoring of an in-flight session, including taking over or releasing control from the automation, which doubles as a containment step. Then treat the recording bucket as one of the most sensitive stores in the workload — it holds the rendered DOM and form input of authenticated sessions, laid out as s3://bucket/prefix/session-id/batch_N.ndjson.gz — so apply KMS encryption, Block Public Access, a TLS-only bucket policy, tight read access for responders only, and a retention/lifecycle rule. Enable CloudTrail data events for AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Browser / ::BrowserCustom (and ::BrowserProfile when used), then verify which required browser API operations appear in delivered events. These resource types are listed in the CloudTrail guide; that listing is not proof of DOM/action replay. Correlate the API audit with a recorded synthetic browser session and CloudWatch spans to demonstrate that responders can reconstruct pages visited and actions taken.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Does the application enforce which user owns each tool/agent session, given that the platform does not bind sessions to users on its own?
controls.h: Session isolation keeps sessions apart, but the runtime does not enforce which user a session belongs to — the application backend must map users to sessions and cap sessions per user. Confirm this mapping and lifecycle control exists, so one user cannot resume or hijack another user's tool session.
controls.ev: Application-side user-to-session mapping + session lifecycle limits
controls.rec: AgentCore Runtime authorizes an invocation against the agent runtime ARN, not against an individual session: it validates the FORMAT of the supplied runtimeSessionId but does not verify that the session belongs to the calling identity. So wherever one IAM principal invokes on behalf of many end users, session ownership is entirely an app-layer control. Derive the runtimeSessionId server-side from the authenticated end user and never accept it from client input; store a user-to-session mapping; validate on every InvokeAgentRuntime call that the session being resumed belongs to the authenticated user; and cap max sessions per user. AWS's strongest documented control is structural: use DISTINCT IAM principals per user or tenant for high-security multi-tenant deployments, so a cross-user session ID fails IAM rather than relying on backend logic being correct. Do not treat the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-User-Id header as verified identity — AWS states the header path does not verify the userId against an authenticated end-user identity and relies on the calling workload passing the correct value, so it is only as trustworthy as the caller. It requires bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser on top of bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime and drives GetWorkloadAccessTokenForUserId; scope that permission to specific runtime ARNs for trusted principals only, derive the value from the authenticated principal's context, and where user-id delegation is not needed add an explicit Deny on bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser so the header cannot be accepted at all. For production, prefer JWT bearer authentication (GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT), which validates the token's issuer, signature and expiry and so gives cryptographic proof of the end user. Detect what these controls miss: CloudTrail records the authenticated principal and the target sessionId (and runtimeUserId) in the same InvokeAgentRuntime event, so alert on one principal presenting session IDs bound to different users. Use StopRuntimeSession (runtimeSessionId + agentRuntimeArn) to terminate a user's sessions on logout, revocation, or a suspected takeover.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Where agent sessions use persistent file storage, is access fine-grained through the runtime execution role, and is per-session isolation handled correctly for shared (bring-your-own) mounts?
controls.h: Runtime session storage comes in two forms: service-managed storage is isolated per session by the platform; bring-your-own mounts (S3 Files, EFS) are SHARED across sessions and agents, so isolation becomes the application's responsibility. Confirm the execution role's file-access permissions are least-privilege and scoped to the specific access point, and that shared mounts enforce per-session partitioning in code.
controls.ev: Execution-role S3 Files/EFS permissions scoped to access-point ARN + per-session partitioning for shared mounts
controls.rec: Distinguish the two session-storage models. Service-managed session storage is isolated per session by the platform (a session can only reach its own storage) — prefer it where it fits. Bring-your-own mounts (S3 Files, EFS) are SHARED across all sessions and agents, so per-session isolation is the application's responsibility: enforce file-per-session naming/partitioning in code. Scope the runtime execution role to least privilege on the mount — for S3 Files grant only s3files:ClientMount, s3files:ClientWrite, and s3files:GetAccessPoint (NOT s3files:ClientRootAccess) constrained with ArnEquals on s3files:AccessPointArn to the specific access point (POSIX UID/GID + access-point root directory are the real scoping mechanism), and back it with the S3 Files file-system resource policy and security groups (inbound TCP 2049 on the mount-target SG referencing the runtime SG). BYO mounts require VPC network mode and are available on the serverless (microVM) compute, not on AgentCore Instances. Do not assume the two mount types are secured identically: S3 Files is NFSv4.2 over TLS with mandatory IAM authentication — TLS and IAM are always on and cannot be disabled — whereas EFS is NFSv4.1 over TLS and IAM authentication is used only when the execution role holds elasticfilesystem:ClientMount with an AccessPointArn condition, so on the EFS path you must grant those permissions to get IAM enforcement rather than inherit it. Either way the filesystem must be in the same account and VPC as the runtime; cross-account VPC configurations are not supported. Budget for failure modes too: a failed mount returns HTTP 424 with a 30-second per-mount timeout, and the limits are 5 filesystem configurations total (max 2 S3 Files, 2 EFS, 1 session storage) with mount paths of the form /mnt/<name>.

controls.section_title: Bedrock AgentCore — runtime, tool & code-execution isolation
controls.q: Is invocation of the agent runtime restricted to an approved network path AND an approved caller, so neither the internet nor a direct call that bypasses the gateway can reach the agent?
controls.h: Two distinct restrictions, both on the runtime. Network: confirm the runtime is invoked only through its PrivateLink endpoint — Private DNS on, security group scoped to application SGs on 443, resource-based policy denying invocation unless it arrives via an approved VPC/VPC-endpoint, so a leaked credential alone cannot reach the agent from the internet. Caller: where a gateway fronts the runtime to apply policy, guardrails, and rate limits, confirm the runtime also rejects invocations that did not come from that gateway — otherwise a caller inside the approved VPC can invoke the runtime ARN directly and skip every gateway control.
controls.ev: Runtime VPCE + Private DNS + SG scope + resource-policy aws:SourceVpc/SourceVpce deny; plus gateway-source restriction (SigV4 resource policy scoped to the gateway role, or allowedWorkloadConfiguration on customJWTAuthorizer)
controls.rec: Front the runtime with the data-plane interface endpoint com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore (which also serves Built-in Tools, Memory, and Identity), enable Private DNS, and scope its ENI security group to specific application security groups on TCP 443 rather than the whole VPC CIDR. Constrain the Runtime resource-based policy with aws:SourceVpc or aws:SourceVpce (add Bool aws:ViaAWSService:false on the Deny so legitimate AWS service-to-service traffic is not blocked) across the runtime invoke actions — InvokeAgentRuntime, InvokeAgentRuntimeForUser, InvokeAgentRuntimeCommand, InvokeAgentRuntimeCommandShell, InvokeAgentRuntimeWithWebSocketStream, and InvokeAgentRuntimeWithWebSocketStreamForUser (note InvokeGateway is a Gateway action, not a Runtime action). For OAuth-auth runtimes the resource policy must use Principal '*' with the VPC conditions carrying enforcement, and the endpoint policy must also allow GetRuntimeProtectedResourceMetadata (Principal '*') or OAuth discovery returns HTTP 403. Enforce the private path at create time with an SCP denying CreateAgentRuntime/UpdateAgentRuntime when bedrock-agentcore:subnets/securityGroups is null. SEPARATELY, close the gateway-bypass path: where the runtime is fronted by an AgentCore Gateway so that policy authorization, Guardrails, interceptors, and rate limits apply, a caller who invokes the runtime ARN directly skips every one of those controls — AWS states the gateway is only useful if it cannot be bypassed. Restrict the source on the RUNTIME, not the gateway, and the mechanism depends on inbound auth: for IAM (SigV4) runtimes attach a resource-based policy restricting invocation to the gateway's execution role (with the trust-policy hardening that requires, so the role cannot be assumed by anything else); for OAuth (JWT) runtimes set allowedWorkloadConfiguration on the customJWTAuthorizer to allow only the gateway's workload. Prefer IAM outbound authorization on the Runtime target so access can be restricted exclusively to the gateway role — token-passthrough outbound auth leaves the runtime doing its own authorization, which reintroduces the bypass unless the runtime itself validates the source. A network-path restriction alone does NOT close this: a caller inside the approved VPC can still reach the runtime directly.

controls.q: When the gateway exposes tools or APIs to a model, does it enforce its own inbound authentication and authorization, independent of what the model requests?
controls.h: Confirm the gateway requires a validated identity on every inbound call (JWT from your IdP, or SigV4) and authorizes the caller itself — rather than trusting that the model would only ask for permitted things. An unauthenticated (NONE) gateway in production is a critical gap.

controls.q: Is there an org-wide preventive control that blocks creating or updating a gateway with no inbound authorizer?
controls.h: Look for an SCP that denies gateway create/update when the authorizer type is NONE, so no team in the org can stand up an unauthenticated gateway — enforced at the control plane, not left to per-account discipline.
controls.ev: SCP denying CreateGateway/UpdateGateway when GatewayAuthorizerType is NONE
controls.rec: Deploy an AWS Organizations SCP at the OU level that denies bedrock-agentcore:CreateGateway and bedrock-agentcore:UpdateGateway unless bedrock-agentcore:GatewayAuthorizerType equals CUSTOM_JWT (use StringNotEquals so NONE, AWS_IAM, and an absent value all fail closed). GatewayAuthorizerType is a real request condition key on both actions with valid values AWS_IAM, CUSTOM_JWT, NONE (note AUTHENTICATE_ONLY is a valid authorizerType but is not an enumerated value of this condition key, so validate behavior for that case). Back it with a detective audit of GetGateway/ListGateways that alarms on any gateway whose authorizerType is not CUSTOM_JWT. Note that BOTH IAM artifacts disagree with the developer guide here — neither the machine-readable service model nor the Service Authorization Reference attaches this key to CreateGateway (the SAR lists only aws:RequestTag/${TagKey} and aws:TagKeys) — so prove the SCP in a test OU before relying on it: create a gateway with CUSTOM_JWT and confirm it succeeds, then repeat with a deliberately misspelled key name and confirm that one is denied. That pair distinguishes a key being evaluated from one being ignored. The StringNotEquals shape above is what makes this safe to deploy either way: if the key is not evaluated the condition is true, the deny fires, and gateway creation breaks visibly rather than silently permitting NONE. controls.q: Do the gateway's resource-based policy and target execution-role trust prevent a confused-deputy attack when an AWS service or another account is allowed to invoke it?
controls.h: Confirm any statement allowing a service principal (e.g. Lambda) or a broad principal to InvokeGateway — and any target execution-role trust of the AgentCore service — is constrained with both aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn to a specific account and function/gateway ARN, and that the resource policy targets the exact gateway ARN (no wildcard).
controls.ev: Gateway resource policy + execution-role trust with SourceAccount/SourceArn conditions
controls.rec: On the Gateway resource-based policy (PutResourcePolicy) and on each target execution role's trust policy, constrain the granted principal with both aws:SourceAccount = your account and aws:SourceArn scoped to the specific invoking function/gateway ARN, so a confused-deputy caller cannot make the service invoke the gateway or assume the role. Trust only bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com as the target execution-role principal, and scope the resource policy to the exact gateway ARN — wildcard Resource is rejected. For OAuth callers the resource policy must use Principal '*' (identity is in the JWT, not IAM), so pair it with the network conditions in AIR-ACR-GW-04. If a consent portal is attached to this gateway, audit a third trust policy: the portal assumes an executionRoleArn that lets the service principal bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com call sts:AssumeRole, and the documented setup tells you to create that role with the Condition block OMITTED, because the portal ARN does not exist until the portal does. That leaves a role any caller in the partition can have the service assume on their behalf, and nothing in the service re-checks it later. Treat the unconditioned role as a bootstrap state with a deadline: once CreateConsentPortal returns, put aws:SourceAccount = your account id and ArnLike aws:SourceArn = arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:<region>:<account-id>:consent-portal/<portal-id> back on the trust policy, and confirm both are present rather than assuming the setup guide's last step was done.

controls.q: Is the network path to the gateway restricted to approved private endpoints, rather than reachable over any network path?
controls.h: Confirm the gateway is reached through its dedicated PrivateLink endpoint with the ENI security group limited to specific application security groups on 443 (not the whole VPC CIDR), Private DNS enabled, and the resource policy constrained by aws:SourceVpc/aws:SourceVpce/aws:SourceIp so only the approved path is allowed.
controls.ev: Gateway VPCE + endpoint policy + SG scope + resource-policy network conditions
controls.rec: Restrict the gateway network path: create the Gateway-specific interface endpoint com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-agentcore.gateway (distinct from the Runtime data-plane endpoint), enable Private DNS, and scope its ENI security group to specific application security groups on TCP 443 rather than 0.0.0.0/0 or the full VPC CIDR. Constrain the Gateway resource-based policy with aws:SourceVpc or aws:SourceVpce (and aws:SourceIp where relevant) so only the approved private path can InvokeGateway; for OAuth-auth gateways the endpoint policy must use Principal '*' (endpoint policies match IAM principals, not OAuth users) with the VPC conditions carrying the enforcement. A future AgentCore Resource Control Policy (RCP) would let you enforce this private-path condition org-wide from Organizations regardless of caller account, but bedrock-agentcore is NOT in the RCP-supported service list (re-verified 2026-08-19 against the AWS Organizations list of services that support RCPs — RCPs cover S3, STS, KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager, ECR, OpenSearch Serverless and others, and no AgentCore prefix appears). So the per-resource policy plus SCP control-plane keys (e.g. bedrock-agentcore:PrivateEndpointType on targets) remain the enforcement mechanisms, and because RCPs constrain resources rather than principals, an SCP is not a substitute for the cross-account case an RCP would cover. controls.q: Is the gateway protected against volumetric abuse and malicious requests with rate limiting and a web-application firewall, given it is a public-facing agent entry point?
controls.h: The gateway is an AI-gateway entry point for agent traffic. Confirm native gateway rate limits cap per-caller consumption (requests, tokens, and connections) on a bounded dimension, an AWS WAF web ACL is associated for request-inspection and volumetric rules, and service quotas are treated as a ceiling — rather than assuming the managed service rate-limits per caller on its own.
controls.ev: ListGatewayRateLimits showing an ACTIVE limit on a bounded dimension + WAF web ACL associated to the gateway
controls.rec: Cap per-caller consumption with native gateway rate limits, then keep WAF in front for request inspection. Create limits with bedrock-agentcore-control create-gateway-rate-limit (or batch-put-gateway-rate-limits, which is upsert-idempotent and safe to run from CI), using each metric only where the service supports it: requests (catches retry loops) at second or minute on any target type, tokens (catches reasoning-heavy abuse) at minute only and only on inference targets, and connections (caps concurrent in-flight sessions rather than a rate) at second only. An unsupported metric/period pair — tokens on an MCP or Lambda gateway, or connections per minute — is a ValidationException, so it fails at creation rather than silently protecting nothing. Key them on a BOUNDED dimension: targetName, toolName, qualifiedModelId, $.context.jwt.<claim> (sub/team/tier), $.context.iam.principal, or $.context.iam.sourceIdentity. Never key on a per-request claim such as $.context.jwt.jti or nonce: that creates one bucket per request and silently disables throttling. Use rate 0 to block a caller outright during an incident (propagation is up to 30s). dimensionKeys are immutable after creation, so plan the dimension structure before production; * is allowed only in trailing positions and most-specific entry wins. CRITICAL — rate limits are FAIL-OPEN by design: if the rate-limit service times out or a dimension cannot be resolved, the request is ALLOWED, so they are abuse and cost protection, never an authorization boundary. Keep authentication (AIR-ACR-GW-01) and policy authorization (AIR-ACR-POL-01) as the security boundary. Separately associate a REGIONAL WAF web ACL with the gateway ARN (wafv2:AssociateWebACL + bedrock-agentcore:GatewayAssociateWebACL; one web ACL per gateway, CloudFront/global web ACLs unsupported), keep its failure mode at the default FAIL_CLOSE, and monitor WafBlocks/WafFailOpens/WafFailCloses. Treat adjustable service quotas (e.g. 5000 concurrent connections at both gateway and account level — 1000 is the separate quota for gateways per account) as a ceiling beneath which your own limits apply — the effective rate is the minimum of yours and the service-managed limit. Alarm on throttling via the aws.agentcore.gateway.throttle.customer.decision OTEL span attribute or the built-in Throttles metric.

controls.q: Where the gateway performs per-tool or per-tenant access control in a Lambda interceptor, is the interceptor fail-safe and does it avoid logging raw credentials?
controls.h: Request interceptors run before the target and can extract JWT claims, enforce per-tool/per-tenant decisions, and inject headers. Confirm they deny when authorization cannot be determined (never fail open), that passRequestHeaders is set deliberately (it is off by default), and that the interceptor never logs raw auth tokens.
controls.ev: Interceptor fail-safe tests + all-header propagation review + synthetic secret-header logging/destination checks
controls.rec: Configure Gateway Lambda interceptors fail-safe: a REQUEST interceptor (at most one per gateway) that denies when authorization cannot be determined — never fail open — for per-tool/per-tenant/parameter-level checks and token exchange, and a separate RESPONSE interceptor for output-side security (filtering unauthorized tools from tools/list, PII redaction) and observability. Set inputConfiguration.passRequestHeaders deliberately: false (default) excludes headers; true forwards ALL request headers to the interceptor Lambda, including any bearer tokens or credentials. It is not a header allowlist. Minimize propagation, sanitize before logging, and verify synthetic secret headers do not reach logs or unauthorized downstream destinations. Keep each interceptor lightweight with its own least-privilege role and bound external lookups. Scope the gateway service role's lambda:InvokeFunction to the specific interceptor ARNs, not a wildcard. Prefer the native primitives where they now cover what an interceptor used to have to implement: per-caller consumption caps belong in gateway rate limits (AIR-ACR-GW-05) and authorization decisions — including multi-step and per-tenant-budget rules — belong in the policy engine (AIR-ACR-POL-01, AIR-ACR-POL-07). Reserve interceptors for context enrichment and checks the policy engine genuinely cannot express, so the deterministic decision boundary stays in policy rather than in Lambda code (AIR-ACR-POL-05).

controls.q: Are the headers, query parameters, and tokens the gateway forwards to targets minimized to only what each target needs, so sensitive headers are not leaked downstream?
controls.h: Gateway targets have per-target allowlists for request/response headers and query parameters. Confirm they are minimized to essentials, that the Authorization header is injected only via an interceptor (it cannot be allowlisted at target creation), and that token propagation follows least privilege per target.
controls.ev: Target metadataConfiguration header/query allowlists minimized + Authorization via interceptor only
controls.rec: Minimize per-target header/query propagation: on each target's metadataConfiguration keep allowedRequestHeaders, allowedResponseHeaders, and allowedQueryParameters to only essential values (max 10 entries each, and each entry is a NAME not a value — header names are capped at 100 characters and query-parameter names at 40, per the CreateGatewayTarget service model; the allowlist bounds which names propagate, not payload size, so it is not a size control). The Authorization header cannot be allowlisted at target creation — it is forwarded only when an interceptor Lambda injects it (interceptor-provided Authorization overrides the credential-provider token), which is the intended path for custom auth; headers starting with X-Amzn- are prohibited except X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Custom-*. Optionally enforce the allowlist size/content org-wide with the bedrock-agentcore:AllowedRequestHeaders / AllowedResponseHeaders / AllowedQueryParameters condition keys on CreateGatewayTarget/UpdateGatewayTarget.

controls.q: Does each gateway target use an appropriate, least-privilege outbound authentication method, with no unauthenticated targets in production and no wildcard target permissions?
controls.h: Confirm the outbound auth per target matches the target type (Lambda via scoped service-role SigV4, MCP/OpenAPI via scoped OAuth or API key), that no production target uses No-Auth, and that a Lambda target's execution role grants invoke on the specific function ARN — not a wildcard.
controls.ev: Per-target outbound-auth enumeration + Lambda target scoped to specific function ARN
controls.rec: Enumerate gateway targets (ListGatewayTargets/GetGatewayTarget) and confirm each uses least-privilege outbound auth for its type: Lambda targets use the gateway service role (SigV4) scoped to the specific function ARN (no lambda:InvokeFunction wildcard); API Gateway targets use scoped service-role SigV4 or API key; MCP and OpenAPI targets use OAuth 2LO/3LO or API key (avoid No-Auth in production) with per-target scoped tokens rotated via Token Vault; token-exchange (RFC 8693 OBO) requires the gateway inbound auth to be JWT. Flag any target configured with No-Auth outbound (no credential provider) in production — the CredentialProviderType enum is GATEWAY_IAM_ROLE, OAUTH, API_KEY, CALLER_IAM_CREDENTIALS, or JWT_PASSTHROUGH, and No-Auth is expressed by omitting the credential-provider configuration rather than a NONE value — and prefer OAuth Client Credentials over No-Auth for MCP-on-Runtime targets. Where a target needs per-user consent, only grantType AUTHORIZATION_CODE (3LO) does: a CLIENT_CREDENTIALS target is machine-to-machine, needs no consent, and never appears on a consent portal's Connections page, so reaching user-owned data through one is a finding rather than a configuration choice. On each AUTHORIZATION_CODE target served by a consent portal, set defaultReturnUrl to exactly <portalUrl>/connect/callback. A missing or wrong value does not fail closed: the outbound provider returns the user somewhere other than the portal and the consent never binds to the session, which is the cross-user grant this flow exists to prevent. Targets created BEFORE the portal existed carry a different defaultReturnUrl or none at all, so enumerate and update the pre-existing ones instead of only the new ones. Review the target and outbound credential-provider NAMES before a portal goes live, because the consent portal renders them to end users verbatim on its Connections page. A name chosen for an operator audience is the text a user reads when deciding what to hand an agent access to, so a vague or misleading one turns a consent screen into a place users approve grants they did not understand.

controls.q: For gateway targets in private networks or on-premises, is egress routed through a private connection with least-privilege network controls, rather than over the public internet?
controls.h: Gateway can reach VPC-hosted or on-prem targets through a VPC Lattice Resource Gateway (an ENI in your subnets). Confirm private egress is used for private targets, the ENI security groups restrict to the needed ports/protocols, and outbound authorization to the target is configured (not 'no authorization').
controls.ev: VPC Lattice Resource Gateway egress config + ENI security-group scoping
controls.rec: Route gateway egress to VPC-hosted/on-prem MCP-server and OpenAPI targets through a VPC Lattice Resource Gateway (an ENI AgentCore places in your subnets; managed or self-managed) rather than the public internet, and scope the ENI security groups to the specific ports/protocols the target needs (typically 443). Ensure outbound authorization to the target is configured (SigV4/OAuth/API key, not No-Auth). In managed mode AgentCore creates, reuses and deletes the resource gateway and resource configuration for you and they are read-only in your account (no customer Lattice auth policy or VERIFIED_DOMAINS_ONLY knob, and no vpc-lattice:* IAM permissions, SCP change, or approval process needed); self-managed Lattice is the only cross-account path (shared to the gateway account with AWS RAM), requires vpc-lattice:* permissions (CreateResourceGateway, CreateResourceConfiguration, CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociation) and may need an SCP update or approval. Neither mode hands you a private-DNS preference on this path: AgentCore always creates and manages the service-network resource association itself in both modes, and privateDnsPreference is a Lattice resource-consumer setting rather than an AgentCore egress knob. Plan subnet IP capacity: ENI count equals the number of designated subnets. Enforce private-only targets with the bedrock-agentcore:PrivateEndpointType condition key on CreateGatewayTarget/UpdateGatewayTarget.

controls.q: Is an agent's persisted memory (conversation history, learned facts) encrypted with organization-controlled keys and partitioned so one agent or user cannot read another's records?
controls.h: Confirm memory is encrypted with a customer-managed key and that retrieval is scoped per agent/user — access checked against the caller's identity before records are returned, rather than any caller reading the whole store. The correct actor/scope must be supplied on every request; the service does not infer it.
controls.ev: Memory CMK + caller-bound actor/namespace configuration + positive and cross-tenant negative tests for each used access path
controls.rec: Encrypt AgentCore Memory with a customer-managed KMS key by setting encryptionKeyArn at CreateMemory, and enforce it org-wide with an SCP that denies bedrock-agentcore:CreateMemory when bedrock-agentcore:KmsKeyArn is null. The native controls are the bedrock-agentcore-memory-encryption-enabled Config rule / Security Hub BedrockAgentCore.3. For same-account partitioning, bind the requested actor and namespace to the authenticated caller before access. Apply action-appropriate IAM conditions, including bedrock-agentcore:namespace for supported long-term operations and actorId/sessionId for short-term event APIs, and test the exact read/write operations used. Normalize namespace values consistently with the documented leading/trailing slash behavior. The caller must supply the correct actorId/namespace on every request since the service never infers it. The current namespace developer guide names bedrock-agentcore:namespace and bedrock-agentcore:namespacePath in IAM guidance, while authorization-reference mappings differ. Record this conflict; do not blanket-rename conditions or infer effectiveness from either omission alone. namespacePath is also an API parameter and Cedar context field, so verify the IAM policy shape separately. Require an allowed same-tenant case and denied cross-tenant cases for every applicable API, including namespace prefixes, missing scope and direct record-ID access where used. Retain the exact condition keys/operators and observed results. Restrict direct paths that cannot enforce the intended boundary, or use the Gateway/Cedar boundary below; no documentation example replaces this tenant-isolation evidence. To bind memory access to an OAuth/JWT identity rather than an IAM principal — actorId must equal the token's sub claim, or a namespace path carried in a claim — front Memory with a Gateway whose policy engine evaluates Cedar policies, and pair it with a resource policy on the memory restricting direct access to that gateway ARN; roll out in LOG_ONLY first, because a Cedar policy that references a field the request does not carry reaches ACTIVE and then denies with a 403. Memory now supports resource-based policies: attach one via PutResourcePolicy on the exact memory ARN (a wildcard Resource is rejected as a validation error) to grant cross-account access — the caller in account B passes the full memory ARN as the memoryId, and AWS evaluates both the resource-based policy and the caller's identity-based policy — constrained with aws:SourceArn/aws:SourceAccount to avoid a confused deputy. (Residual drift, this one failing closed: the IAM service model still lists only gateway/runtime/runtime-endpoint as PutResourcePolicy resource types, so confirm a PutResourcePolicy + GetResourcePolicy round trip against a memory ARN before depending on it.) The sibling AgentCore resources that also take a customer-managed key at create time — Gateway, Policy Engine, and Evaluator — should likewise be set to a CMK rather than left on an AWS-owned or AWS-managed key.

config_rule.note: AWS managed. NON_COMPLIANT if AgentCore Memory has no customer-managed EncryptionKeyArn. Records AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Memory. Regional: launched in a subset of regions (incl. us-east-1); not yet GovCloud.

controls.q: For each memory resource, is the strategy type (built-in vs. custom) chosen deliberately against your LLM-governance rules, and does any custom strategy use a dedicated least-privilege execution role?
controls.h: Built-in strategies run extraction LLM calls in the AWS service account (no Bedrock permissions needed in yours). Custom strategies — including built-in-with-overrides — run bedrock:Invoke* in YOUR account via a passed execution role. Confirm the choice is intentional and that custom-strategy roles grant only the two InvokeModel actions, not a broad bedrock:* grant.
controls.ev: Per-memory strategy-type decision + custom-strategy execution-role policy (scoped bedrock:Invoke*)
controls.rec: Decide each Memory resource's strategy type against your LLM-governance requirements. Built-in strategies run extraction LLM calls in the AWS service account (uses AWS-managed Bedrock quotas, needs no bedrock:InvokeModel and no execution role in your account) — the simplest path where direct Bedrock access is restricted. Custom strategies (INCLUDING built-in-with-overrides) run bedrock:InvokeModel / bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream in your account under a passed memoryExecutionRoleArn (via iam:PassRole): make that a dedicated least-privilege role granting only those two InvokeModel actions on the specific model ARNs (never a shared role or bedrock:*), and scope its trust policy to bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com with aws:SourceAccount + aws:SourceArn. Where an SCP denies bedrock:* org-wide but a custom strategy is required, scope the exception to the specific execution-role ARN using aws:PrincipalArn (the InvokeModel call is attributed in CloudTrail to the assumed execution role, not a bare service principal) — or prefer built-in strategies / a self-managed strategy routed through your approved LLM gateway.

controls.q: Is sensitive data (PII/PHI) filtered out of the content before it is written into long-term memory, not only at the model's language boundary?
controls.h: Long-term memory persists extracted facts that may contain PII. Confirm a content-safety layer strips or blocks sensitive data before it is consolidated into a durable memory record — so an agent's memory does not become an unmanaged store of personal data — distinct from masking it later in logs.
controls.ev: PII-filtering step on the memory write/extraction path (Guardrail or interceptor)
controls.rec: Keep PII/PHI out of durable memory at write time rather than remediating it later: run the content destined for long-term memory through a Bedrock Guardrail sensitive-information filter (piiEntitiesConfig set to BLOCK or ANONYMIZE, plus custom regexesConfig for secrets/identifiers). Apply it via ApplyGuardrail on the extraction path, or a Gateway request interceptor / Cedar guardrails block ahead of any tool that writes memory — so personal data is masked or rejected before a record is consolidated. For custom/self-managed extraction strategies, apply the filter inside the extraction step (memoryExecutionRoleArn) before records are stored. This complements, not replaces, the log-side masking in the observability controls.

controls.ev: Memory record deletion/correction workflow

controls.q: Is content validated or attributed to a trusted source before it is written into an agent's persistent memory, so false or manipulated facts cannot be silently persisted?
controls.h: Distinct from purging bad data after the fact (AIR-ACR-MEM-02): confirm a write-time control (source attribution, validation, or provenance tagging) governs what enters long-term memory, so an attacker cannot inject a false 'fact' — a fabricated VIP status, a poisoned project-context cache, or a contradictory record — that the agent later trusts as its own memory.
controls.ev: Write-time provenance/validation + caller-bound namespaceVariables + namespace-key constraints and replacement-update review + extraction-failure alert evidence
controls.rec: Govern what enters long-term memory at write time: restrict bedrock-agentcore:CreateEvent to trusted principals scoped by actorId/sessionId condition keys so only attributable sources can seed memory. Use a custom or self-managed extraction strategy (memoryExecutionRoleArn) to validate/attribute content before records are consolidated. Tag provenance using CreateMemory indexedKeys plus record metadata so retrieval can filter by source (RetrieveMemoryRecords metadataFilters). Place a Gateway request Lambda interceptor / Cedar policy ahead of tools that write memory to reject unvalidated or untrusted content rather than persisting it as a trusted fact. For custom namespaces, configure namespaceKeys on CreateMemory/UpdateMemory and bind CreateEvent extractionConfig.namespaceVariables to trusted tenant/session context. Keys and values must be lowercase; use allowedValues and regexPattern for the permitted values. If both constraints are configured, a value must satisfy BOTH. Treat input validation as distinct from authorization: an allowed tenant name must still belong to the caller. Treat UpdateMemory namespaceKeys as a full replacement: read GetMemory, merge the intended change with the complete approved key set, and review the replacement before updating. Remove strategy-template references before removing a key; a still-referenced key cannot be removed. Exercise a missing variable referenced by a strategy template: CreateEvent can succeed and store the short-term event while extraction is skipped for that strategy. Enable the relevant vended logs/metrics and alert on NamespaceResolutionFailure; a successful write response alone is not evidence that long-term extraction or tenant routing succeeded.
