controls.q: Is model bias or fairness evaluated as part of the approval process for models that inform decisions about individuals?
controls.h: Look for a bias/fairness evaluation step in the approval workflow where the model's decisions affect people, measured against defined thresholds (e.g. a four-fifths / disparate-impact ratio for protected classes) rather than a subjective judgment. For regulated decisions (lending, employment, insurance), confirm the evaluation is tied to the applicable rule.
controls.ev: Bias/fairness evaluation record with thresholds
controls.rec: Add a bias step to the approval workflow that computes the standardized pre-training and post-training bias metrics against defined thresholds — in particular Disparate Impact (DI) held to the four-fifths / 0.8-1.25 ratio for protected classes, alongside Difference in Positive Proportions in Predicted Labels (DPPL) and the pre-training Difference in Proportions of Labels (DPL). SageMaker Clarify is no longer open to new customers, so do not build a new workflow on Clarify processing jobs, SageMakerClarifyProcessor, clarify.BiasConfig or run_bias(); existing customers can continue as normal. New accounts should compute the same published DI/DPPL/DPL formulas with pandas/scikit-learn in a SageMaker Processing step (replacing ClarifyCheckStep) — the metric definitions remain documented on the Clarify pre-training and post-training bias metrics pages — using the AWS-published open-source SageMaker AI monitoring solutions as the reference implementation and logging results to a SageMaker AI MLflow App. Amazon Bedrock Evaluations and Guardrails are not a substitute: AWS scopes them to foundation-model evaluation, not predictive/tabular bias detection. For regulated decisions (lending, employment, insurance) tie the threshold to the governing rule (e.g. ECOA/Reg B) and store the bias report as the evaluation record on the Model Card rather than relying on subjective judgment.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — compute & container image security
controls.q: Are container images used for self-hosted AI/agent workloads scanned for known vulnerabilities before deployment?
controls.h: Confirm image scanning runs as a gate before deployment, with findings above an agreed severity blocking release. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) the image still lives in ECR, so check the registry-level configuration (`aws ecr get-registry-scanning-configuration`, expect `scanType: ENHANCED` with `CONTINUOUS_SCAN`) and confirm Inspector's `ecrImageInUseCount` / `ecrImageLastInUseAt` filters tie findings back to live workloads — AWS states this in-use mapping "is also supported on Fargate with Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS." For Lambda container-image agents check that same ECR configuration; for .zip agents check Inspector Lambda standard scanning and Lambda code scanning are both activated (standard is a prerequisite for code), that the function has been invoked or updated in the last 90 days and is `$LATEST`, and that it is not excluded by the `InspectorExclusion` / `InspectorCodeExclusion` tags. On Lambda MicroVMs this does not apply as a registry gate, because a MicroVM image is not an ECR artifact and Inspector has no MicroVM resource type — verify instead that CI scans the Dockerfile base image and lockfiles before the artifact is uploaded to S3.
controls.ev: Image scan results + block-on-severity policy
controls.rec: Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector integration) with scan-on-push plus continuous re-scan on the repositories holding AI/agent images, so images are scanned for both OS and language-package CVEs. Route Inspector findings via EventBridge to gate the CI/CD deploy stage, failing promotion when any finding meets or exceeds the agreed severity threshold. Configure this at the registry level: the repository-level scan-on-push setting has been deprecated in favor of registry-level scan configurations. ECS and Lambda container-image agents pull from ECR, so enhanced scanning applies unchanged. For Lambda .zip agents use Amazon Inspector Lambda standard scanning (dependencies) plus Lambda code scanning (custom code), which rescan automatically on deploy and whenever a newly published CVE becomes relevant; record the two coverage holes — standard scanning "doesn't scan the AWS SDK dependency installed by default in the Lambda runtime environment," and Inspector "does not support scanning Lambda functions encrypted with customer managed keys," so a CMK-encrypted agent function needs a CI-side equivalent. On Lambda MicroVMs there is no post-build scan target, so shift the gate left into CI over the Dockerfile base image and lockfiles, and rely on ECR enhanced scanning only for a private-ECR base image you `FROM`.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — compute & container image security
controls.q: Are only images from an approved, controlled registry allowed to run in the environment hosting AI workloads?
controls.h: Check for enforcement that blocks pulling images from unapproved public registries into the AI workload environment. On ECS check the enforcement path rather than IAM — the ECS condition-key set contains no key for the image, image URI, registry or repository — so look for a CloudFormation Guard Hook (`AWS::CloudFormation::GuardHook`, `FailureMode: FAIL`) covering the IaC path, an ECR VPC endpoint policy covering the pull path, or a `PRE_SCALE_UP` deployment lifecycle hook covering service deployments; confirm whether standalone `RunTask` agents exist, since they pass through no deployment hook. On Lambda the source is structurally ECR in the same Region and account as the function, so check the IAM/SCP conditions on `lambda:CreateFunction`/`lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` instead of looking for a launch-time allow-list. On Lambda MicroVMs check the OS layer uses a Lambda-published managed base image (`base-image-arn`) and that the build role's `s3:GetObject` and `ecr:BatchGetImage` are scoped to your own artifact bucket and repositories.
controls.ev: Registry allow-list / admission-control configuration
controls.rec: Standardize on private Amazon ECR repositories as the single approved source, and use ECR pull-through cache rules (with a scoped-down registry permissions policy and repository creation templates) so upstream public images are vetted and mirrored rather than pulled directly. On EKS, enforce with an admission controller (e.g. an OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno policy) that rejects any pod whose image is not from the approved ECR registry. On ECS enforce provenance outside IAM, because no ECS condition key can express "images must come from this registry": combine a CloudFormation Guard Hook (which intercepts CloudFormation-mediated changes only, not a direct `RegisterTaskDefinition` call), an ECR interface-endpoint policy on both `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.dkr` and `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api` (load-bearing from Fargate platform version 1.4.0, when image-pull traffic moved onto the task ENI), and a `PRE_SCALE_UP` lifecycle-hook Lambda for service deployments. Write that endpoint policy as two statements or it will break every pull: scope `ecr:BatchGetImage`, `ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer` and `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability` to `arn:aws:ecr:<region>:<account_id>:repository/*`, but keep `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken` on `"Resource": "*"` because it does not support resource-level permissions — a policy that scopes it to a repository ARN authorizes no auth token, so no task can pull at all. Add `aws:PrincipalOrgID` as the cross-account bound. On Lambda the platform already constrains the source to ECR, so the remaining work is restricting which repository — scope `lambda:CreateFunction`/`UpdateFunctionCode` to a pipeline role, pin `ImageUri` by `@sha256:` digest, and set ECR `imageTagMutability: IMMUTABLE`. Do not extend the pull-through-cache pattern to a container-image function, though: AWS states "AWS Lambda doesn't support pulling container images from Amazon ECR using a pull through cache rule," so the cache repository cannot be the function's image source — add a CI step that copies the vetted image into an ordinary private repository in the function's own Region and account, and point `ImageUri` at that digest. On Lambda MicroVMs the OS base image must be Lambda-published (`base-image-arn` takes a Lambda-managed base image found through `ListManagedMicrovmImages`) and so cannot come from an arbitrary registry; restrict the container base you `FROM` by scoping the build role's `ecr:BatchGetImage`, `ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer` and `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability` to your own repository ARNs while leaving `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken` on `"Resource": "*"` — the same two-statement split as the endpoint policy above, and worth stating because AWS's own build-role example leaves all four unscoped.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — compute & container image security
controls.q: Do containers running AI workloads run as non-root with the minimum OS-level privileges needed, rather than elevated/privileged mode by default?
controls.h: Verify pod/container security context disallows privileged mode and root execution unless explicitly justified. On ECS check the container definition for `user` (a non-root uid), `readonlyRootFilesystem: true` and `linuxParameters.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`, with Security Hub [ECS.20] and [ECS.5] as the detective backstop. On the Fargate launch type, privileged mode, host namespace sharing, `linuxParameters.devices`, `maxSwap`, `pidMode: host` and `networkMode: host` are all unavailable, so that class of hardening is moot rather than failing — note that [ECS.4] therefore passes vacuously on Fargate, since `privileged` cannot be set there at all, making it evidence of the launch type rather than of hardening. On ECS Managed Instances those knobs are settable again, so [ECS.4] carries real signal there. On Lambda this is satisfied by construction — "Lambda follows security best practices by defining a default Linux user with least-privileged permissions. This means that you don't need to specify a USER in your Dockerfile," on a filesystem where only `/tmp` is writable — so verify only that the agent image does not depend on root-owned files. On Lambda MicroVMs check `additionalOsCapabilities` is unset, since its only valid value is `["ALL"]`.
controls.ev: Container security-context configuration review
controls.rec: Apply the EKS Pod Security Standards restricted profile via Pod Security Admission namespace labels (enforce mode) so pods must set runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, privileged: false, and drop all Linux capabilities. Codify the same securityContext requirements in a Kyverno/Gatekeeper policy for exceptions handling, granting privileged access only to explicitly justified system workloads. On ECS set `user` to a non-root uid, `readonlyRootFilesystem: true` and `linuxParameters.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` — on Fargate the only documented addable capability is `SYS_PTRACE`, for in-task observability tooling — and add a preventive IAM guardrail at `RegisterTaskDefinition` denying `ecs:privileged`. Two caveats on that guardrail: AWS's own published example uses the `Bool` operator while the Service Authorization Reference types `ecs:privileged` as String, so verify it actually denies by attempting a privileged `RegisterTaskDefinition` or running `aws iam simulate-principal-policy` rather than assuming attachment equals enforcement; and scope the settings to Linux, since `user`, `readonlyRootFilesystem` and `linuxParameters` are unsupported for Windows containers and Security Hub marks those task definitions `NOT_APPLICABLE`. On Lambda this is the platform default and there is no securityContext to configure; the only work is keeping the agent image free of root-owned file dependencies. On Lambda MicroVMs leave `additionalOsCapabilities` unset and treat a request for `["ALL"]` as an exception requiring justification, noting AWS bounds the consequence — "capabilities are applied within the VM isolation boundary and do not affect the host or other MicroVMs" — so root inside a Firecracker microVM is not the shared-kernel breakout risk it is in a pod.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — compute & container image security
controls.q: Is the underlying host/node OS patched on a defined cadence, with a way to detect nodes that have fallen behind?
controls.h: Look for automated patch management and drift detection for the compute layer hosting AI workloads. On ECS/Fargate, Lambda and Lambda MicroVMs this does not apply as written, because AWS owns and patches the host: "When using Fargate, customers are not responsible for securing the compute infrastructure that runs their containers," and Lambda workers are AWS-managed Nitro instances in an account customers cannot see, where "neither customers nor AWS operators can connect to a host running customer workloads" — so there is no AMI to pin, no node to cordon and no Inspector EC2 scanning target. controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — compute & container image security
controls.q: Is there a signed/verified supply chain for the AI application code and dependencies deployed into these workloads?
controls.h: Confirm build artifacts are signed and verified at deploy time, with dependency provenance checked, not an unauthenticated pull-and-run. On ECS check for ECR managed signing (`ecr:PutSigningConfiguration` carrying a `signingConfiguration.rules[].signingProfileArn`) plus a verification gate at deploy — an ECS service `DeploymentLifecycleHook` at `PRE_SCALE_UP` whose Lambda runs the Notation CLI and returns `hookStatus: FAILED` to force rollback. Confirm the Lambda enforces rather than logs (in AWS's reference implementation this is the sample function's own failure-behavior switch, not an ECS API setting) and that `timeoutConfiguration.action` is `ROLLBACK` rather than `CONTINUE`; confirm too that no standalone `RunTask` agents exist, since every documented lifecycle stage is a service-deployment stage. On Lambda .zip agents check a code signing configuration is attached with `UntrustedArtifactOnDeployment` set to `Enforce` rather than the default `Warn`, that layers are signed by an allowed profile too, and that `lambda:CodeSigningConfigArn` is required org-wide. On Lambda container-image agents and Lambda MicroVMs there is no platform-side signature check, so verify signing happens in CI, verification happens in the pipeline before `UpdateFunctionCode` / `CreateMicrovmImage`, and the deployed reference is digest-pinned against an `IMMUTABLE` ECR repository.
controls.ev: Artifact signing/verification configuration
controls.rec: Sign container images with AWS Signer and the Notation client (via a Signer signing profile) so signatures are stored with the image in ECR, and verify them at deploy time on EKS using an admission controller with an AWS Signer plugin - Gatekeeper+Ratify or Kyverno (kyverno-notation-aws) - configured against a Notation trust store and trust policy, so only signed, verified images are admitted. Establish dependency provenance by exporting a software bill of materials per image with Amazon Inspector SBOM export (CreateSbomExport, CycloneDX 1.4/SPDX 2.3), and treat ECR enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector) as a separate CVE vulnerability gate, not a provenance or signing control. Signed source/build attestations (e.g. SLSA/in-toto provenance) remain a CI-layer control outside these AWS services. On ECS use Amazon ECR managed signing, which signs images with AWS Signer on push (the pushing principal needs `signer:SignPayload`), and verify at deploy with a service deployment lifecycle hook at `PRE_SCALE_UP` — AWS itself notes that "many people refer to this as an admission controller." State the two ways it is not equivalent to a Kubernetes validating webhook: it is a service-deployment construct only, so a standalone `RunTask` — a common shape for a batch or on-demand agent — passes through no hook, and enforcement is rollback-shaped (`FAILED` rolls the deployment back to the last successful service revision) rather than rejecting the task-definition revision at registration. On Lambda .zip agents use AWS Signer with a code signing configuration set to `UntrustedArtifactOnDeployment: Enforce`; Lambda then validates integrity, expiry, mismatch and revocation, and covers layers — but note it only prevents new deployments of unsigned code, so existing unsigned code keeps running until redeployed. This does not apply to Lambda container-image agents, because code signing configurations are .zip-only and Lambda verifies no signature on an image it pulls; nor to Lambda MicroVMs, where neither `CreateMicrovmImage` nor `AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage` accepts a signing-profile parameter and there is no hook at `RunMicrovm`. For those two, sign with Notation in CI, verify in the pipeline before the deploy call, and compensate with digest pinning, ECR `IMMUTABLE` tags, IAM restriction of the deploy action to a pipeline role, and — on MicroVMs — the version-activation gate (`update-microvm-image-version --status INACTIVE`, where the request field is `status`, not the `state` the user-guide example writes, which is a separate read-only lifecycle field with no `INACTIVE` value) as the release control.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — compute & container image security
controls.q: Are compute resources for self-hosted agents isolated per workload/tenant at the node or namespace level, preventing one workload from accessing another's resources?
controls.h: Check for namespace/node-level isolation between distinct AI workloads, not a single shared, undifferentiated pool. On ECS/Fargate this is inherited and stronger than namespace isolation — "Each task running on Fargate has its own isolation boundary and does not share the underlying kernel, CPU resources, memory resources, or elastic network interface with another task." Establish the capacity type by two fields rather than one: the task definition's `requiresCompatibilities` should be `FARGATE`, and the service or task should resolve to Fargate capacity either through `launchType: FARGATE` or a `capacityProviderStrategy` naming only `FARGATE`/`FARGATE_SPOT`. A Managed Instances workload is identified by a `capacityProviderStrategy` with `launchType` omitted — you cannot request `MANAGED_INSTANCES` as a `launchType`, though `DescribeTasks` can return it — and on EC2, Managed Instances and ECS Anywhere "there is no task isolation," so containers can potentially reach credentials, environment variables and temporary files belonging to other tasks on the same instance. Verify each agent has its own `taskRoleArn` distinct from the execution role, and assess any sidecar tool-executor separately, since containers in one task share a network namespace and "can inter-communicate over localhost." On Lambda verify one function and one execution role per agent — "runtime environments are never reused across functions, function versions, or AWS accounts" — and that the handler scopes data to local variables and deletes `/tmp` files, since reuse within one function is possible. On Lambda MicroVMs verify one MicroVM per session or tenant and that tenant-specific material arrives via `runHookPayload`, not image-level `environmentVariables`, which are shared across every MicroVM run from that image version.
controls.ev: Namespace/node isolation configuration
controls.rec: Isolate distinct AI workloads/tenants into separate EKS namespaces with Kubernetes network policies enforcing default-deny ingress/egress between them, and scope credentials per workload using IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) or EKS Pod Identity so each pod assumes only its own IAM role. For stronger separation, pin sensitive workloads to dedicated managed node groups (via node taints/affinity) rather than a single shared node pool. On ECS/Fargate this comes for free and is the reason to prefer Fargate for agents — "each workload runs on its own single use, single tenant compute instance" — so the remaining work is giving each agent its own task role (where `bedrock:InvokeModel` and tool permissions belong, kept separate from the execution role, whose credentials "aren't directly accessible by the containers in the task") and not co-locating an untrusted tool-executor as a sidecar. On ECS Managed Instances a per-task role is necessary but not sufficient, because there is no task isolation on the shared instance; separate hostile tenants onto different instances or move them to Fargate. On Lambda the boundary is a per-environment Firecracker microVM on AWS-managed Nitro workers; one function plus one dedicated execution role per agent is the isolation unit, and the residual risk to ask about is intra-function reuse, since "it is possible for data from one Lambda function to be shared with another invocation of the same function instance." Where tenants genuinely have to share one function, that residual risk has a native answer: Lambda tenant isolation mode routes each tenant identifier to its own execution environments, which "are never reused across different tenants." Assess its edges, because they constrain the design rather than just the setting — it can only be turned on at function creation and is immutable afterwards, the tenant ID then becomes mandatory on every invoke or the call fails, the execution role still applies to all tenants (so it is an environment boundary, not a permissions boundary), and it is unsupported with function URLs, provisioned concurrency and SnapStart. On Lambda MicroVMs run one microVM per tenant session — the resource "represents an isolated compute environment for a single tenant, user session, or job" — and pass tenant-scoped credentials through the `/run` hook, because a MicroVM has exactly one `executionRoleArn`; AWS documents no metadata service, token requirement or hop limit for the guest, so assume any process in the sandbox can use that role and do not rely on an IMDSv2-style shield that is not documented to exist.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — compute & container image security
controls.q: Is there a tested ability to quickly isolate or terminate a specific compromised container/instance without taking down the entire cluster or fleet?
controls.h: Confirm a documented, exercised containment procedure exists for isolating a single compromised workload. On ECS confirm the runbook uses `ecs:StopTask` with a `reason` string, and that egress containment works by stripping rules from a security group the agent service owns exclusively — the deny-all-SG swap ported from EC2 fails because the task ENI is a fully managed ECS feature that your account "can't detach or modify." Confirm `ListTasks` is used to find sibling tasks running the same image, and that isolation (blocking inbound and outbound traffic, per GuardDuty's ECS remediation guidance) is preferred over termination so evidence survives. On Lambda confirm the runbook sets reserved concurrency to 0 and that a code or configuration update is used to force running execution environments to be replaced. On Lambda MicroVMs confirm containment is `TerminateMicrovm` or `SuspendMicrovm` plus halting token minting, and that in-guest evidence is captured over the shell before termination, because "network connectors are specified when you call run-microvm and cannot be changed while a MicroVM is running." On all of these, confirm the runbook does not call for a memory dump or disk image: the host is unreachable and there is no exec path into a Lambda execution environment at all.
controls.ev: Containment runbook + exercise record
controls.rec: Maintain a tested runbook to isolate a single compromised workload: apply a deny-all Kubernetes network policy to the affected pod, cordon and drain the node to stop new scheduling, and — if the underlying EC2 instance is suspected compromised — swap it to an isolation security group before terminating the node. Automate this containment (e.g. GuardDuty EKS Protection finding triggering an SSM/EventBridge response) and rehearse it regularly so a single container/instance can be quarantined without disrupting the rest of the cluster or fleet. On ECS give every agent service its own security group so containment can strip that group's ingress and egress rules surgically — a deny-all NACL takes out the whole subnet, and the SG swap is blocked because the task ENI is service-managed. Terminate with `ecs:StopTask` (SIGTERM, 30-second default timeout, then SIGKILL) only after evidence capture, and automate on an EventBridge `ECS Task State Change` or a GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring finding — Runtime Monitoring does cover ECS on Fargate, delivered as a GuardDuty-managed sidecar, so phrase the sensor requirement as "automated agent configuration is enabled and coverage shows the agent on every task," never as a node DaemonSet, which Fargate cannot schedule; and read the capacity types carefully, because the names collide — Runtime Monitoring's EC2 coverage "also supports Amazon ECS Managed EC2 Instances," meaning container instances you run yourself, while AWS separately states it "doesn't support applications running on Amazon ECS Managed Instances," the AWS-managed capacity type, which offers no SSH, no SSM and no agent-install path, so there is no runtime sensor to fall back to there and the containment trigger has to come from CloudTrail, CloudWatch Logs and the agent's own telemetry. On Lambda use `put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0` — AWS's documented off-switch — plus `PutFunctionRecursionConfig` set to `Terminate` for self-triggering agent loops. On Lambda MicroVMs containment is kill-the-sandbox rather than quarantine-the-sandbox: `TerminateMicrovm` or `SuspendMicrovm`, plus stopping `CreateMicrovmAuthToken`; connectors are immutable for a running MicroVM and editing a shared one disrupts every MicroVM using it. Across all of these, host-level acquisition (disk image, memory capture, EBS snapshot) is unavailable — GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 "doesn't support malware scans for AWS Fargate workloads," and there is no instance ARN or attached volume to snapshot — so pre-arrange the evidence set ante-mortem: CloudWatch Logs, VPC Flow Logs on the task or connector ENI, CloudTrail with `taskArn` in the session context, and ECS Exec or MicroVM shell transcripts.

controls.q: For self-hosted models, are the model weights obtained from a verified source and integrity-checked before they are loaded, rather than pulled from a public hub and trusted on arrival?
controls.h: The weights are the asset in a self-hosted deployment, and the load path is where they are most exposed. Confirm two things: that the artifact came from a source you control or verified (a digest or signature checked against a recorded value, not just a repository name), and that it is checked immediately before load rather than only on download — a file staged on a shared volume can be replaced between the two. Distinct from AIR-SLF-CMP-01/02, which govern the container image; the weights are usually mounted or downloaded separately and never pass through image scanning. On ECS/Fargate verify the weights are mirrored into S3 or an EFS volume you control (with `transitEncryption: ENABLED` on the `efsVolumeConfiguration`) rather than pulled from a public hub at task start, that the digest re-check runs in the container entrypoint, and that the read permission sits on the task role rather than the execution role; Fargate ephemeral storage is already encrypted with an AES-256 key managed by Fargate and can take a customer-managed key at the cluster level, gated by the `ecs:fargate-ephemeral-storage-kms-key` condition key. On Lambda verify the digest check runs immediately before load in the handler or container entrypoint, sized against the 10 GB image limit or the `/tmp` ceiling (512–10,240 MB, encrypted at rest with an AWS-managed key). On Lambda MicroVMs verify weights are fetched or verified in the `/run` hook rather than baked into the snapshot, since build-time content is shared across every MicroVM run from the same image version. On all of these the IMDSv2 (`HttpTokens=required`) and Nitro Enclave / NitroTPM steps below do not apply, because there is no customer EC2 instance, no metadata service you configure and no attestation document — the substitute is least-privilege scoping of the single task or execution role plus egress restriction.
controls.ev: Recorded expected digest for each deployed model + the load-time verification step that compares against it, plus the KMS key protecting the artifact at rest
controls.rec: Treat model weights as a signed build artifact rather than a download. Mirror the model into an S3 bucket or ECR repository you control instead of pulling from a public hub at start-up, record the artifact's SHA256 digest at ingest, and re-verify that digest in the container entrypoint immediately before load so a substituted or truncated file fails closed rather than serving. Encrypt the artifact at rest with a customer-managed KMS key (SSE-KMS on the bucket, or ECR encryption with a CMK for weights packaged as an OCI artifact) and scope read access to the inference workload's own role — not the whole node role — so the blast radius of a compromised sidecar is not the weights. Where weights ship inside the image, AIR-SLF-CMP-05's AWS Signer/Notation signing already covers provenance and this control is answered by that pipeline. For the highest-sensitivity case, where the operator of the instance must not be able to read the weights either, escalate to hardware-attested key release per AIR-FND-DAT-10: a GPU-served model cannot run inside a Nitro Enclave, so the applicable mechanism is an Attestable AMI with NitroTPM gating the decryption key on the instance's boot measurement. Enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) on any instance whose role can read the artifact, since IMDSv1 turns a server-side request forgery in the inference server into weight-exfiltration credentials. On ECS/Fargate keep the mirror-and-verify pattern, but note GPUs are unavailable on the Fargate launch type: `resourceRequirements` of `type: GPU` needs either EC2 container instances running the ECS GPU-optimized AMI with `ECS_ENABLE_GPU_SUPPORT=true` in the agent config, or ECS Managed Instances, where AWS pre-installs the NVIDIA drivers and CUDA toolkit and there is no AMI or agent setting to configure. So a Fargate agent serves a CPU-sized model within the task size ceiling or calls a remote endpoint. Scope the S3 or EFS read to the task role rather than the execution role or a shared node role, and consider a customer-managed key for Fargate ephemeral storage — the key policy needs `kms:GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext`, `kms:CreateGrant` and `kms:DescribeKey`, spelled as in the AWS page's JSON example rather than its prose bullet, which carries a capitalization typo (`WithoutPlainText`) that IAM will not reject and that fails the task launch with an opaque encryption error. Note also that multi-Region keys and KMS aliases are unsupported there, it requires platform version 1.4.0 or later, it is unavailable for Windows task clusters, and the store is destroyed with the task. On Lambda apply the same digest-at-load rule inside the handler or entrypoint. On Lambda MicroVMs fetch or re-verify in the `/run` hook rather than at image build, and re-validate in `/resume`, because a suspended microVM can hold stale credentials and connections in preserved memory. The hardware-attested escalation path above is EC2-only: none of ECS/Fargate, Lambda or Lambda MicroVMs exposes an enclave, a vTPM or an attestation document, and compute runs in an AWS-owned account, so where the operator must be unable to read the weights the answer is to move the workload to EC2 rather than to reconfigure these platforms.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Are secrets and credentials used by self-hosted agent workloads injected at runtime from a managed secrets store, rather than baked into images or environment files?
controls.h: Confirm secrets are pulled from a managed store at runtime; scan images/config for embedded credentials. On ECS (Fargate or ECS Managed Instances), confirm the container definition uses a `secrets` array of `valueFrom` ARNs (Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store) with a task execution role, and that Security Hub [ECS.8] / AWS Config `ecs-no-environment-secrets` is clean — that check fails when `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, or `ECS_ENGINE_AUTH_DATA` appear in `environment`, and it evaluates only the latest active task-definition revision. On Lambda, confirm the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension or an in-process SDK fetch rather than a plaintext environment variable. On Lambda MicroVMs, confirm per-session material arrives through `runHookPayload` and is resolved in the `/run` hook — image-level `environmentVariables` are set at image build time and injected into the snapshot, so every MicroVM launched from that image version shares them and nothing baked there is per-session or per-tenant.
controls.ev: Secrets-injection configuration + image scan for embedded secrets
controls.rec: Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager (or Parameter Store) and inject them at runtime rather than baking them into images or env files. On EKS, mount them via the Secrets Store CSI Driver with the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider (ASCP), or fetch in-memory with the Secrets Manager Agent, granting pod-scoped access through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA. On EC2, retrieve at boot using the instance role and require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required), since a retrieval path that depends on the instance role is only as strong as the metadata service that hands out that role's credentials. Scan images and manifests to confirm no embedded secrets remain. Note the residual exposure this control does not remove: an injected secret is plaintext in the workload's memory, so anyone with host or node access can read it. Where a specific secret must stay inaccessible even to the host — a signing key, a model-decryption key — that is the case for hardware-attested isolation rather than better injection hygiene, and AIR-FND-DAT-10 covers binding its release to an attested measurement. The same rule holds on every host; only the injection primitive changes. On ECS (Fargate or ECS Managed Instances) use `secrets: [{"name":...,"valueFrom":"<secret-or-parameter-ARN>"}]` plus `logConfiguration.secretOptions` for log-driver credentials, granting retrieval to the task execution role — the role the ECS container and Fargate agents assume to make those calls on your behalf — while the agent's own AWS permissions stay on the separate task role. On ECS Managed Instances add the co-tenancy caveat AWS states plainly: unlike Fargate there is no task isolation, so containers can potentially read credentials, environment variables, and temporary files belonging to other tasks on the same instance, including data left by previously running tasks — so an agent handling restricted material belongs on Fargate. On Lambda use the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension (localhost HTTP interface on port 2773, cache TTL 300 seconds by default and settable only in the 0–300 second range via `SECRETS_MANAGER_TTL` / `SSM_PARAMETER_STORE_TTL`) or a direct SDK call under the function's own execution role. Prefer that over encrypting environment variables: `KmsKeyArn` does encrypt the function's environment variables (and its SnapStart snapshots and the optimized container image, though not the image in ECR) with a customer-managed key, but Amazon Inspector does not scan Lambda functions encrypted with customer managed keys for either standard or code scanning, so setting it forfeits the Inspector tier AIR-SLF-RT-04 asks for; keeping secrets out of environment variables entirely avoids the trade-off. On Lambda MicroVMs pass only a reference — a Secrets Manager path, a session token, or a signed URL — in `runHookPayload` and resolve it in the `/run` hook under the execution role, because the snapshot model makes any build-time value shared across every MicroVM from that image version; AWS documents no customer-managed KMS key parameter for a MicroVM image or its snapshot, so do not treat a secret written into the image as protected by your own key. On Fargate, ECS Managed Instances, Lambda, and Lambda MicroVMs the IMDSv2 `HttpTokens=required` step does not apply because there is no customer-configurable instance metadata service to harden — but on ECS the risk it mitigates does not disappear: the task role's credentials are still vended over a link-local HTTP path (`AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI` at `169.254.170.2`) that an SSRF in the agent can reach, so the mitigations are a least-privilege task role kept distinct from the execution role plus the egress restriction in AIR-SLF-RT-02. Lambda and each MicroVM have a single execution role, so scoping that one role tightly is the whole of it. Where the escalation to hardware-attested isolation is warranted, note that it lands on EC2-based hosts only — EC2 directly, or EKS on an enclave-enabled managed node group with the Nitro Enclaves Kubernetes device plugin — and not on Fargate, ECS Managed Instances, Lambda, or MicroVMs, none of which expose an enclave, a vTPM, or an attestation document; on EKS keep node-level separation too, because every pod and container on a node running the device plugin can communicate with that node's enclave.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Is outbound network egress from self-hosted agent workloads restricted to an approved allow-list of destinations?
controls.h: Look for an egress control (network policy, firewall, proxy) limiting outbound destinations rather than open egress. On ECS/Fargate, check the security group attached to the task's own ENI — `awsvpc` is the only network mode available to Fargate tasks, so a per-task egress firewall already exists and the question is whether its outbound rules are scoped. On ECS Managed Instances, check the task is in `awsvpc` mode rather than `host` mode: `awsvpc` gives each task its own ENI and security group, while in `host` mode tasks share the instance's network namespace and there is no per-task egress boundary to scope. On Lambda, check `VpcConfig.SubnetIds` / `SecurityGroupIds` are populated (AWS Config `lambda-inside-vpc`, Security Hub [Lambda.3]) — a function with no `VpcConfig` has unrestricted internet egress and no security group, NACL, or route table to constrain it. On Lambda MicroVMs, check `run-microvm` passes `--egress-network-connectors` pointing at a customer VPC egress connector rather than the Lambda-managed `INTERNET_EGRESS` connector, since public internet access is the documented default on the egress path.
controls.ev: Egress policy configuration
controls.rec: Enforce a default-deny egress posture and allow only approved destinations. Use Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall domain allow-lists to control which domains workloads can resolve, AWS Network Firewall stateful domain/rule groups to filter outbound HTTP/S and other traffic, and restrictive security group outbound rules (including security groups for pods on EKS) so agents can reach only their declared endpoints. Translate that to each host's chokepoint. On ECS/Fargate every task already carries its own ENI and security group, so scope those outbound rules per agent service, layer subnet NACLs, and route the subnet through Network Firewall; the ECS Developer Guide's network-security best-practices page names the control-plane endpoints a strict allow-list must permit (`ecs-a-*.<region>.amazonaws.com` for agent management, `ecs-t-*.<region>.amazonaws.com` for telemetry, `ecs-sc.<region>.api.aws` for Service Connect Envoy management). Two additions belong in the same allow-list or the detection AIR-SLF-RT-04 mandates silently fails: from Fargate platform version 1.4.0 secret-retrieval and image-pull traffic flows over the task ENI, so an ECR PrivateLink path now needs both the `ecr.dkr` and `ecr.api` endpoints plus the S3 gateway endpoint rather than `ecr.dkr` alone; and where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is on, the task must be able to reach the ECR repository hosting the GuardDuty sidecar image (public subnet with a public IP, a NAT gateway, or ECR interface endpoints) and, with restricted security groups, reach the S3 managed prefix list on port 443. On ECS Managed Instances the same per-task security group applies only in `awsvpc` mode; in `host` mode the enforceable boundary is the instance's security group, shared by every task on it. On Lambda attach the agent function to private subnets with a per-function security group, and enforce it organizationally with an SCP on the `lambda:VpcIds`, `lambda:SubnetIds`, and `lambda:SecurityGroupIds` condition keys against `lambda:CreateFunction` and `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration`. On Lambda MicroVMs create a Lambda network connector with a `VpcEgressConfiguration` (`SubnetIds`, `SecurityGroupIds`, `NetworkProtocol`, `AssociatedComputeResourceTypes: ["MicroVm"]`) plus its operator role, wait for `ACTIVE`, and reference it with `--egress-network-connectors` at `run-microvm` — this matters more than on other hosts because a MicroVM left on the default internet egress lets a sandboxed agent reach tool endpoints directly and bypass any gateway in front of it. Enforce that one preventively somewhere other than on the launch call, because the launch call cannot carry it: `lambda:RunMicrovm` defines no action condition keys at all, so no policy can require that a particular egress connector be attached, and a Deny written against a connector ARN or attribute on that action is silently ignored rather than refused. The enforceable surrogates are an SCP on `lambda:CreateNetworkConnector` conditioned on `lambda:SubnetIds` and `lambda:SecurityGroupIds` so only approved VPC egress connectors can exist, plus restricting `lambda:RunMicrovm` itself to a deployment role and auditing the launches through the CloudTrail data events in AIR-SLF-RT-03. Scope the DNS layer honestly: DNS Firewall filters queries that leave your VPC through the Route 53 VPC Resolver, so it covers Fargate and `awsvpc` ECS tasks (whose ENI is in your subnet) and VPC-attached Lambda functions, and covers nothing on a Lambda function that is not VPC-attached. Scope what it inspects honestly too, since this rec leads with it: AWS states DNS Firewall only filters on the domain name, does not resolve that name to an IP address to be blocked, and does not filter other application-layer protocols such as HTTPS, SSH, TLS or FTP — so an agent that connects to a raw IP address, or resolves a name through a resolver other than the VPC Resolver, never touches the rule group. Network Firewall stateful rules and security group egress rules are what actually stop that traffic, and DNS Firewall should be read as one allow-list layer plus a detection signal rather than the egress boundary. For MicroVM egress AWS documents the enforcement surface as security group rules and network ACLs on the VPC egress connector and says nothing about DNS Firewall, so do not claim DNS-layer coverage there.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Is access to the underlying host or cluster control plane restricted and separately audited from application-level access to the AI workload?
controls.h: Confirm control-plane/host administrative access is distinct from and more tightly controlled than application access. On Fargate there is no host plane to inspect — AWS states neither customers nor AWS operators can connect to a host running a Fargate task — so verify instead that the ECS control plane (`ecs:RegisterTaskDefinition`, `ecs:UpdateService`) and interactive container access via ECS Exec are separately gated: `ecs:ExecuteCommand` held by a distinct role, `enableExecuteCommand` off unless needed, and the `ExecuteCommand` call itself in CloudTrail. On ECS Managed Instances the host plane is likewise unreachable by design — AWS lists no SSH access and no SSM Session Manager access as its responsibility — so ECS Exec and the ECS API are again the only planes to separate. On Lambda, verify the split between `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (the deploy plane, in CloudTrail management events by default) and `lambda:InvokeFunction` (the application plane, which requires opting `AWS::Lambda::Function` data events into CloudTrail before invocations are recorded at all). On Lambda MicroVMs, verify `lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken` is granted separately from `lambda:RunMicrovm`, that production MicroVMs are launched without the `SHELL_INGRESS` connector, and that CloudTrail data events are enabled for `AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage` — without that opt-in every `RunMicrovm` and every shell-token mint is unaudited.
controls.ev: Control-plane access policy + separate audit trail
controls.rec: Separate cluster/host administration from application access. On EKS, gate control-plane access with EKS access entries and Kubernetes RBAC bound to least-privilege IAM principals, and enable control-plane logging (audit and authenticator log types) to CloudWatch Logs so administrative API activity is recorded distinctly from workload behavior. On EC2, restrict host administration to SSM Session Manager under a dedicated IAM role with CloudTrail/session logging, separate from the app's runtime role. On Fargate and ECS Managed Instances the host-administration plane does not exist to separate, so put the effort into the two planes that do: restrict ECS control-plane actions to a deployment role, and treat ECS Exec as the privileged path — it runs over SSM Session Manager (the agent binaries are bind-mounted into the container), and it is recorded in CloudTrail as the `ExecuteCommand` event. Scope it with the condition keys the action actually defines: `ecs:ExecuteCommand` accepts `ecs:cluster`, `ecs:task`, `ecs:container-name` and `aws:ResourceTag/${TagKey}`, and nothing else. Do NOT add `ecs:enable-execute-command` to that statement — it is a condition key of `ecs:RunTask` and `ecs:UpdateService`, not of `ecs:ExecuteCommand`, so a Deny scoped to `ExecuteCommand` and keyed on it is silently ignored and fails OPEN, permitting exactly the interactive access it was written to block (the same defect shape recorded in AIR-SGM-EP-02; an Allow keyed on it would instead fail closed and break the caller visibly). Use it where it is defined, which is also the stronger control: Deny `ecs:RunTask` and `ecs:UpdateService` when `ecs:enable-execute-command` is true, so the exec channel is never provisioned on a production task rather than being policed after the fact. Configure the cluster's `executeCommandConfiguration` with `logging: OVERRIDE` and a `logConfiguration` naming `cloudWatchLogGroupName` and/or `s3BucketName` (both must already exist) so transcripts land separately from application logs, and set `cloudWatchEncryptionEnabled` / `s3EncryptionEnabled` to true, because AWS documents both as off when unspecified; `kmsKeyId` is a separate concern — it encrypts the session data in transit between the local client and the container, not the stored transcripts. Also deny `ssm:StartSession` on your task ARNs, since a session started outside `execute-command` is not logged by this configuration. Where GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is on you must name the container explicitly because the security agent runs as a sidecar and you cannot exec into it. On Lambda this control is largely satisfied by construction — there is no shell, session, or host-administration API — so the remaining scope is IAM separation between deploy/lifecycle actions and invocation, and the honest consequence to record is the flip side: there is no live triage path into a compromised workload, so the evidence set must be arranged in advance (structured logs, traces, CloudTrail). On Lambda MicroVMs the shell is a real but explicitly denyable capability: grant `lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken` to break-glass principals only and launch production MicroVMs without the `SHELL_INGRESS` connector, since AWS documents that a MicroVM must have been run with that connector attached for a shell token to be created — treat the connector, not the IAM grant alone, as the thing that removes the capability, and because AWS does not document which error a missing connector returns, confirm the failure in your own account rather than writing a specific exception into the runbook. Keep shell tokens short-lived, and enable CloudTrail data-event logging with `put-event-selectors` on an advanced event selector matching `eventCategory: Data` and `resources.type: AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage` so all six documented data events are on the trail — `RunMicrovm`, `TerminateMicrovm`, `SuspendMicrovm`, `ResumeMicrovm`, `CreateMicrovmAuthToken`, and `CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken`. Suspend and resume in particular must be captured, because AIR-SLF-RT-07 treats suspend as a containment action and resume restores preserved memory and disk state.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Is runtime behavior of self-hosted agent workloads (process activity, file access, network calls) monitored for anomalies, not just container-level health checks?
controls.h: Check for runtime security monitoring capturing process/file/network behavior, distinct from simple liveness/readiness probes. On ECS/Fargate this is a genuine yes: check GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is enabled with automated agent configuration for Fargate (Amazon ECS only) and that the ECS clusters runtime coverage shows the cluster healthy — then check the prerequisites that silently drop coverage: Linux only (Windows platform versions are not supported), platform version at least 1.4.0 or LATEST, a task execution role present with the ECR pull permissions, and — the prerequisite most often broken by AIR-SLF-RT-02's own egress allow-list — a network path from the task to the ECR repository hosting the GuardDuty agent (public IP, NAT gateway, or ECR interface endpoints) plus access to the S3 managed prefix list on port 443 where security groups restrict egress. Because a Fargate task is immutable, already-running tasks are not retrofitted — they must be stopped and started — and if the sidecar cannot launch healthy the task still runs, so read coverage statistics rather than treating enablement as coverage. On ECS Managed Instances this mechanism is unavailable: AWS states Runtime Monitoring is not supported for applications running on Amazon ECS Managed Instances, so the answer there is the lower tier below. On Lambda, check GuardDuty Lambda Protection is on (AWS Config `guardduty-lambda-protection-enabled`) together with Amazon Inspector Lambda standard and code scanning — and check the function does not set a customer-managed `KmsKeyArn`, because Inspector does not scan CMK-encrypted functions and that silently voids this half of the evidence. On Lambda MicroVMs, check VPC Flow Logs on the egress connector's ENIs, an execution role that actually forwards stdout/stderr to CloudWatch, and that `--logging` is not set to `{"disabled":{}}`, plus whatever in-guest instrumentation the customer added, because nothing managed watches process activity inside a MicroVM.
controls.ev: Runtime monitoring configuration + example alert
controls.rec: Enable Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for behavioral threat detection at the process, file, and network level. On EKS, deploy the `aws-guardduty-agent` EKS add-on to detect container breakouts, reverse shells, and privilege escalation, and pair it with GuardDuty EKS Protection for control-plane audit-log analysis; configure it under Runtime Monitoring rather than looking for a separate EKS Runtime Monitoring product, since that capability is now consolidated there. Confirm the cluster is in scope before claiming this control, because the unsupported cases are silent rather than blocking: AWS supports EKS clusters on EC2 instances and EKS Auto Mode, and does not support EKS Hybrid Nodes or EKS clusters running on Fargate — a cluster on either falls back to the lower tier described below. With automated agent configuration GuardDuty also creates a VPC endpoint and security group in each VPC hosting a monitored cluster, which the egress allow-list in AIR-SLF-RT-02 has to accommodate. For EC2 and ECS-on-EC2 workloads use GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring with the agent. Route findings to Security Hub/EventBridge for alerting, distinct from liveness/readiness probes. On ECS/Fargate specifically, enable automated agent configuration for Fargate (Amazon ECS only) at account level or per cluster via GuardDuty's include/exclude tagging; GuardDuty attaches its security agent as a sidecar container to each task, analyzes on-host behavior such as file access, process execution, and network connections, and creates a VPC endpoint and security group in each VPC hosting a cluster. On ECS Managed Instances that path is closed — Runtime Monitoring does not support it — so the achievable answer is task-level and network-level telemetry (VPC Flow Logs on the task ENI in `awsvpc` mode, CloudWatch Logs, CloudTrail) plus, if you accept the documented risk, a self-managed sensor running under the opt-in privileged Linux capabilities the capacity provider can enable; say plainly that managed process- and file-level behavioral detection does not exist there. On Lambda there is no runtime security agent and no way to install one, so state the narrower tier as such: GuardDuty Lambda Protection derives findings from Lambda network activity logs and covers every function in the account including those not using VPC networking, and Amazon Inspector provides continuous Lambda standard (dependency) and code scanning — pair them with CloudTrail `Invoke` data events and the agent's own structured decision logs rather than claiming process-level visibility, and remember that a customer-managed `KmsKeyArn` on the function removes the Inspector half, in which case the dependency and code-CVE evidence has to come from scanning the artifact in CI or in ECR instead (see AIR-SLF-RT-01). Check the other two Inspector eligibility conditions as well, because they drop coverage without producing an error: a function is scanned only while it is marked `$LATEST` and has been invoked or updated within the last 90 days — so a break-glass, seasonal, or standby agent function is automatically excluded once it goes quiet, and resumes being scanned only when it is invoked or its code changes — and any function tagged `InspectorExclusion` is skipped by design, which is worth grepping for rather than assuming. On Lambda MicroVMs there is likewise no managed behavioral agent and MicroVMs are not a Runtime Monitoring resource type, so the substitute is VPC Flow Logs on the VPC egress connector, application telemetry to CloudWatch Logs under the execution role, CloudTrail data events on the lifecycle and token APIs, and any sensor built into the image — do not describe this as equivalent to on-host runtime monitoring.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Are network policies enforced between pods/instances so that an agent workload can only reach the specific services it needs?
controls.h: Verify network policy (or security-group equivalent) restricts pod-to-pod/instance-to-instance reachability to declared dependencies. On ECS there is no NetworkPolicy object to read because ECS uses no overlay network — verify instead that each agent service has its own security group whose rules reference the security groups of its declared dependencies rather than broad CIDR ranges. On Fargate that boundary is meaningful because every task gets a dedicated ENI and shares no network interface, ephemeral storage, CPU, or memory with another task; on ECS Managed Instances verify `awsvpc` mode first, since `host` mode collapses every task on the instance onto one namespace, and note that AWS documents no task isolation there at all. On Lambda, verify a per-function security group in `VpcConfig` with the destination's inbound rules referencing it; the inbound half of this control does not apply because a function has no network listener and can only be reached through the Lambda Invoke API. On Lambda MicroVMs, verify the egress connector's security groups are scoped and that ingress is either the `NO_INGRESS` connector or a port-scoped auth token rather than an all-ports token.
controls.ev: Network policy configuration between workloads
controls.rec: Enforce micro-segmentation so each agent workload reaches only its declared dependencies. On EKS, enable Kubernetes network policy support in the Amazon VPC CNI add-on (enableNetworkPolicy=true) and author NetworkPolicy resources restricting pod-to-pod traffic, ideally with strict (default-deny) enforcement mode. Layer security groups for pods (SecurityGroupPolicy) to control access to VPC resources such as RDS. On EC2, use per-workload security groups referencing each other rather than broad CIDR allowances. Keep the outcome — an agent reaches only its declared dependencies — and use each platform's actual boundary. On ECS give every agent service its own security group and write rules referencing the dependency's security group, following the ECS best-practices guidance to allow inbound traffic only from other resources using the same security group. Be explicit with reviewers that this is L3/L4 security-group and CIDR matching with no namespace selector, no label selector, no default-deny-per-namespace primitive, and no L7 policy engine bound to the task, and that ECS Service Connect with AWS Private CA gives short-lived TLS between services — transport encryption and telemetry, not an authorization layer. Note too that the boundary inside a task is weaker than between tasks: Linux containers in one task share network namespaces including the IP address and ports and can intercommunicate over localhost, which matters when an agent's tool executor runs as a sidecar. On ECS Managed Instances add that co-located tasks share the kernel, network interface, ephemeral storage, CPU, and memory, so the security-group boundary is per-task only in `awsvpc` mode and the instance is the real trust boundary. On Lambda use a per-function security group and reference it from the destination's inbound rules; there is nothing to segment on the ingress side. On Lambda MicroVMs there is no Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, label selector, or security-groups-for-pods counterpart to configure, and each MicroVM has its own kernel and its own dedicated endpoint with no load balancing across MicroVMs — AWS documents no shared workload network or east-west service discovery between them. Do not read that as isolation you get for free: a single connector is intended to be reused across many MicroVMs, so MicroVMs sharing one egress connector share its subnets and security groups. The reviewable asks are therefore the two that exist — egress scoped through the VPC egress connector's security groups and NACLs, and ingress set to `NO_INGRESS` or a port-scoped token instead of an all-ports one.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Is secret and credential rotation for self-hosted agent workloads automated on a defined schedule, rather than performed manually and irregularly?
controls.h: Look for scheduled, automated rotation with evidence of recent successful rotations, not a manual process that lapses. The rotation schedule is a Secrets Manager property and is checked the same way everywhere; what differs is whether the rotated value ever reaches the running agent, so check that second half per platform. On ECS (Fargate or ECS Managed Instances), injection happens only when the container starts — AWS states that if the secret is subsequently updated or rotated the container will not receive the updated value automatically — so confirm either a runtime fetch by the agent under its task role, or automation that calls `update-service --force-new-deployment` on rotation. On Lambda, confirm the function reads through the Parameters and Secrets extension at all rather than holding the value in a module-scope variable or a plaintext environment variable that never refreshes. On Lambda MicroVMs, confirm a `/resume` hook exists and re-fetches credentials — a suspended MicroVM is restored from a memory and disk checkpoint, so credentials established before suspend may have expired by the time it resumes, and a rotation schedule alone would pass a sandbox that never re-reads the secret.
controls.ev: Rotation schedule + recent rotation history
controls.rec: Configure AWS Secrets Manager automatic rotation on a defined schedule (rotation-rules ScheduleExpression as a rate or cron, e.g. at least every 30 days) using a Lambda rotation function or managed rotation for supported services, so updated credentials are available to any workload that re-fetches them. Confirm success via CloudTrail rotation events and the secret's rotation history rather than relying on manual updates. Then add the propagation step each host needs, because on most of them a rotation alone does not reach the running agent. On ECS (Fargate or ECS Managed Instances) either have the agent call `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` at runtime under its task role — moving the control out of `secrets`/`valueFrom` into application code with least-privilege scoping — or wire the rotation event to an `update-service --force-new-deployment` so a fresh task picks up the new value; there is no CSI-driver-style mounted-secret refresh and no rotation sidecar on ECS. On Lambda the Parameters and Secrets extension comes closest to zero-touch: it invalidates and re-fetches a cached entry once its TTL expires, and because `SECRETS_MANAGER_TTL` and `SSM_PARAMETER_STORE_TTL` accept 0 to 300 seconds with a 300-second default, the extension already bounds staleness at five minutes and the TTL can only be lowered, never stretched to match a rotation cadence — so the reviewable question is whether the function reads through the extension at all. A value injected as an environment variable will not refresh until the function is updated. On Lambda MicroVMs implement the `/resume` lifecycle hook to refresh credentials, re-establish connections, and validate state, keeping it inside the 1–60 second `resumeTimeoutInSeconds` budget so a slow secret fetch does not become the failure mode, and re-generate any per-instance values in the `/run` hook, since anything created at image build time is shared by every MicroVM started from that image version.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Can outbound network access for a specific compromised self-hosted agent workload be cut off immediately without disrupting unrelated workloads?
controls.h: Confirm a tested, granular egress-kill capability exists targeting a single workload, not an all-or-nothing network shutdown. On ECS/Fargate, confirm the runbook does not assume a security-group swap: the task ENI is a fully managed ECS feature your account cannot detach or modify, and changing a service's `networkConfiguration` launches new tasks rather than re-tagging running ones. The workable moves are stripping the rules from the security group the task already holds — so check each agent service has its own security group, otherwise rule-stripping hits every service sharing it — a deny-all NACL on the task's subnet (blast radius is the whole subnet), or `ecs:StopTask`. On ECS Managed Instances confirm the same and check `awsvpc` mode, since in `host` mode the only network lever is the instance's security group and it is shared by every task on that instance. On Lambda, confirm `put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0` is the exercised off-switch, plus a security-group edit for VPC-attached functions. On Lambda MicroVMs, confirm the runbook is terminate-or-suspend rather than quarantine, because network connectors are specified at `run-microvm` and cannot be changed while a MicroVM is running.
controls.ev: Targeted egress-kill runbook + exercise record
controls.rec: Maintain a tested runbook to isolate a single compromised workload without disrupting others: on EKS, apply a default-deny NetworkPolicy or swap the pod's SecurityGroupPolicy to a quarantine security group with no egress rules (or cordon/label the affected pods). On EC2, replace the instance's security group with a locked-down one so outbound rules are removed immediately. Layer Route 53 DNS Firewall/Network Firewall rule changes for destination-specific cutoff, and record periodic exercises. Per-agent containment survives on the other hosts too, but the mechanism differs and two of them break an EC2-derived runbook outright. On ECS/Fargate you cannot hot-swap a running task onto a quarantine security group — the task ENI is service-managed and your account cannot detach or modify it — so give each agent service its own security group precisely so that stripping its inbound and outbound rules is surgical, keep a deny-all subnet NACL as the coarser fallback, and reach for `ecs:StopTask` (which issues the equivalent of `docker stop`, then `SIGKILL` after a 30-second timeout, and records an optional `--reason` visible in `DescribeTasks`) only when you accept the evidence loss. GuardDuty's compromised-ECS remediation guidance is to isolate by blocking all inbound and outbound traffic to the affected task first, and to use `ListTasks` to find sibling tasks running the same image. Automate detection-to-action with EventBridge `ECS Task State Change` events. On ECS Managed Instances the same applies with one caveat: because tasks are co-located and share the instance, a `host`-mode agent cannot be network-isolated without affecting its neighbors, so `StopTask` is the only per-agent lever there. On Lambda set reserved concurrency to zero, which AWS documents as stopping the function from processing any events until the limit is removed, then revoke or deny the execution role's permissions and update the function's code or configuration — the next invocation cold-starts and existing environments running the previous version are reaped — and combine with the ordinary security-group edit where the function is VPC-attached. On Lambda MicroVMs containment is kill-the-sandbox rather than quarantine-the-sandbox: connectors cannot be re-scoped on a running MicroVM and AWS warns that modifying a connector actively in use can break connectivity for every MicroVM using it, so call `terminate-microvm` or `suspend-microvm` and stop minting auth tokens. That is acceptable because sessions are ephemeral, but it means in-guest evidence must be collected over the shell before termination, and `--maximum-duration-in-seconds` should already be set as a backstop ceiling.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — runtime isolation, secrets & egress
controls.q: Is a serverless function that hosts agent or tool code invocable only by authenticated, authorized callers, rather than reachable by anyone holding its URL?
controls.h: Check the function's URL config and its resource-based policy, not just its execution role — the execution role governs what the function may do, this control governs who may run it. Run `aws lambda get-function-url-config` and confirm AuthType is AWS_IAM, not NONE: with NONE, Lambda auto-creates a resource policy whose Principal is "*", so any unauthenticated caller with the URL can invoke the function. Then run `aws lambda get-policy` and confirm no statement has Principal "*" without a narrowing condition. Two traps worth checking explicitly. First, deleting a function URL does NOT delete the resource-based policy Lambda created for it, so a function can show no URL config while still carrying a public-access statement — inspect the policy even when there is no URL. Second, when NONE is genuinely required (a browser-facing endpoint), confirm the policy includes the lambda:InvokedViaFunctionUrl condition, or the public grant extends to ordinary Invoke calls and not just the URL path. Also confirm the CORS allow-origin is not a bare wildcard where the endpoint is browser-facing.
controls.ev: Function URL AuthType + resource-based policy for each agent/tool function
controls.rec: Set the function URL AuthType to AWS_IAM so Lambda authenticates every request with SigV4 and the caller needs both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction, and keep the resource-based policy scoped to named principals with no "*" Principal. Enforce it preventively rather than per function: `lambda:FunctionUrlAuthType` is a real IAM condition key and is accepted by CreateFunctionUrlConfig, UpdateFunctionUrlConfig and AddPermission, so an SCP with StringEquals on lambda:FunctionUrlAuthType = NONE and Effect Deny stops a public URL being created or an existing one being loosened anywhere in the OU. Where a public endpoint is a genuine requirement, do not expose the function URL directly — front it with CloudFront and AWS WAF, move authentication into an authorizer or the handler, and include the lambda:InvokedViaFunctionUrl condition in the resource policy so the public grant cannot be replayed against plain Invoke. Audit existing functions for the orphaned-policy case: removing a URL leaves its auto-created public statement behind, so run lambda:GetPolicy across the account and strip any "*" Principal statement that no longer has a URL to serve. Restrict the CORS allow-origin to known origins rather than a wildcard.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — agent identity, orchestration & guardrails
controls.q: Does each self-hosted agent instance authenticate with its own distinct identity, rather than a shared service credential used across all agent instances?
controls.h: Confirm identity assignment is per-instance/per-agent, enabling individual attribution and revocation. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) check the task definition's taskRoleArn is distinct per agent and separate from executionRoleArn, and note every container in a task shares the task role, so a sidecar tool-executor is not separately attributable. On EC2, ECS Managed Instances and ECS Anywhere also check what else runs on the same instance, because AWS states there is no task isolation there and containers can potentially reach credentials for co-located tasks and for the container instance role via IMDS. On Lambda confirm each agent function has its own execution role rather than one shared across agents. For Lambda MicroVMs check the executionRoleArn passed at RunMicrovm and that buildRoleArn is a separate role.
controls.ev: Per-agent identity assignment configuration
controls.rec: Assign each agent its own distinct IAM role: on EKS use EKS Pod Identity associations (or IRSA) to map a dedicated IAM role to each agent's Kubernetes service account, and on EC2 use a per-instance IAM instance profile role. Never share one service account/role across agent instances, so actions are individually attributable in CloudTrail and a single agent's credentials can be revoked independently. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) the grain is the task role: give each agent its own taskRoleArn for the agent's own permissions (bedrock:InvokeModel, tool access) and keep it distinct from the task execution role, which exists for image pull, awslogs, private-registry auth and secret retrieval and whose credentials AWS states aren't directly accessible by the containers in the task; task-role credentials carry a taskArn session context, so CloudTrail shows which task a call came from. Prefer Fargate where per-agent attribution has to hold under compromise — each Fargate task has its own isolation boundary, whereas on EC2, ECS Managed Instances and ECS Anywhere co-located tasks can reach one another's credentials, so a per-task role is necessary but not sufficient and the placement has to isolate too. On Lambda the per-function execution role is already the native grain; keep one role per agent function and right-size it with IAM Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail. For Lambda MicroVMs RunMicrovm accepts exactly one executionRoleArn, so every process in the sandbox runs with that single role's permissions and the MicroVM — not the request — is the tenant boundary: run one MicroVM per tenant session, pass tenant-specific configuration and secret references through runHookPayload rather than widening the role, and keep buildRoleArn separate (the build hooks /ready and /validate run under the build role, the runtime hooks /run, /resume, /suspend and /terminate under the execution role). Do not assume an IMDSv2-style shield inside the sandbox: AWS documents no metadata service, no token requirement and no hop limit for the MicroVM guest, so treat every process in it as able to use that single role and size the role for that.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — agent identity, orchestration & guardrails
controls.q: Is a content-safety and action-safety guardrail applied to self-hosted agent input/output and intended actions, equivalent to what a managed platform would enforce?
controls.h: Check that a guardrail layer (built or integrated) filters both language output and proposed actions, not left unenforced because the platform is self-managed. This is an application-layer call, so verify it identically on every host: confirm the role the agent code actually runs under carries bedrock:ApplyGuardrail — the Pod Identity/IRSA role on EKS, the instance profile role on EC2, taskRoleArn on ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances), the execution role on Lambda and on Lambda MicroVMs — and that tool execution is gated on the result. On Lambda MicroVMs also confirm egress is pinned to a customer-managed VPC egress network connector, since a sandbox on the default egress path can reach tools without traversing your guardrail.
controls.ev: Guardrail integration configuration for self-hosted agent
controls.rec: Integrate Amazon Bedrock Guardrails via the ApplyGuardrail API, which evaluates content against configured policies (content filters, denied topics, PII/sensitive-information, word filters, and prompt-attack detection) without invoking a Bedrock model and works with self-hosted/third-party models. Call ApplyGuardrail with source INPUT on incoming prompts and source OUTPUT on generated responses, and gate any proposed tool/action on a NONE (not GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED) result before executing it. This transfers unchanged to ECS on Fargate, ECS Managed Instances, Lambda and Lambda MicroVMs: none of them provides a managed guardrail layer, none of them blocks the call, and only the role that needs bedrock:ApplyGuardrail changes — used standalone against a self-hosted or third-party model, that single permission is enough and no InvokeModel grant is required. What does change is how easily the guardrail can be bypassed. On Lambda MicroVMs AWS documents that MicroVMs have public internet access on the egress path by default, so a sandboxed tool can call a model or an external API directly; creating a Lambda network connector with your VPC configuration and passing it as the MicroVM's egress connector is what makes the guardrail path non-optional rather than advisory, since outbound traffic is then subject to your security groups and network ACLs.
