controls.q: Is the orchestration logic that sequences agent steps and tool calls protected from unauthorized modification, with changes reviewed before deployment?
controls.h: Confirm orchestration/workflow definitions go through code review and access control like any other production code, and ask which platform gate actually blocks an unreviewed build — the Kubernetes signed-image verification step below exists only on EKS and self-managed Kubernetes. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) look for a PRE_SCALE_UP deployment lifecycle hook on the agent's service that verifies the signature, and check whether the agent also runs as a standalone RunTask, which passes through no hook at all. On Lambda .zip functions check the code signing configuration sets UntrustedArtifactOnDeployment to Enforce rather than the Warn default; for container-image functions no such gate exists, so check the CI verification step and who holds lambda:UpdateFunctionCode. For Lambda MicroVMs check who holds lambda:CreateMicrovmImage and lambda:UpdateMicrovmImage, and whether image-version status (ACTIVE/INACTIVE) is used as the release gate.
controls.ev: Change-control record for orchestration logic
controls.rec: Keep all orchestration/workflow definitions (agent step sequencing, tool wiring, prompts) in version control with peer-reviewed pull requests, and deploy only through a CI/CD pipeline (e.g. AWS CodePipeline) rather than manual edits. Enforce the review technically: add a CodePipeline manual approval action as a release gate, sign the resulting container image with AWS Signer using the Notation CLI (Notary Project) and verify the signature at deployment (Amazon EKS / self-managed Kubernetes signed-image verification) so unsigned or unreviewed builds cannot run, and set the ECR repository to IMMUTABLE tag mutability so a deployed tag cannot be overwritten. Restrict who can push images or change the running workload with least-privilege IAM (ECR repository policies, EKS RBAC) so orchestration logic cannot be altered out-of-band. The signing, IMMUTABLE-tag and least-privilege steps above apply to every ECR-sourced platform; what does not carry over is the Kubernetes admission path (the Gatekeeper+Ratify / kyverno-notation-aws controllers AIR-SLF-CMP-05 prescribes), which exists only on EKS and self-managed Kubernetes — record that rather than substituting a lookalike, because off EKS the control is answered by pipeline gating plus IAM on the deploy action, not by a platform admission gate. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) you can automate the signing side with ECR managed signing (ecr:PutSigningConfiguration against an AWS Signer signing profile, with the pushing principal permitted to sign payloads with that profile) and verify at deploy with an ECS deployment lifecycle hook Lambda at PRE_SCALE_UP that runs notation verify; state its two limits, because both are silent bypasses — lifecycle hooks are configured on an ECS service, so an agent launched by a standalone RunTask is never intercepted, and enforcement is rollback-shaped (returning hookStatus FAILED rolls the deployment back to the last successful one) rather than rejecting the task-definition revision at registration. ECS already resolves image tags to digests at deployment unless a container sets versionConsistency to disabled, but no ECS condition key names the image, image URI, registry or repository, so an IAM guardrail cannot pin an approved registry — that has to come from the lifecycle hook or an ECR VPC endpoint policy on the pull path. On Lambda .zip functions the platform gate is a code signing configuration with UntrustedArtifactOnDeployment set to Enforce, since the Warn default allows the deployment and only emits the SignatureValidationErrors metric and a CloudTrail warning; pin it org-wide with the lambda:CodeSigningConfigArn condition key on CreateFunction, and note two edges — any layers the function uses must also be signed by an allowed profile, and the configuration only blocks new deployments, so unsigned code already deployed keeps running until it is replaced. Lambda container-image functions have no equivalent: Signer's Lambda signing platform (AWSLambda-SHA384-ECDSA) signs zip code packages staged in S3, while container images are signed under the separate Notation-OCI-SHA384-ECDSA platform that nothing in Lambda verifies at deploy time — so verify the Notation signature in CI before UpdateFunctionCode, deploy by digest, and rely on IAM. For Lambda MicroVMs nothing verifies a signature at RunMicrovm and neither CreateMicrovmImage nor the image-version APIs accept a signing-profile or code-signing parameter: restrict lambda:CreateMicrovmImage and lambda:UpdateMicrovmImage to the CI role, scope the build role's s3:GetObject to the single artifact bucket, and use update-microvm-image-version --status INACTIVE as the release gate, which disables a bad sandbox image version without deleting it. Write that flag as --status: the API's request field is status with valid values ACTIVE and INACTIVE, while the same resource separately carries a read-only state field (PENDING, IN_PROGRESS, SUCCESSFUL, FAILED, DELETING, DELETED, DELETE_FAILED) that has no INACTIVE value at all — so the --state INACTIVE form the AWS user guide's example shows names the wrong field, and the release gate you thought you had does not exist.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — agent identity, orchestration & guardrails
controls.q: Are calls between self-hosted agents and the tools/APIs they invoke logged with enough detail to reconstruct an agent's full decision path?
controls.h: Verify logging captures each tool call, parameters, and result linked to the originating agent session. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) look for an ADOT Collector sidecar in the agent's task definition, a task role carrying the X-Ray write and sampling permissions plus the logs: actions, and awslogs or awsfirelens shipping the agent's structured logs; correlate on TaskARN from the task metadata endpoint V4. On Lambda check advanced logging controls set the log format to JSON with a per-agent log group, that tracing mode is Active, and that CloudTrail data events are enabled for resources.type AWS::Lambda::Function, since data events are not logged by default. For Lambda MicroVMs check an execution role with logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents is supplied (without one, runtime stdout and stderr are silently not forwarded), that logging has not been disabled, and that CloudTrail data events are opted in on resources.type AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage so RunMicrovm and the token APIs are recorded.
controls.ev: Agent decision-path log sample
controls.rec: Instrument the agent with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK/Collector to emit distributed traces (each tool call, its parameters, and result) correlated to an agent session ID, sending them to CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray, and write structured decision logs to CloudWatch Logs. Rely on AWS CloudTrail for the API-level record of the AWS actions each agent role invokes, giving a reconstructable end-to-end decision path. Where the Collector runs and what supplies the correlation key differ per host. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) run the ADOT Collector as a sidecar container in the agent's own task definition and give the task role xray:PutTraceSegments, xray:PutTelemetryRecords, the X-Ray sampling reads and the logs: actions; ship decision logs with the awslogs or awsfirelens driver and use TaskARN from the task metadata endpoint V4 as the correlation key — task-role credentials already carry a taskArn session context in CloudTrail, so the AWS API-level half of the path is attributable per task without extra work. On Lambda use advanced logging controls to emit structured JSON into a per-agent log group — the requestId is added automatically, which gives per-invocation correlation without a custom field — set tracing mode to Active, and add the ADOT Lambda layer with AWS_LAMBDA_EXEC_WRAPPER set to /opt/otel-instrument for auto-instrumentation; separately enable CloudTrail data events on AWS::Lambda::Function, because Invoke is a data event and CloudTrail does not log most data events by default, so without the opt-in there is no record of who drove the agent. For Lambda MicroVMs the agent's stdout and stderr reach CloudWatch in the default log group /aws/lambda-microvms/<image-name> — spelled with the hyphen, which the MicroVM monitoring page uses for both the build logs and the runtime logs, though one AWS page writes /aws/lambda/microvms, so look under both before concluding logs are missing — with the log stream defaulting to the MicroVM ID, but only when an execution role carrying the three logs: permissions is supplied — a sandbox launched without one, or with logging set to disabled, produces no runtime log at all, and build logs likewise need the build role. RunMicrovm, TerminateMicrovm, SuspendMicrovm, ResumeMicrovm, CreateMicrovmAuthToken and CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken are CloudTrail data events requiring an explicit opt-in via put-event-selectors with an advanced event selector on resources.type AWS::Lambda::MicrovmImage; the image-management calls are management events and are logged by default.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — agent identity, orchestration & guardrails
controls.q: In multi-agent orchestration, is one agent prevented from impersonating or acting with another agent's authority without an explicit, checked handoff?
controls.h: Confirm agent-to-agent delegation requires an explicit, authorized handoff rather than implicit trust between co-located agents. STS source identity is platform-independent, so check it identically everywhere; what varies is the transport that carries the handoff. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) confirm each agent has its own task role and its own security group, and treat Service Connect TLS as transport encryption, not authorization — ECS has no NetworkPolicy analogue and matches on L3/L4 only. On Lambda inspect the function's resource-based policy for who may invoke it and confirm no Function URL uses AuthType NONE. For Lambda MicroVMs confirm one MicroVM per agent session, that CreateMicrovmAuthToken tokens are port-scoped and short-lived, and that lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken is denied where interactive shell is not needed.
controls.ev: Delegation/handoff authorization configuration
controls.rec: Give each agent its own IAM role and require an explicit, authenticated handoff for delegation: a calling agent gets short-lived scoped credentials via sts:AssumeRole (never shared credentials), and inter-agent endpoints (e.g. API Gateway or an internal service) use IAM authorization so requests must be SigV4-signed with the caller's own identity. To stop one agent acting with another's authority across the handoff, bind the originating identity into the delegated session with STS source identity (sts:SetSourceIdentity permission plus the sts:SourceIdentity trust-policy condition): once set it persists through role chaining, cannot be changed during the session, and appears as aws:SourceIdentity on every downstream request and in CloudTrail — so the target role's trust policy can require and pin the caller, and each handoff is authorized against least-privilege policies rather than implicit co-location trust. That mechanism works unchanged on every host; only the transport-side authorization differs. On ECS (Fargate or Managed Instances) give each agent its own task role and its own security group: each Fargate task gets its own ENI and security group, which is a genuine per-task firewall but matches on L3/L4 only, and on ECS Managed Instances or EC2 several tasks share an instance and can reach one another's credentials, so the checked handoff has to live in IAM/SigV4 at the inter-agent endpoint rather than in network placement. ECS Service Connect with an AWS Private CA has ECS generate, rotate and distribute TLS 1.3 certificates between agent components, but scope the claim when you assess it: the seven-day maximum validity applies only when the private CA runs in short-lived mode — AWS's recommendation, because Service Connect does not support certificate revocation and relies on frequent rotation — whereas general-purpose mode allows any expiration date, communications fail if the rotation frequency exceeds seven days, and only traffic passing through the ECS agent is encrypted. Encryption is not an authorization layer either way. On Lambda the resource-based policy is the inbound gate: grant lambda:InvokeFunction only to the specific calling agent's role, never a wildcard principal, and if a Function URL is used set AuthType to AWS_IAM, because with NONE Lambda performs no authentication and the function's resource-based policy has to grant public access for the URL to work at all. For Lambda MicroVMs the boundary is the MicroVM itself, since it holds exactly one executionRoleArn: run one MicroVM per agent session, mint short-lived port-scoped JWE tokens with CreateMicrovmAuthToken (the documented examples use a 30-minute expiration) with allowedPorts limited to the ports actually in use, so a request to any other port returns 403 Forbidden, and deny lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken separately so API access to a sandbox does not imply interactive shell — shell additionally requires the MicroVM to have been launched with the SHELL_INGRESS ingress connector, and simply not attaching that connector is the stronger control because create-microvm-shell-auth-token then fails with a ValidationException.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — agent identity, orchestration & guardrails
controls.q: Is there monitoring that specifically detects an agent behaving outside its intended task scope (scope creep) before it causes broader impact?
controls.h: Look for behavioral monitoring tuned to detect deviation from expected task scope, not just error-rate or uptime metrics. On ECS on Fargate you also get a host-level behavioral tier: check GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring is enabled with automated agent configuration for Fargate (Amazon ECS only) and that runtime coverage statistics show the security-agent sidecar present on every agent task. On ECS Managed Instances, Lambda and Lambda MicroVMs no such tier exists, so the custom-metric and log-based checks are the entire detection surface — verify the agent itself publishes the task-scope signals rather than treating the control as unanswerable. On Lambda additionally check an alarm on RecursiveInvocationsDropped and that GuardDuty Lambda Protection is on.
controls.ev: Scope-deviation detection configuration + example
controls.rec: Publish custom CloudWatch metrics for task-scope signals (e.g. tool-call mix, invocation of tools outside the expected set, target resources touched) and apply CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms that learn each metric's normal baseline and fire when behavior falls outside the band. Complement with a CloudWatch Logs metric filter / Contributor Insights on the decision-path logs to flag out-of-scope tool or API usage, and trigger notification/containment before broad impact. Those mechanisms are platform-independent and are what answers this control everywhere; the managed behavioral tier on top of them is not. On ECS on Fargate layer GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring over the custom metrics — a GuardDuty-managed sidecar container attaches to each container in the task and analyzes on-host behavior such as file access, process execution and network connections. Record its preconditions in the assessment, because each one is a silent coverage gap: Linux only (Windows platform versions are not supported), Fargate platform version at least 1.4.0 or LATEST, a task execution role carrying the ECR pull permissions or the task simply starts without the sidecar, network reachability to ECR and S3 from the task's subnet and security group, an already-running task must be stopped and started to become covered, and it fails open — if the sidecar cannot launch in a healthy state the task is not prevented from running. Runtime Monitoring covers only EKS, ECS on Fargate and EC2, and AWS states it does not support applications running on Amazon ECS Managed Instances; nothing extends it to Lambda or Lambda MicroVMs. On those platforms say plainly that process- and file-level anomaly detection is unavailable, so scope-creep detection rests entirely on the metrics the agent publishes itself, CloudWatch Logs from its own output, and CloudTrail on its role's API calls — a coverage difference, not an exemption. On Lambda add GuardDuty Lambda Protection, which is network-derived rather than on-host: it monitors Lambda network activity logs, including VPC flow logs from all Lambda functions in the account even those that don't use VPC networking. Alarm on RecursiveInvocationsDropped, which Lambda emits when a function is invoked approximately 16 times in one chain of requests, but bound the claim: recursion detection covers only loops formed by Lambda, Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS and Amazon S3 and requires a supported AWS SDK version, so a self-trigger routed through DynamoDB, EventBridge, Step Functions or the agent's own HTTP endpoint is not caught and still needs the agent-published task-scope metrics. For Lambda MicroVMs no managed detection plan is documented as covering them, so the available signals are in-guest telemetry the agent writes to CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs on the egress connector's ENIs when VPC egress is configured, and CloudTrail data events on the lifecycle and token APIs.

controls.section_title: Self-hosted agents (VMs, containers & serverless) — agent identity, orchestration & guardrails
controls.q: Is there a tested kill-switch that can pause or stop a specific self-hosted agent's orchestration without requiring a full platform redeploy?
controls.h: Confirm an operational control exists to halt one agent's execution quickly, exercised at least once, distinct from a full redeployment. On ECS check the rehearsed step stops one agent's service without disturbing siblings, and that each agent service has its own security group, because the task ENI is service-managed and your account cannot detach or modify it. On Lambda check put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0 is the rehearsed off-switch. For Lambda MicroVMs check TerminateMicrovm and SuspendMicrovm are exercised per sandbox and that maximumDurationInSeconds is set on every launch.
controls.ev: Kill-switch runbook + exercise record
controls.rec: Define and rehearse a per-agent kill-switch: on EKS scale the agent's Deployment to zero replicas (kubectl scale --replicas=0) or delete/cordon it, on ECS set the service desired count to 0, and on EC2 stop the instance; pair this with immediately revoking or disabling that agent's IAM role/credentials to halt in-flight API calls. Document the steps in a runbook and exercise it at least once to confirm a single agent can be stopped without a full platform redeploy. Know what each platform's stop actually does to work in flight, and what containment short of stopping is possible. On ECS, StopTask issues the equivalent of docker stop — a stop signal (SIGTERM by default, overridable with STOPSIGNAL) followed by SIGKILL after a default 30-second timeout — so an in-flight agent turn gets at most that long. For containment before termination, record what does not work: the task ENI is a fully managed Amazon ECS feature that your account can't detach or modify, so a running task cannot be moved onto a quarantine security group; instead strip the ingress and egress rules from the security group the task already holds, which is surgical only if each agent service has its own, or apply a deny-all NACL to the subnet and accept a whole-subnet blast radius. GuardDuty's compromised-ECS guidance is to isolate impacted tasks by blocking all inbound and outbound traffic rather than terminating them, so isolate first where evidence matters. On ECS Managed Instances the instance is AWS-managed with no SSH access and ECS initiates draining after 14 days, so instance-level containment is not yours to perform — stop the service and revoke the task role. On Lambda the off-switch is put-function-concurrency --reserved-concurrent-executions 0, which stops the function processing any events until the limit is removed, and the non-increasable 900-second timeout bounds any in-flight agent turn. For Lambda MicroVMs call TerminateMicrovm or SuspendMicrovm per sandbox — both are discrete IAM actions, so an orchestrator can be granted kill rights without image-publish rights — and set maximumDurationInSeconds (maximum 28,800) as a platform-enforced ceiling on every launch. Containment here is kill, not quarantine: network connectors are specified at run-microvm and cannot be changed while a MicroVM is running, so a running sandbox cannot be re-scoped. Arrange the evidence path out of band before you need it — CloudWatch Logs via the execution role, VPC Flow Logs on the egress connector's ENIs, CloudTrail data events on the lifecycle and token APIs — because collecting in-guest over the shell only works if the sandbox was launched with the SHELL_INGRESS connector and the responder holds lambda:CreateMicrovmShellAuthToken, which AIR-SLF-AGT-05 recommends denying; treat shell-in as a deliberate, documented exception rather than the default step.

controls.section_title: Physical & edge AI (IoT, ICS/OT, robotics, autonomous systems)
controls.q: Does each physical AI device carry its own unique cryptographic identity with an authorization policy scoped to that device, rather than a shared certificate or one fleet-wide policy granting broad topic access?
controls.h: Check three things, because a fleet can look well-governed and still share one credential. First, per-device identity: each thing has its own X.509 certificate (or its own private key in a hardware secure element) registered to exactly one thing, and provisioning does not ship a common certificate in the device image. Second, the policy is scoped by the device, not merely attached to it: look for AWS IoT Core thing policy variables (iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName, ThingTypeName, or Attributes[attributeName]) in the Resource or Condition, and specifically for the Bool condition iot:Connection.Thing.IsAttached = true, which is what stops a certificate being replayed for a thing it is not attached to. A policy granting iot:Publish or iot:Subscribe on topic/* is fleet-wide access however many certificates exist. Two traps: thing policy variables resolve ONLY over MQTT or MQTT-over-WebSocket, so a device using another transport gets no scoping from them; and where non-exclusive thing association is in use the same certificate may be attached to several things, in which case the MQTT client ID must exactly match the thing name or the variable resolves to the wrong thing. Third, no long-lived AWS credentials on the device: look for the AWS IoT credentials provider (iot:AssumeRoleWithCertificate against a role alias) rather than an access key in the firmware. Run AWS IoT Device Defender Audit and confirm the shared-certificate and permissive-policy checks are clean.
controls.ev: Per-device certificate registration + an IoT policy showing thing policy variables and IsAttached, plus a clean Device Defender Audit
controls.rec: Give every device its own X.509 certificate, held in a hardware secure element or TPM where the platform offers one, and register it to exactly one thing with AttachThingPrincipal — never bake a common certificate into the device image, because recovering one device then yields the fleet. Scope authorization with AWS IoT Core thing policy variables rather than writing one policy per device or one policy for all: template the topic with ${iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName} (or a thing attribute) so a device can only publish and subscribe under its own prefix, and add the Bool condition iot:Connection.Thing.IsAttached = true so the certificate cannot be used for a thing it is not attached to. This fails closed by design: if the certificate is not associated with the thing the variable does not resolve and the request is denied. Note the mechanism's limits and design around them — thing policy variables are available only over MQTT and MQTT over WebSocket, and under non-exclusive thing association the MQTT client ID must exactly equal the thing name or the policy evaluates against the wrong thing. For AWS API access from the device, use the AWS IoT credentials provider (iot:AssumeRoleWithCertificate on a role alias, itself scoped with the same thing policy variables) so the device exchanges its certificate for short-lived credentials instead of carrying an access key. Schedule AWS IoT Device Defender Audit to run continuously and act on its findings, and keep its built-in mitigations ready — add-thing-to-quarantine-thing-group, update the device certificate, replace the default policy version.

controls.section_title: Physical & edge AI (IoT, ICS/OT, robotics, autonomous systems)
controls.q: Are the physical actions an AI agent can take bounded to an explicitly enumerated, safety-reviewed set, with hazardous or irreversible actuation gated on human approval and an interlock outside the agent's control path?
controls.h: This is the control with no AWS toggle, so verify it as a design property with three artifacts. First, an enumerated action space: a reviewed list of every physical action the agent may command, with the permitted parameter RANGE for each — a bound on consequence, not just on API surface. An IAM policy or Cedar policy that allows the actuation API without constraining its payload is not this control, because the harm lives in the parameter, not the call. Second, a consequence classification: which actions are reversible, which are not, and which can injure. Confirm the irreversible and hazardous ones require human approval at run time, and check the approval is enforced in the execution path rather than advisory in a prompt — a system prompt instructing the agent to ask first is not an enforcement point, because the agent is the thing you are bounding. Third, and most important: an interlock the agent cannot reach — a physical E-stop, a hardware limit, a rate or travel limiter, or an independent safety controller that holds even if the agent, its tools and its credentials are fully compromised. Confirm the agent has no permission that can disable, reconfigure or bypass it; if the interlock is reachable through any tool the agent holds, it is part of the agent, not a bound on it. Distinguish this from AIR-FND-GOV-09, which is the governance approval gate on high-impact actions generally; this control asks whether the physical action space itself is bounded.
controls.ev: Enumerated action space with parameter ranges + consequence classification + evidence the interlock is outside the agent's permissions
controls.rec: Bound the action space in the tool layer, not in the prompt. Expose actuation to the agent only through a narrow tool contract that validates each parameter against a reviewed range and rejects anything outside it, so the agent cannot command a value no human approved — the tool, not the model, is the enforcement point. Classify every action as reversible, irreversible or hazardous, and route the second two through an explicit human approval before execution: an AWS Step Functions human-approval task using the wait-for-callback pattern gives you an auditable gate outside the model's control, which a prompt instruction does not. Keep a safety interlock entirely outside the agent's reach — a hardware E-stop, a mechanical or firmware travel and rate limit, or an independent safety controller — and verify by IAM and IoT policy review that no role, tool or credential the agent holds can disable, reconfigure or bypass it; assume the agent is compromised and check the bound still holds. Rehearse the failure: exercise the interlock and the approval path as part of the AI-specific incident response test, because an untested E-stop is a claim rather than a control. On the device side, prefer commanding through a constrained interface (an AWS IoT job or a validated command topic whose handler enforces the same ranges) over granting the agent broad device control, and log every commanded action with its parameters and approval state so a physical incident can be reconstructed.

controls.section_title: Physical & edge AI (IoT, ICS/OT, robotics, autonomous systems)
controls.q: Is the model and agent code deployed to edge devices integrity-verified on the device before it runs, with provenance established before upload rather than inferred from the delivery channel?
controls.h: Separate the two halves, because the managed service covers only one of them. Transport integrity is largely inherited: when you create an AWS IoT Greengrass component, Greengrass calculates a cryptographic digest of each artifact and writes it into the component recipe, and the core device verifies each artifact against that digest on download — so tampering in the cloud or in transit is detected for you. What is NOT covered is provenance: AWS states you are responsible for securing software artifacts BEFORE you upload them to S3, so the digest proves the device got the bytes you uploaded, never that those bytes were the model your pipeline approved. So look upstream for the real control — a signing or attestation step in the build pipeline, a recorded hash of the approved model artifact, and a check that the uploaded object matches it. Confirm the artifact bucket resists silent replacement (versioning, and S3 Object Lock where the artifacts must not be overwritten or deleted at all), because overwriting the object and re-creating the component re-derives a valid digest for the wrong content. Also verify the runtime itself: Greengrass nucleus archives are signed from version 2.9.5 onward and can be checked with jarsigner -verify, which is a separate assurance from component artifact digests. Where the model is a container image, AWS Signer plus Notation gives signature verification rather than digest-only integrity — note the distinction, since an image digest establishes integrity but not authenticity.
controls.ev: Build-pipeline signing or approved-artifact hash record + component recipe digests + bucket versioning/Object Lock configuration
controls.rec: Treat the Greengrass artifact digest as transport integrity and add provenance yourself, because that split is where edge deployments are actually attacked. Sign the model and agent artifacts in the build pipeline — AWS Signer, or a KMS asymmetric key with kms:Sign and kms:Verify — record the approved artifact's hash alongside the model-registry entry that approved it, and verify signature and hash before the artifact is uploaded to the component bucket. Lock the bucket against silent replacement: enable versioning, and use S3 Object Lock where component artifacts must not be overwritten or deleted, since overwriting an object and re-creating the component simply re-derives a valid digest for content nobody approved. Let Greengrass do the part it does well — component recipes carry each artifact's digest and hash algorithm, and core devices verify on download — and verify the runtime separately: from Greengrass nucleus 2.9.5 onward the nucleus archive is signed, so check it with jarsigner -verify -certs before installing. For container-packaged models use AWS Signer with Notation so the device or the deploying pipeline verifies a signature rather than only a digest, which establishes authenticity and not just integrity. Scope the deployment role so it can publish new component versions but cannot rewrite existing artifacts, and log component creation and deployment so a device running unexpected code can be traced to the deployment that put it there.
